What to do: Each month, buy the stocks with the highest returns over the past 12 months (skipping the latest month) and short those with the lowest, e.g. the top and bottom 10%.
Why it pays: Investors under-react to news and then pile in late, so price trends in individual stocks tend to persist for 3–12 months.
Track record: ~1–1.5%/month gross long-short, US 1965–1989; over 1%/month across 12 European markets 1980–1995; near zero in Japan. Weaker in the US since 2000
How it loses money: Sudden 'momentum crashes' when beaten-down losers rebound sharply after a market bottom, as in 1932 and 2009.
Key sources: Jegadeesh & Titman (1993); Rouwenhorst (1998); Fama & French (2012)

Strategy: Diversified trend following (time-series momentum, managed futures)
What to do: In each of many futures markets (stock indices, bonds, currencies, commodities), go long if its past 1–12 month return is positive and short if negative, sizing positions to equal risk.
Why it pays: Investors under-react to news and then herd, and hedgers pay speculators to take price risk, so price moves tend to persist for months.
Markets: Multi-asset; Equity indices & ETFs; Bonds & rates; FX; Commodities
Track record: Significant gross abnormal returns, 58 futures 1985–2009; positive in every decade 1880–2016 after simulated 2/20 fees (backtests)
How it loses money: Choppy, trendless markets and sharp reversals cause strings of losses and multi-year flat spells, as in much of the 2010s.
Key sources: Moskowitz, Ooi & Pedersen (2012); Hurst, Ooi & Pedersen (2017); Huang, Li, Wang & Zhou (2020)

What to do: Each month, buy the stocks trading closest to their 52-week high and short those furthest below it, holding each batch for about six months.
Why it pays: Investors anchor on the 52-week high and hesitate to bid prices above it, so good news gets priced in slowly.
Track record: Around 0.5%/month long-short, US stocks 1963–2001 (gross, six-month holding).
How it loses money: Sharp market rebounds in which beaten-down stocks surge, the classic momentum crash.
Key sources: George & Hwang (2004)

What to do: Each month, buy stocks whose analysts have raised earnings forecasts most over the past 1–6 months and short those with the biggest forecast cuts.
Why it pays: Analysts revise forecasts in small, slow steps and investors under-react, so revisions and prices keep drifting the same way.
Track record: No reliable figure. Revisions predicted 6–12 month returns beyond price momentum, US stocks 1977–1993 (gross)
How it loses money: A crowded quant signal that can reverse sharply when many funds sell at once, as in the August 2007 quant crash.
Key sources: Givoly & Lakonishok (1979); Stickel (1991); Chan, Jegadeesh & Lakonishok (1996)

What to do: Buy a managed-futures replication ETF, or regress a trend-fund (CTA) index's recent returns on a few liquid futures and hold the fitted positions, to copy CTA returns cheaply.
Why it pays: Most CTA returns come from a few shared trend signals, so a cheap rule captures much of them without paying 2%-and-20% hedge-fund fees.
Track record: No reliable figure; simple trend models track managed-futures indices closely in published tests
How it loses money: Tracking error when real CTAs shift positions faster than the model, plus trend following's long flat spells.
Key sources: Fung & Hsieh (2001); Hasanhodzic & Lo (2007); Hurst, Ooi & Pedersen (2013)

What to do: Each month, buy the commodity futures with the strongest past 1–12 month returns and short the weakest, holding for one to several months.
Why it pays: Price trends reflect inventory shortages and gluts that resolve slowly, because supply takes time to respond and hedgers keep paying for protection.
Track record: ~9%/yr average across the profitable long-short versions, 31 commodity futures 1979–2004 (gross)
How it loses money: Supply shocks or policy moves (OPEC, weather, export bans) reverse trends abruptly; crowding raises crash risk.
Key sources: Erb & Harvey (2006); Miffre & Rallis (2007); Gorton, Hayashi & Rouwenhorst (2013)

What to do: Each month, buy the national stock-market indices (via country ETFs or index futures) with the best past 3–12 month returns, and avoid or short the worst.
Why it pays: Investors under-react to country-wide economic news, so national market trends persist for months.
Track record: No reliable figure. Several studies found significant gross long-short profits across developed-country indices, 1970s–2000s
How it loses money: Few, correlated bets; currency swings and sudden regime changes, such as emerging-market crises, cause whipsaws.
Key sources: Chan, Hameed & Tong (2000); Bhojraj & Swaminathan (2006); Asness, Moskowitz & Pedersen (2013)

What to do: Buy corporate bonds whose own returns, or whose issuer's stock returns, were highest over the past 6–12 months, and underweight or short the worst.
Why it pays: Bond prices react slowly to news that stocks and earlier bond moves already reflect, especially in illiquid high-yield bonds.
Track record: Significant momentum profits concentrated in high-yield bonds, US 1973–2011 (long-short, gross); weak in investment grade.
How it loses money: Sharp junk-bond rebounds, as in 2009, crush the shorts on recent losers.
Key sources: Gebhardt, Hvidkjaer & Swaminathan (2005); Jostova, Nikolova, Philipov & Stahel (2013); Haesen, Houweling & van Zundert (2017)

Strategy: Currency trend rules (moving-average and filter rules in FX)
What to do: Buy a currency when it rises above its moving average or a set percentage off its recent low, and sell when it falls back below or a set percentage off its recent high.
Why it pays: Central-bank rate smoothing and slow macro money flows once made currency trends persistent; profits faded as the market deepened and the rules spread.
Track record: Significant gross profits on major currencies in the 1970s–80s; largely gone for major pairs from the 1990s on.
How it loses money: Long sideways stretches and sudden reversals produce strings of small losses that outweigh the occasional big trend.
Key sources: Levich & Thomas (1993); Neely, Weller & Ulrich (2009); Menkhoff & Taylor (2007)

What to do: Each month, buy the currencies with the best total returns (price change plus interest earned) over the past 1–12 months and short the worst performers.
Why it pays: Investors underreact to economic and central-bank news, so currency moves partly continue; high costs in minor currencies stop arbitrageurs closing the gap.
Track record: Up to ~10%/yr long-short before costs, 48 currencies 1976–2010; much smaller after costs, concentrated in minor currencies
How it loses money: Sharp trend reversals and high trading costs in illiquid minor currencies can eat most of the profit.
Key sources: Okunev & White (2003); Menkhoff, Sarno, Schmeling & Schrimpf (2012); Asness, Moskowitz & Pedersen (2013)

What to do: Each month, hold the long-short stock factors (such as value, size, profitability and investment) that made money over the past year, and drop or short those that lost money.
Why it pays: Factor returns tend to persist, and the authors argue stock momentum is largely an indirect bet on this persistence.
Track record: Average factor earned ~0.5%/month after a positive year vs near zero after a losing year, US factors 1960s–2010s, gross
How it loses money: Factor trends can flip abruptly, as in value's violent rebound in late 2020, and it needs many long-short portfolios.
Key sources: Ehsani & Linnainmaa (2022); Gupta & Kelly (2019)

What to do: Trade futures in the direction of very recent price moves using short look-back windows (about one week to two months), so positions flip quickly when markets turn.
Why it pays: Captures short bursts of momentum and reacts quickly in crashes, trading much higher costs for faster crisis protection than slow trend.
Markets: Equity indices & ETFs; Bonds & rates; FX; Commodities
Track record: No reliable figure; 1-month trend signals were profitable before costs in published multi-market futures backtests
How it loses money: High turnover eats returns, and volatile but directionless markets cause frequent whipsaw losses.
Key sources: Hurst, Ooi & Pedersen (2013); Baltas & Kosowski (2013); Hamill, Rattray & Van Hemert (2016)

What to do: Each month, buy government bond futures whose return over the past 12 months (above cash) is positive and short those whose return is negative.
Why it pays: Investors and central banks adjust slowly to news, so interest-rate moves tend to trend over months.
Track record: Positive 12-month time-series momentum returns in all 13 government bond futures studied, data through 2009 (factor sample 1985–2009; gross); ranking countries against each other works much less well.
How it loses money: Abrupt reversals, such as sudden central-bank pivots, cause whipsaw losses.
Key sources: Moskowitz, Ooi & Pedersen (2012); Asness, Moskowitz & Pedersen (2013); Hurst, Ooi & Pedersen (2017)

What to do: Hold a stock-index fund (or another asset-class fund) only while its month-end price is above its 10-month average; otherwise switch to cash or short-term bonds, checking once a month.
Why it pays: Trends persist as investors under-react and then herd, and big bear markets unfold over months, so the filter often exits before most of the damage.
Markets: Equity indices & ETFs; Bonds & rates; Commodities
Track record: Similar returns to buy-and-hold with much lower volatility and drawdowns, US stocks over the 20th century (Faber backtest, gross); gain mostly from avoiding bear markets.
How it loses money: Repeated whipsaw losses in choppy markets, and missing sharp V-shaped rebounds such as 2020.
Key sources: Faber (2007); Zakamulin (2014); Siegel (1994)

What to do: Each month, rank industries by their past 6–12 month returns, then buy stocks in the top-ranked industries and short stocks in the bottom-ranked ones.
Why it pays: Industry-wide news (demand shifts, regulation, input costs) spreads slowly across related firms, so whole sectors keep trending.
Track record: No reliable figure. Significant gross long-short profits, US stocks 1963–1995, strongest with a 1-month ranking period
How it loses money: Concentrated industry bets reverse sharply at turning points, such as tech in 2000 or energy in 2008.
Key sources: Moskowitz & Grinblatt (1999); Grundy & Martin (2001); Hou (2007)

What to do: Instead of the whole market, hold only the large stocks with the strongest 6–12 month returns, rebalanced every 3–6 months, for example through a momentum ETF.
Why it pays: It captures the long half of the momentum premium, which comes from investor under-reaction, without needing to short.
Track record: Long side supplied roughly half of US long-short momentum profits, 1926–2011 (Israel-Moskowitz). No reliable net figure for ETFs
How it loses money: It carries full stock-market risk and can lag badly when market leadership flips, such as sharp rebounds after sell-offs.
Key sources: Israel & Moskowitz (2013); Korajczyk & Sadka (2004); Asness, Frazzini, Israel & Moskowitz (2014)

Also moves with: Calendar & Seasonal; Sentiment, Flows & Alt Data
What to do: Use a stock-index future's return from the prior close through the first half-hour of trading to predict the last half-hour: buy near the close if it was up, sell if down.
Why it pays: Options dealers hedging short-gamma positions and late-day rebalancing (e.g., leveraged ETFs) trade in the day's direction into the close.
Markets: Equity indices & ETFs; Bonds & rates; Commodities; FX
Track record: Significant first-to-last half-hour predictability in the SPY ETF 1993–2013; small edge per trade (gross)
How it loses money: The edge per trade is tiny, so commissions and slippage can erase it; it depends on dealers' options positioning.
Key sources: Gao, Han, Li & Zhou (2018); Baltussen, Da, Lammers & Martens (2021)

Strategy: Moving-average crossover & channel breakout systems (Donchian channels, Turtle rules)
What to do: Buy a futures market when its price tops its highest level of the last 20–55 days, or a fast moving average crosses above a slow one; exit or short on the reverse signal.
Why it pays: Same drivers as time-series momentum (slow reaction to news, herding, hedging demand); preset stops cut losers early while winners run.
Markets: Commodities; FX; Bonds & rates; Equity indices & ETFs
Track record: Profitable after estimated costs in most of 28 commodity futures, 1959–2007; famed 1980s Turtle results are anecdotal
How it loses money: Whipsaws: false breakouts in range-bound markets trigger repeated stop-outs and long drawdowns.
Key sources: Szakmary, Shen & Sharma (2010); Lempérière et al. (2014); Faith (2007)

What to do: Each month, rank stocks on their past 12-month returns after stripping out moves explained by the market, size and value factors, then buy the top and short the bottom.
Why it pays: It removes the hidden factor bets behind plain momentum's crashes, leaving investors' slow reaction to company-specific news.
Track record: About twice the risk-adjusted return of plain momentum, US stocks 1930–2009, gross long-short; also found in international markets
How it loses money: Milder crashes than plain momentum, but it still loses in sharp junk rallies, and results depend on the factor model used.
Key sources: Blitz, Huij & Martens (2011); Gutierrez & Prinsky (2007); Blitz, Hanauer & Vidojevic (2020)

What to do: Run a standard momentum long-short but resize it monthly: cut it when momentum's recent volatility is high or after market crashes, and enlarge it when markets are calm.
Why it pays: Momentum crashes are partly predictable: they cluster after market sell-offs and in volatile periods, when losers are primed to rebound.
Track record: Sharpe ratio (return per unit of risk) rose from ~0.53 to ~0.97 vs plain momentum, US stocks 1927–2011, gross long-short
How it loses money: A crash can hit before volatility rises, and extra leverage used in calm periods magnifies losses when the model misfires.
Key sources: Barroso & Santa-Clara (2015); Daniel & Moskowitz (2016); Cederburg, O'Doherty, Wang & Yan (2020)

What to do: Each month, buy the commodity futures whose nearest contract has outperformed the next-dated contract most over the past year, and short those where it lagged most.
Why it pays: It captures supply-demand imbalances between hedgers and speculators that bend the futures curve; you are paid for absorbing that price pressure.
Track record: No reliable figure; reported to beat standard momentum and carry signals in commodity futures backtests
How it loses money: Rests mainly on one study, so data-mining risk is real; storage or supply surprises can reverse positions quickly.
Key sources: Boons & Porras Prado (2019)

What to do: Time each country's stock and bond futures using both markets' past 12-month returns: past bond gains signal buying stocks, past stock gains signal selling bonds.
Why it pays: Falling yields support later equity gains while equity rallies foreshadow higher rates, and investors are slow to link the two markets.
Track record: No reliable figure; one paper reports a higher Sharpe than plain time-series momentum (gross backtest, developed markets)
How it loses money: Single-paper evidence; the stock-bond relationship can change with the inflation regime and flip the signals.
Key sources: Pitkäjärvi, Suominen & Vaittinen (2020)

What to do: Each week, buy the coins with the highest returns over the past 1–4 weeks and short or avoid the worst performers; the effect tends to reverse beyond about a month.
Why it pays: Investor attention and herding push recent winners further for a few weeks before prices overshoot and revert.
Track record: No reliable net figure; significant gross weekly long-short returns 2014–2018 (coins above $1m market value), but a monthly test found no momentum
How it loses money: Sharp reversals and high trading costs in thin coins eat the gains, and shorting small coins is often impossible.
Key sources: Liu, Tsyvinski & Wu (2022); Grobys & Sapkota (2019); Cong, Karolyi, Tang & Zhao (2021)

What to do: Hold bitcoin (or another major coin) while its price is above a moving average (e.g., 50- or 200-day) or its return over recent weeks is positive; otherwise switch to cash (or go short).
Why it pays: With no cash flows to anchor value, investors extrapolate past prices and herd, so trends tend to persist for weeks.
Track record: Moving-average rules beat buy-and-hold on Sharpe ratio out of sample in daily bitcoin data, 2010s, mainly by dodging crashes; no robust net-of-cost figure
How it loses money: Whipsaws in choppy, sideways markets, and sudden crashes that hit before the signal turns.
Key sources: Liu & Tsyvinski (2021); Detzel, Liu, Strauss, Zhou & Zhu (2021); Corbet, Eraslan, Lucey & Sensoy (2019)

Strategy: Dual momentum ETF rotation (Antonacci's Global Equities Momentum)
What to do: Each month, hold whichever of US or international stocks rose more over the past 12 months, but switch to bonds if that winner's 12-month return is below Treasury bills.
Why it pays: Combines relative momentum (leaders keep leading) with absolute momentum (a trend filter that sidesteps long bear markets).
Track record: No reliable independent figure; headline results come from the author's own in-sample backtests
How it loses money: Few assets and one look-back make it fragile; whipsaws at sharp V-shaped rebounds lock in losses and miss recoveries.
Key sources: Antonacci (2014); Moskowitz, Ooi & Pedersen (2012)

What to do: Among last year's biggest winners, buy those whose gains came from many small daily rises rather than a few big jumps, and short losers that fell in the same gradual way.
Why it pays: Investors notice dramatic news but under-react to a steady trickle of small news, so gradual trends last longer.
Track record: No reliable figure. In US data, momentum profits were concentrated in smooth-path stocks and largely absent in jumpy ones (gross)
How it loses money: It is still a momentum bet, so it shares momentum crashes, and independent tests since publication are few.
Key sources: Da, Gurun & Warachka (2014); Gray & Vogel (2016)

What to do: Each month, rank stocks on their returns from 12 to 7 months ago, ignoring the latest six months, then buy the top performers and short the bottom.
Why it pays: Proposed to capture slow-moving under-reaction to news, but the mechanism is unclear and the effect may be a statistical quirk.
Track record: Beat recent (6-2 month) momentum in US data since 1926, gross long-short; Goyal-Wahal found no such edge in dozens of other countries
How it loses money: Its edge over standard momentum may be a US-only quirk, and it still carries momentum's crash risk.
Key sources: Novy-Marx (2012); Goyal & Wahal (2015)

Also moves with: Size & Illiquidity; Short-Term Reversal & Stat Arb
What to do: Use the latest returns of large, heavily traded stocks or industry leaders to predict and trade the next-day or next-week move of related small, thinly traded stocks in the same direction.
Why it pays: News hits big, liquid stocks first and seeps slowly into small, neglected stocks because of limited investor attention and trading frictions.
Track record: No reliable figure
How it loses money: Much of the effect is stale small-stock prices that can't actually be traded at those quotes after costs.
Key sources: Lo & MacKinlay (1990); Boudoukh, Richardson & Whitelaw (1994); Hou (2007)

Strategy: Leveraged 200-day trend rotation ('Leverage for the Long Run')
What to do: Hold a 2x or 3x leveraged S&P 500 or Nasdaq ETF while the index closes above its 200-day moving average (average of the last 200 daily closes); otherwise hold Treasury bills.
Why it pays: Volatility clusters in downtrends, so sitting out below the average avoids the turbulent stretches that most erode daily-reset leveraged funds.
Track record: Authors' 1928–2015 S&P 500 simulation: higher return and Sharpe, smaller drawdowns than leveraged buy-and-hold; in-sample, before taxes.
How it loses money: Repeated whipsaw trades, and fast crashes that hit before the signal flips (as in February 2020), cause big losses at 3x.
Key sources: Gayed & Bilello (2016); Faber (2007); Avellaneda & Zhang (2010)

What to do: Each month, score every stock on its price relative to moving averages from 3 days to about 4 years, then buy the fifth with the strongest score and short the weakest fifth.
Why it pays: It blends short-, medium- and long-horizon price signals, exploiting news that spreads gradually and under-reaction at several speeds.
Track record: ~1.6%/month gross long-short vs ~0.8% for standard momentum, US stocks ~1930–2014
How it loses money: High turnover, much of it in small stocks, so trading costs can eat a large share of the paper profits.
Key sources: Han, Zhou & Zhu (2016); Han, Yang & Zhou (2013)

What to do: Mark the high and low of the first 5–30 minutes of trading; buy if price breaks above that range (short if below), exit at the other side, and close by day's end.
Why it pays: Early moves on news or heavy volume tend to continue as slower traders react, especially in unusually active 'stocks in play'; evidence is mostly from practitioners.
Track record: Authors' own backtest: ~1,600% total, Sharpe ~2.8, US 'stocks in play' 2016–2023, using intraday leverage; not independently replicated.
How it loses money: False breakouts cause repeated stop-outs, and spreads, slippage and commissions on frequent trades can wipe out a thin edge.
Key sources: Crabel (1990); Holmberg, Lönnbark & Lundström (2013); Zarattini, Barbon & Aziz (2024)

What to do: Each month, buy straddles (call plus put) on stocks whose straddles earned the highest returns over the past several months to three years, and sell straddles on those with the lowest.
Why it pays: Option prices appear to underreact to persistent differences in volatility risk across stocks, so past option winners keep outperforming.
Track record: No reliable figure; documented in US stock options from 1996 to the late 2010s, before trading costs; no out-of-sample test yet
How it loses money: Recent, mostly in-sample finding; option trading costs and volatility regime shifts can erase gains.
Key sources: Heston, Jones, Khorram, Li & Mo (2023)

What to do: Each month, hold the 1–3 of the roughly 11 S&P sector ETFs with the best past 3–12 month returns, often switching to cash or bonds when every sector is falling.
Why it pays: It is a simple long-only version of industry momentum, relying on sector news spreading slowly and investors herding into leading sectors.
Track record: No reliable figure. Mostly practitioner backtests, which vary widely with lookback length and choice of sectors
How it loses money: With only about 11 sectors, a few whipsaws or one bad concentrated bet can erase years of gains.
Key sources: O'Neal (2000); Faber (2010); Moskowitz & Grinblatt (1999)

Strategy: Speed-blended trend at turning points ("Breaking Bad Trends")
What to do: Run slow (12-month) and fast (1-month) trend signals together; when they disagree, signalling a possible turning point, shrink or blend positions instead of following the slow signal alone.
Why it pays: Slow trends lag at reversals and fast trends are noisy; choosing speed by market state limits losses at turning points, where most trend losses occur.
Markets: Equity indices & ETFs; Bonds & rates; FX; Commodities
Track record: No reliable figure; published backtests only, too recent for meaningful out-of-sample evidence
How it loses money: Little live track record; speed rules can be overfit and still get whipsawed in choppy markets.
Key sources: Garg, Goulding, Harvey & Mazzoleni (2021); Goulding, Harvey & Mazzoleni (2023)

Strategy: Value Line Timeliness rankings (the 'Value Line enigma')
What to do: Buy the stocks the weekly Value Line Investment Survey ranks 1 (top) for 'Timeliness' and avoid or short those ranked 5, switching holdings whenever the ranks change.
Why it pays: The ranks combine earnings momentum, price momentum and recent earnings surprises, so they profit from investors' slow reaction to news.
Track record: No reliable figure; older studies found rank 1 beat rank 5, but the gap is largely explained by momentum and earnings drift and shrinks after costs
How it loses money: Frequent rank changes bring heavy trading costs, and the edge mostly duplicates cheaper momentum and earnings-drift signals.
Key sources: Copeland & Mayers (1982); Affleck-Graves & Mendenhall (1992); Choi (2000)

Strategy: Moving-average & range-breakout rules on a single stock index (Brock-Lakonishok-LeBaron)
What to do: Buy the stock index when its price crosses above a moving average (e.g., 50 or 200 days) or breaks out of its recent range; sell when it crosses back below.
Why it pays: Originally credited to slow-moving trends and under-reaction; later work shows much of the edge was data mining and pre-1987 market conditions.
Track record: Strong in Dow Jones backtests 1897–1986; no outperformance 1987–1996, nor after costs and data-snooping controls
How it loses money: The in-sample edge vanished out of sample; whipsaws plus trading costs tend to lose against buy-and-hold.
Key sources: Brock, Lakonishok & LeBaron (1992); Sullivan, Timmermann & White (1999); Bajgrowicz & Scaillet (2012)

What to do: Each year, buy the stocks whose total assets grew least (or shrank) over the past year and short those whose assets grew most.
Why it pays: Fast growers overinvest and investors extrapolate their growth; also, firms invest less when investors demand a high return, so low investment flags higher expected returns.
Track record: ~20%/yr spread equal-weighted, ~8%/yr value-weighted; US 1968–2003 (long-short, gross)
How it loses money: Shares value's long droughts; the large equal-weighted gains shrink sharply in tradable large caps.
Key sources: Cooper, Gulen & Schill (2008); Fama & French (2015); Hou, Xue & Zhang (2015)

What to do: Once a year, buy the stocks with the highest book value (accounting net worth) relative to market value, i.e. the cheapest, and short or underweight those with the lowest.
Why it pays: Cheap firms may carry more business risk, and investors over-extrapolate past growth, overpaying for glamour stocks and dumping unloved ones.
Track record: Significant positive HML premium, US 1963–1991 (gross, long-short); then a drawdown lasting over a decade, roughly 2007–2020
How it loses money: Long value droughts, such as roughly 2007–2020, when cheap stocks lagged growth stocks for over a decade.
Key sources: Fama & French (1992); Fama & French (1993); Jensen, Kelly & Pedersen (2023)

Strategy: Earnings, cash-flow and enterprise-multiple value (P/E, P/CF, EV/EBITDA)
What to do: Buy the stocks with the highest earnings, cash flow or operating profit relative to share price or to enterprise value (debt plus equity), and short or avoid the lowest.
Why it pays: Investors extrapolate recent earnings trends too far; earnings and cash flow measure cheapness more directly than book value, which misses intangible assets.
Track record: No reliable single figure; earnings, cash-flow and EBITDA/EV yields predict US returns at least as well as book-to-market (gross)
How it loses money: Value traps (cheap firms in permanent decline) and long stretches when growth stocks lead.
Key sources: Basu (1977); Lakonishok, Shleifer & Vishny (1994); Loughran & Wellman (2011)

What to do: Apply value sorts (book-to-market, earnings yield and similar) inside non-US developed and emerging stock markets: buy each market's cheapest stocks and short or avoid the most expensive.
Why it pays: Same risk and overreaction story as US value; separate markets give independent out-of-sample confirmation and diversify the US version.
Track record: Global value beat global growth by ~7.7%/yr; value won in 12 of 13 major markets, 1975–1995 (gross)
How it loses money: Global value droughts, currency swings, and political or liquidity shocks in emerging markets.
Key sources: Fama & French (1998); Rouwenhorst (1999); Fama & French (2012)

Strategy: Net share issuance and shareholder yield (buybacks)
What to do: Buy firms shrinking their share count or paying high dividends plus buybacks (shareholder yield), and short or avoid firms issuing the most new shares.
Why it pays: Managers issue shares when their stock is overpriced and buy back when it's cheap, and investors underreact to these signals.
Track record: No reliable single figure; post-1970 US predictive power stronger than size, value or momentum; works across 41 countries
How it loses money: Underperforms in issuance-fuelled booms, and overlaps heavily with value.
Key sources: Pontiff & Woodgate (2008); McLean, Pontiff & Watanabe (2009); Boudoukh, Michaely, Richardson & Roberts (2007)

Strategy: Value + momentum combined across asset classes ("Value and Momentum Everywhere")
What to do: In each asset class (stocks, country indices, bonds, currencies, commodities), hold a 50/50 mix of a cheap-minus-expensive value bet and a past-winners-minus-losers momentum bet.
Why it pays: Value and momentum are strongly negatively correlated, so combining them smooths returns; both likely reflect behavioural mispricing plus some liquidity risk.
Markets: Multi-asset; Stocks; Equity indices & ETFs; Bonds & rates; FX; Commodities
Track record: Value and momentum premia in all 8 markets/asset classes; 50/50 global combo has a higher Sharpe than either alone (gross, long-short), c. 1972–2011
How it loses money: Long value droughts (2018–2020) or momentum crashes (2009) can sink the combo; the leverage needed magnifies losses.
Key sources: Asness, Moskowitz & Pedersen (2013); Blitz & Van Vliet (2008); Ilmanen et al. (2021)

Strategy: Betting against analyst growth optimism (low vs high long-term growth forecasts)
What to do: Once a year, buy the tenth of stocks with the most pessimistic analyst forecasts of long-term (3–5 year) earnings growth and short the tenth with the most optimistic forecasts.
Why it pays: Analysts and investors over-extrapolate recent good news into rosy growth stories, so hyped stocks disappoint and unloved ones surprise on the upside.
Track record: About 12 points/yr (≈15% vs 3%), most pessimistic minus most optimistic growth-forecast tenth, US stocks 1981–2015, gross
How it loses money: The short side holds high-beta glamour stocks that can soar in speculative booms such as the late-1990s tech bubble.
Key sources: La Porta (1996); Dechow & Sloan (1997); Bordalo, Gennaioli, La Porta & Shleifer (2019)

Strategy: Country equity index value (incl. long-term reversal)
What to do: Overweight or buy the national stock markets that look cheapest on valuation ratios (e.g., cyclically adjusted P/E, book-to-market) or fell most over 3–5 years; underweight or short the most expensive.
Why it pays: Cheap markets carry real economic risk and investors over-extrapolate bad news, so valuations tend to mean-revert over several years.
Track record: No reliable figure
How it loses money: Cheap markets can stay cheap for a decade, as when expensive US stocks beat cheaper markets through the 2010s.
Key sources: Asness, Liew & Stevens (1997); Richards (1997); Asness, Moskowitz & Pedersen (2013)

What to do: Buy corporate bonds whose spreads are wide relative to a model of default risk (leverage, volatility, rating) and short or underweight bonds whose spreads look too tight.
Why it pays: Spreads overreact to news and fund flows, so bonds paying more than their risk warrants tend to outperform as prices correct.
Track record: Positive alphas vs the bond market, US investment-grade and high-yield bonds 1994–2015 (gross); smaller with cleaned data and trading costs.
How it loses money: Cheap bonds are often cheap for a reason and go on to default, and shorting corporate bonds is costly.
Key sources: Correia, Richardson & Tuna (2012); Houweling & van Zundert (2017); Israel, Palhares & Richardson (2018)

What to do: Buy the currencies that look cheapest on purchasing-power parity (inflation-adjusted exchange rate far below its long-run level) and short the most expensive, rebalancing monthly or quarterly.
Why it pays: Real exchange rates drift back toward fair value over several years as trade and inflation adjust, and few investors are willing to wait that long.
Track record: No reliable single figure; modest long-short returns in 1970s–2010s academic tests, stronger when adjusted for productivity and other fundamentals
How it loses money: Cheap currencies can stay cheap or get cheaper for years, especially during crises or structural economic shifts.
Key sources: Rogoff (1996); Asness, Moskowitz & Pedersen (2013); Menkhoff, Sarno, Schmeling & Schrimpf (2017)

What to do: Hold a broad stock index weighted by company size measures such as sales, cash flow, book value and dividends instead of market value, and rebalance yearly.
Why it pays: It automatically underweights overpriced stocks and overweights cheap ones, so it earns a value tilt plus a rebalancing effect.
Track record: ~2%/yr above the cap-weighted index, US 1962–2004 (long-only backtest, gross)
How it loses money: Lags market-cap indexes when growth stocks lead, as in the 2010s; largely a value tilt in disguise.
Key sources: Arnott, Hsu & Moore (2005); Perold (2007)

What to do: Buy the stocks with the worst returns over the past 3–5 years and short the biggest winners, holding for about 3 years.
Why it pays: Investors over-extrapolate long runs of good or bad news and prices later revert; it is largely the same bet as buying cheap value stocks.
Track record: Past 3-year losers beat past winners by ~25% over the next 3 years, US stocks 1926–1982, gross
How it loses money: Losers can keep losing (value traps), and returns are concentrated in tiny stocks and in January.
Key sources: De Bondt & Thaler (1985); Chopra, Lakonishok & Ritter (1992); Fama & French (1996)

Also moves with: Trend & Momentum; Defensive, Quality & Low Risk; Size & Illiquidity
What to do: Hold one long-only portfolio of stocks that score well on several factors at once (cheap, rising, profitable, low-volatility, smaller), rebalanced a few times a year.
Why it pays: Factors pay off at different times and are weakly or negatively correlated, so combining them smooths returns and cuts trading.
Track record: No reliable single figure; combinations beat single factors on Sharpe in backtests, but many live funds lagged cap-weighted US indices since the mid-2010s
How it loses money: Can lag cap-weighted indices for years when mega-cap growth leads, and crowding and fees erode the edge.
Key sources: Asness, Moskowitz & Pedersen (2013); Fitzgibbons, Friedman, Pomorski & Serban (2017); Ilmanen, Israel, Moskowitz, Thapar & Lee (2021)

Strategy: Net external financing (avoid firms raising capital)
What to do: Each year, measure the net cash a firm raised from new debt and shares (minus repayments, buybacks and dividends) relative to its assets; buy the biggest net payers-out and short the biggest net raisers.
Why it pays: Firms tend to raise money when their shares look overvalued and analysts are over-optimistic; investors underreact, and fast-investing firms also earn lower expected returns.
Track record: ~15.5%/yr long-short, extreme tenths of net external financing, US stocks 1971–2000, gross; equity-only ~11%, debt-only ~8%
How it loses money: It overlaps heavily with accruals, asset-growth and share-issuance signals, and lags when markets reward capital-hungry growth firms.
Key sources: Bradshaw, Richardson & Sloan (2006); Cohen & Lys (2006); Jensen, Kelly & Pedersen (2023)

What to do: Each year, short firms with high net operating assets (operating assets minus operating liabilities) relative to total assets and buy firms with low ones.
Why it pays: Investors focus on earnings and overlook that bloated balance sheets, built from past accruals and investment, signal earnings that won't last.
Track record: No reliable figure
How it loses money: Overlaps with asset growth and accruals, and has weakened since publication.
Key sources: Hirshleifer, Hou, Teoh & Zhang (2004)

What to do: Among the cheapest fifth of stocks by book-to-market, buy those scoring 8–9 on nine yes/no financial-health tests (profits, cash flow, debt, margins) and short or avoid those scoring 0–1.
Why it pays: Investors neglect cheap firms and react slowly to improving financial statements, so cheap firms with strengthening fundamentals are underpriced.
Track record: ~23%/yr long-short among cheap US stocks, 1976–1996 (gross); later out-of-sample results mixed
How it loses money: The edge sits mostly in small, illiquid stocks, and later out-of-sample tests are mixed.
Key sources: Piotroski (2000); Piotroski & So (2012)

What to do: Each year, buy stocks whose research-and-development spending is large relative to their market value, and underweight or short firms that spend little.
Why it pays: Accounting rules expense R&D immediately, depressing reported profits, so investors undervalue research-heavy firms whose payoffs arrive later.
Track record: No reliable figure
How it loses money: Concentrated in small, volatile tech and biotech stocks whose research may fail; overlaps with value and intangibles.
Key sources: Lev & Sougiannis (1996); Chan, Lakonishok & Sougiannis (2001); Eberhart, Maxwell & Siddique (2004)

What to do: Estimate from company accounts how far in the future each firm's cash flows lie (its 'equity duration'); buy the shortest-duration stocks, short the longest-duration growth stocks, and rebalance yearly.
Why it pays: Debated: long-dated growth stories attract over-optimistic buyers that short sellers can't easily correct, or near-term cash flows carry a risk premium.
Track record: Short- minus long-duration ~1.1%/month, equal-weighted US stocks 1963–2013, gross; factor models explain only about half
How it loses money: It is effectively a bet against growth stocks, so it suffers when falling rates or growth manias lift long-duration stocks, as in 1999 and 2020.
Key sources: Dechow, Sloan & Soliman (2004); Weber (2018); Gormsen & Lazarus (2023)

What to do: Rank stocks on book-to-market using today's share price instead of one up to 18 months old, or on an average of several cheapness ratios; buy the cheapest, short the dearest, rebalance monthly.
Why it pays: Current prices measure cheapness more accurately, and averaging book, earnings, cash-flow and sales ratios reduces noise from any one accounting number.
Track record: HML-Devil: ~3.1–3.8%/yr alpha vs standard factor models including classic HML and momentum, US long-short (gross)
How it loses money: Same long value droughts as classic value; its extra edge shows up mainly when combined with momentum.
Key sources: Asness & Frazzini (2013); Israel, Laursen & Richardson (2021)

What to do: Buy stocks that are both cheap and highly profitable or high quality, usually by adding the two scores together, to avoid cheap-but-deteriorating 'value traps'.
Why it pays: Cheap stocks are often cheap for a reason; a profitability filter avoids value traps, and the two factors hedge each other's bad periods.
Track record: No reliable single figure; adding profitability to value sharply raised risk-adjusted returns vs value alone, US 1963–2010
How it loses money: Both legs can lag together when speculative growth stocks lead, causing long tracking error vs the market.
Key sources: Novy-Marx (2013); Asness, Frazzini & Pedersen (2019); Fama & French (2015)

What to do: Buy stocks with high advertising spending relative to market value, but avoid firms that just sharply raised ad budgets, which tend to underperform later.
Why it pays: Advertising is booked as an immediate cost so brand value is overlooked, while sudden ad spikes buy only temporary investor attention.
Track record: No reliable figure
How it loses money: Evidence is weak and inconsistent, ad data are patchy, and the effect overlaps with value and size.
Key sources: Chan, Lakonishok & Sougiannis (2001); Lou (2014)

What to do: Buy the commodities whose price has fallen most relative to its level about five years ago and short those that have risen most.
Why it pays: High prices spur new supply and curb demand over years (and low prices do the reverse), so extreme multi-year moves partly reverse.
Track record: No reliable figure; weak standalone premium in published tests
How it loses money: Structural shifts (new extraction technology, demand changes) can keep a commodity cheap or expensive for many years.
Key sources: Asness, Moskowitz & Pedersen (2013); Ilmanen (2011)

What to do: Buy coins whose market value is low relative to network fundamentals (such as user numbers or on-chain activity) and short those that look expensive, rebalancing weekly or monthly.
Why it pays: Either a risk premium for less-established networks or slow pricing of adoption fundamentals; the explanation is unsettled.
Track record: No reliable net figure; significant gross value and adoption premia across thousands of crypto assets in one main working paper
How it loses money: Cheap-looking coins stay cheap or die, and the evidence rests on short, noisy data from one boom-bust era.
Key sources: Cong, Karolyi, Tang & Zhao (2021); Bhambhwani, Delikouras & Korniotis (2019); Liu & Tsyvinski (2021)

What to do: Buy stocks priced below their current assets minus all liabilities (Benjamin Graham's 'net-net' rule) and hold a diversified basket for about a year.
Why it pays: Tiny, neglected, troubled firms get dumped below liquidation value, and few institutions can buy them, so the mispricing lasts.
Track record: ~29%/yr vs ~11.5% for the NYSE-AMEX index, US 1970–1983 (long-only, gross, mostly tiny stocks); few independent tests since
How it loses money: Tiny, illiquid stocks with high trading costs; some burn their cash and go bust; qualifying US stocks are now rare.
Key sources: Graham & Dodd (1934); Oppenheimer (1986)

What to do: Buy government bond futures of countries with high real (inflation-adjusted) yields or yields that rose most over about five years, and short those with low real yields.
Why it pays: Higher real yields compensate for inflation and duration risk, and yields tend to partly mean-revert after large multi-year moves.
Track record: No reliable figure
How it loses money: Bonds can be cheap for a reason: rising inflation or fiscal fears can push their yields higher still.
Key sources: Asness, Moskowitz & Pedersen (2013); Brooks & Moskowitz (2017); Ilmanen (2011)

What to do: Rank stocks on earnings yield (operating profit divided by enterprise value) and return on capital, buy the 20–30 with the best combined rank, and hold each for a year.
Why it pays: It buys good businesses (high returns on capital) at bargain prices, combining the value and quality premiums.
Track record: Author's backtest 30.8%/yr vs 12.4% for the S&P 500, US 1988–2004 (long-only); independent tests far lower
How it loses money: Concentrated portfolio with big tracking error; long losing stretches make investors quit; results sensitive to universe choice.
Key sources: Greenblatt (2005); Gray & Carlisle (2012)

Strategy: Growth at a reasonable price (GARP / PEG ratio below 1)
What to do: Buy stocks whose price-to-earnings ratio is below their forecast yearly earnings growth in percent (PEG below 1, e.g. P/E 15 with 20% growth), refreshing the list about yearly.
Why it pays: Pitched as paying fairly for growth; any edge mostly comes from the low-P/E value tilt, since analysts' forecasts for fast growers are systematically too optimistic.
Track record: No reliable figure; small studies found low-PEG stocks beat high-PEG ones, much like plain low-P/E value investing
How it loses money: Over-optimistic growth forecasts make stocks look cheap until earnings disappoint; it also suffers when value lags, as in 2007–2020.
Key sources: Peters (1991); La Porta (1996); Bordalo, Gennaioli, La Porta & Shleifer (2019)

What to do: Buy the stocks with the highest dividend yield (annual dividend divided by share price), often screened for dividend stability, and rebalance yearly.
Why it pays: High-yield stocks mostly earn the value and low-beta premiums; investors' love of dividend income adds no reliable extra premium.
Track record: No reliable figure; returns largely explained by value and low-beta exposure
How it loses money: Concentrated in rate-sensitive sectors, exposed to dividend cuts, and lags when growth stocks lead.
Key sources: Litzenberger & Ramaswamy (1979); Fama & French (1993); Hartzmark & Solomon (2019)

What to do: Add estimated intangible capital (capitalised R&D plus part of overhead spending) to book value, then buy the stocks that are cheapest on this adjusted book-to-market and short the most expensive.
Why it pays: Book value ignores R&D, brands and know-how, so adjusting for them stops tech and pharma firms from being wrongly labelled expensive.
Track record: No reliable figure
How it loses money: May be a fix found with hindsight; intangible estimates are rough, and it still suffers value droughts.
Key sources: Eisfeldt, Kim & Papanikolaou (2022); Arnott, Harvey, Kalesnik & Linnainmaa (2021); Lev & Srivastava (2022)

What to do: Buy stocks with high debt relative to their stock-market value and short low-debt ones; note that this mostly repeats a value bet and the sign flips with book-value measures.
Why it pays: Debt raises equity risk, but the apparent premium is largely absorbed by book-to-market, and book leverage alone predicts lower, not higher, returns.
Track record: No reliable figure
How it loses money: Mostly repackages value while adding bankruptcy risk, without a reliable extra return.
Key sources: Bhandari (1988); Fama & French (1992); Penman, Richardson & Tuna (2007)

What to do: Buy tax-exempt municipal bonds when their yields are high relative to same-maturity Treasuries (ratio near or above 100%), and cut back when the ratio is low.
Why it pays: Munis are held mostly by tax-sensitive retail investors whose flows swing prices, and long munis yield more than taxes alone justify (the 'muni puzzle').
Track record: No reliable figure; the extra yield on long munis is well documented, but evidence for timing the ratio is mostly practitioner.
How it loses money: Panic selling of muni funds (2008, March 2020), defaults or tax changes push munis cheaper still.
Key sources: Green (1993); Chalmers (1998); Longstaff (2011)

What to do: Each year, buy firms with the most 'organisation capital' (accumulated selling, general and administrative spending relative to assets, versus industry peers) and short those with the least.
Why it pays: Much of these firms' value can walk out the door with key staff, a risk shareholders must be paid to bear.
Track record: ~4.6%/yr higher average returns, high- vs low-organisation-capital firms, US stocks 1970s–2000s (gross)
How it loses money: Evidence rests mainly on one paper, and intangible-heavy firms can sell off together on tech or talent shocks.
Key sources: Lev & Radhakrishnan (2005); Eisfeldt & Papanikolaou (2013)

Strategy: Value timing using the value spread
What to do: Tilt toward value stocks when the valuation gap between cheap and expensive stocks (the 'value spread') is unusually wide, and away from them when it is narrow.
Why it pays: A wide spread may mean cheap stocks are unusually cheap and due to recover, though it can also mean they are genuinely riskier.
Track record: No reliable figure; gains from timing value were modest and statistically weak in US tests
How it loses money: Spreads can keep widening for years, as in 1999–2000 and 2020, so timing bets lose long before paying off.
Key sources: Asness, Friedman, Krail & Liew (2000); Cohen, Polk & Vuolteenaho (2003); Asness, Chandra, Ilmanen & Israel (2017)

What to do: Each month, buy (via currency forwards) the currencies with the highest short-term interest rates and sell those with the lowest, pocketing the rate gap unless exchange rates move against you.
Why it pays: You are paid for crash risk: high-yield currencies tend to fall together in global sell-offs, when funding dries up and speculators unwind.
Track record: About 5%/yr long-short after bid-ask spreads (Sharpe ~0.6), developed and emerging currencies, 1983–2007; G10 carry weak after 2008
How it loses money: Sudden carry unwinds (1998, 2008, the August 2024 yen unwind) can wipe out years of interest gains in days.
Key sources: Lustig, Roussanov & Verdelhan (2011); Burnside, Eichenbaum, Kleshchelski & Rebelo (2011); Brunnermeier, Nagel & Pedersen (2009)

Also moves with: Short Volatility & Insurance Selling; Arbitrage & Relative Value
What to do: Hold government-guaranteed mortgage-backed securities, hedged against interest-rate moves, to earn the extra spread paid for bearing homeowners' option to prepay.
Why it pays: Investors are paid for prepayment and 'negative convexity' risk (gains capped, losses amplified) that only specialised, capital-limited buyers will hold.
Track record: No reliable figure; studies find positive average rate-hedged excess returns on US agency MBS since the 1990s.
How it loses money: Big rate moves shift prepayment speeds and trigger hedging spirals (1994, 2003), and spreads widen when rate volatility jumps (2022).
Key sources: Gabaix, Krishnamurthy & Vigneron (2007); Duarte, Longstaff & Yu (2007); Boyarchenko, Fuster & Lucca (2019)

What to do: In each asset class (currencies, bonds, equity indices, commodities, credit, index options), buy the instruments with the highest carry (what you earn if prices don't change) and short the lowest, then combine them.
Why it pays: Carry pays for risks that bite in global recessions, liquidity crunches and volatility spikes; spreading it across asset classes makes the premium steadier.
Track record: Gross Sharpe ~1.1 for a diversified global carry factor across nine asset classes (~0.7 within single asset classes), 1972–2012 (Koijen et al.)
How it loses money: Carry positions in different markets tend to crash at the same time in global recessions and liquidity crises.
Key sources: Koijen, Moskowitz, Pedersen & Vrugt (2018); Baz, Granger, Harvey, Le Roux & Rattray (2015); Ilmanen (2011)

What to do: Each month, buy the commodity futures in steepest backwardation (near-dated contracts priced above later ones) and short those in steepest contango, earning the roll yield.
Why it pays: Backwardation signals scarce inventories and hedgers paying for insurance, so buyers earn a premium for taking price risk when supply is tight.
Track record: ~12.7%/yr abnormal return for the term-structure (roll-yield) long-short in a pre-2008 sample, before costs (Fuertes, Miffre & Rallis 2010); basis-sorted spreads ~8–14%/yr (Szymanowska et al.)
How it loses money: Backwardated markets can collapse when a supply squeeze ends, e.g. oil in 2014 or energy in recessions.
Key sources: Erb & Harvey (2006); Fuertes, Miffre & Rallis (2010, J. Banking & Finance); Szymanowska, de Roon, Nijman & van den Goorbergh (2014, J. Finance)

Also moves with: Short Volatility & Insurance Selling; Macro & Asset Allocation
What to do: Hold corporate bonds (investment-grade or high-yield), optionally shorting Treasuries of matched maturity so you earn only the extra credit spread over government bonds.
Why it pays: Investors are paid for default, illiquidity and losses that cluster in recessions; spreads have historically exceeded actual default losses.
Track record: Modest positive returns over maturity-matched Treasuries, larger for high yield (US data since the 1930s); no single agreed figure.
How it loses money: Spreads blow out in recessions; US high-yield bonds lost roughly a quarter of their value in 2008.
Key sources: Elton, Gruber, Agrawal & Mann (2001); Huang & Huang (2012); Asvanunt & Richardson (2017)

What to do: Run the FX carry trade, but also buy out-of-the-money currency options on each position so that a sudden crash in the high-yield currencies is capped.
Why it pays: Carry pays for more than crash risk alone, so a smaller premium remains even after you pay for crash insurance.
Track record: Crash-hedged G10 carry stayed profitable; crash-risk premia explain at most about one-third of carry excess returns, 1990–2012 (Jurek)
How it loses money: Option premiums eat into returns, and slow grinding losses that never reach the option strike are not protected.
Key sources: Burnside, Eichenbaum, Kleshchelski & Rebelo (2011); Jurek (2014)

What to do: Buy 10-year government bond futures in countries with the steepest curves (bond yield minus cash rate, plus roll-down) and short those with the flattest, sizing positions to equal risk.
Why it pays: A steep curve usually signals a high term premium, paid for bearing inflation and rate-rise risk, and you also earn roll-down as bonds age.
Track record: No reliable single figure; positive risk-adjusted long-short returns across ~10 developed bond markets, 1980s–2012, before costs (Koijen et al.)
How it loses money: A sudden rate surge in the high-carry markets, as in the 2022 inflation shock, can cause sharp losses.
Key sources: Koijen, Moskowitz, Pedersen & Vrugt (2018); Asness, Ilmanen, Israel & Moskowitz (2015); Ilmanen (2011)

What to do: When the yield curve slopes upward, buy a bond that matures after your holding horizon and sell it early, profiting as its yield 'rolls down' toward the lower yields of shorter bonds.
Why it pays: Forward rates (the future rates implied by today's curve) tend to over-predict actual future rates, so holders keep much of the extra yield.
Track record: No reliable single figure; studies find small extra returns over holding to maturity in US and other bill and note markets.
How it loses money: Yields rise more than the curve implied, erasing the gain; there is no edge when the curve is flat or inverted.
Key sources: Dyl & Joehnk (1981); Grieves & Marcus (1992); Bieri & Chincarini (2005)

Strategy: CLO equity and debt tranches (structured leveraged-loan credit)
Also moves with: Short Volatility & Insurance Selling; Size & Illiquidity
What to do: Buy slices of CLOs (pools of risky corporate loans split into safe AAA notes down to a first-loss 'equity' piece) via CLO ETFs, listed closed-end funds or directly, and hold for years.
Why it pays: Banks and insurers pay up for highly rated tranches under capital rules, so the loans yield more than CLO debt costs; manager fees capture much of that gap.
Track record: US CLO equity beat risk-matched benchmarks before fees, but manager fees absorbed most of that; debt tranches beat same-rated corporate bonds
How it loses money: A wave of loan defaults or price drops trips CLO safety tests, diverting cash from equity, which can lose most of its value.
Key sources: Benmelech, Dlugosz & Ivashina (2012); Cordell, Roberts & Schwert (2023)

Strategy: Commodity curve positioning (optimal roll and calendar spreads)
What to do: Within each commodity, hold the delivery month whose price curve offers the best roll yield instead of the front month, or trade calendar spreads that profit from the curve's slope.
Why it pays: Index and ETF money crowds the front-month contracts and hedging demand differs by maturity, so different points on the same curve earn different premiums.
Track record: No reliable single figure; enhanced-roll indices have historically lost less to contango than front-month indices
How it loses money: Curve shapes can flip fast in supply shocks, and thinly traded deferred contracts cost more to trade.
Key sources: Szymanowska, de Roon, Nijman & van den Goorbergh (2014); de Groot, Karstanje & Zhou (2014)

What to do: Buy commodities whose inventories are unusually low versus normal (usually also in backwardation) and avoid or short those with unusually high stockpiles.
Why it pays: Scarce inventories leave no buffer against supply shocks, so prices become volatile and holders demand a higher risk premium.
Track record: No reliable figure; low-inventory commodities earned higher premiums in multi-decade data, largely captured by the futures curve (basis) signal
How it loses money: Inventory data is slow, revised and patchy, and supply can rebound quickly once prices spike.
Key sources: Working (1949); Gorton, Hayashi & Rouwenhorst (2013)

What to do: Within corporate bonds, overweight those with the widest credit spreads (extra yield over Treasuries) for their rating and maturity, and underweight or short the tightest, rebalancing monthly.
Why it pays: Wider spreads pay for default, liquidity and crash risks that many investors prefer to avoid.
Track record: Positive risk-adjusted long-short returns, US corporate bonds late 1990s–2015 (gross); later studies question bond factor premia on cleaned data.
How it loses money: High-spread bonds fall the most in credit sell-offs, so it behaves like a leveraged bet on credit.
Key sources: Israel, Palhares & Richardson (2018); Dickerson, Mueller & Robotti (2023)

Also moves with: Arbitrage & Relative Value; Short Volatility & Insurance Selling
What to do: Buy bitcoin or ether (or a spot ETF) and sell the same amount of a dated futures contract priced above spot, locking in the premium, which shrinks to zero by expiry.
Why it pays: Trend-chasing leveraged buyers bid futures above spot, and the arbitrageurs who close the gap want paying for tying up margin and bearing crash risk.
Track record: Annualised futures premium at times above 40% a year in 2021 booms, near zero or negative in busts; BTC/ETH, gross of costs
How it loses money: A rally triggers margin calls on the short futures leg and forces an early exit, or the exchange or custodian fails.
Key sources: Schmeling, Schrimpf & Todorov (2023)

What to do: Hold a basket of foreign currencies against the US dollar when average foreign interest rates exceed US rates, and short it when they are below (dollar-index ETFs give a rough version).
Why it pays: Foreign rates exceed US rates mainly in US bad times, so you are paid for being short the dollar exactly when risk is high and the dollar can spike.
Track record: No reliable headline figure; authors report large excess returns with low correlation to standard carry, 1980s–2010 sample
How it loses money: It is one concentrated dollar bet, so a sharp flight-to-safety dollar rally hits the whole position at once.
Key sources: Lustig, Roussanov & Verdelhan (2014)

Strategy: Equity index carry (dividend yield minus interest rate)
What to do: Across country stock-index futures, buy those whose expected dividend yield most exceeds the local short-term interest rate and short those with the smallest gap, rebalancing monthly.
Why it pays: A big gap between dividend yield and local rates signals a higher risk premium, largely compensation for recession and crash risk in that market.
Track record: Positive but noisy long-short returns across developed-market index futures, late 1980s–2012 (Koijen et al.); no robust headline figure
How it loses money: High-carry markets can be cheap for good reason and fall further in global equity sell-offs.
Key sources: Koijen, Moskowitz, Pedersen & Vrugt (2018)

Strategy: FX global-imbalance strategy (debtor vs creditor currencies)
What to do: Using national external balance-sheet data, buy currencies of large net-debtor countries (especially those whose foreign debt is in their own currency) and sell currencies of large net-creditor countries.
Why it pays: Debtor-country currencies fall in global downturns, so holders demand extra return for bearing that risk, much like carry.
Track record: No reliable figure
How it loses money: Debtor currencies tend to crash together in global risk-off episodes, just like carry trades.
Key sources: Della Corte, Riddiough & Sarno (2016)

Also moves with: Arbitrage & Relative Value; Short Volatility & Insurance Selling
What to do: Buy a coin on the spot market and short the same amount of its perpetual future (a futures contract with no expiry date), collecting the 'funding' payments that longs pay shorts while the perp trades above spot.
Why it pays: Leveraged buyers pay up for long exposure in booms, and arbitrage money is scarce because exchanges demand margin and can liquidate positions.
Track record: Sharpe around 2 with retail fees (higher fee-free), BTC perp-vs-spot backtest c. 2019–2022; ignores exchange-failure risk; price gaps shrank over time
How it loses money: An exchange fails (as FTX did in 2022), funding turns negative, or a sharp rally forces margin calls on the short leg.
Key sources: He, Manela, Ross & von Wachter (2022); Schmeling, Schrimpf & Todorov (2023)

Also moves with: Size & Illiquidity; Short Volatility & Insurance Selling
What to do: Invest in private funds or exchange-listed business development companies (BDCs) that make floating-rate loans directly to mid-sized, often private-equity-owned firms, collecting above-market interest.
Why it pays: Lenders are paid for illiquidity and default risk in lending banks retreated from after 2008; net of fees, the extra yield roughly just covers that risk.
Track record: Positive alpha gross of fees but insignificant alpha net of fees vs stock and bond benchmarks; 532 private debt funds, 1992–2015 vintages
How it loses money: A recession brings defaults among highly levered borrowers, while model-based valuations hide losses and lockups block exit.
Key sources: Erel, Flanagan & Weisbach (2024)

What to do: Buy exchange-traded futures on the next 1–5 years of index dividends (e.g. Euro Stoxx 50 dividend futures), betting they are priced below the dividends companies will actually pay.
Why it pays: Banks selling structured products end up long dividends and hedge by selling dividend futures, pushing prices down; buyers also bear dividend-cut risk in recessions.
Track record: Option-implied S&P 500 short-term dividend claims beat the index, 1996–2009 (van Binsbergen et al.); later work disputes size and robustness
How it loses money: Recessions bring deep dividend cuts (2008–09, 2020), causing large losses on dividend futures.
Key sources: van Binsbergen, Brandt & Koijen (2012); van Binsbergen, Hueskes, Koijen & Vrugt (2013); Bansal, Miller, Song & Yaron (2021)

Strategy: Short-rate futures risk premium (fed funds / SOFR futures)
What to do: Buy fed funds or SOFR futures, which profit if policy rates end up lower than the market priced, and buy more when economic indicators suggest a large built-in risk premium.
Why it pays: Futures prices carry a risk premium that grows in bad times, and markets kept over-predicting rates during the long 1980s–2010s decline.
Track record: No reliable strategy figure; futures-implied rates averaged above later-realised fed funds rates, US late 1980s–2000s.
How it loses money: Surprise hiking cycles, as in 1994 and 2022, produce large losses.
Key sources: Piazzesi & Swanson (2008); Gürkaynak, Sack & Swanson (2007); Cieslak (2018)

What to do: Lock up proof-of-stake coins (e.g., ether) to help secure the network, or lend coins or stablecoins on platforms such as Aave or Compound, and collect the interest-like yield.
Why it pays: Networks pay stakers new coins (diluting non-stakers) plus fees for security; borrowers pay interest for leverage, which rises when speculation is high.
Track record: ETH staking roughly 3–5% a year in ETH terms 2022–2025, falling as more ETH is staked, before price moves; DeFi lending rates swing widely
How it loses money: Coin price falls swamp the yield, and hacks, slashing penalties or lender collapses (e.g., Celsius in 2022) can wipe out principal.
Key sources: Gudgeon, Werner, Perez & Knottenbelt (2020); John, Rivera & Saleh (2021)

Also moves with: Value & Long-Term Reversal; Trend & Momentum; Macro & Asset Allocation
What to do: Using positions matched for rate sensitivity, buy short-term and short long-term bonds (a 'steepener') or do the reverse (a 'flattener'), picking the side with carry, value or momentum signals.
Why it pays: The extra return each maturity pays shifts across the curve and through the rate cycle, and these shifts are partly predictable.
Track record: No reliable figure; carry, value and momentum signals reported to predict slope returns across developed bond markets, mostly in working-paper backtests.
How it loses money: The curve reshapes the wrong way; US steepeners lost as the curve inverted to its deepest since the early 1980s in 2022–2023.
Key sources: Brooks & Moskowitz (2017); Campbell & Shiller (1991); Koijen, Moskowitz, Pedersen & Vrugt (2018)

Strategy: Variance risk premium harvesting (selling hedged index volatility)
What to do: Sell one-month index straddles (a call plus a put at the current price) and hedge out market direction with futures, profiting when actual volatility turns out lower than the volatility priced into the options.
Why it pays: Investors overpay for crash insurance, so option-implied volatility usually exceeds the volatility that follows; sellers are paid for bearing crash risk.
Markets: Equity indices & ETFs; Options & volatility; Bonds & rates; FX; Commodities
Track record: Zero-beta at-the-money S&P 500 straddles lost buyers ~3% per week on average (the sellers' gain) in an early-1990s sample, gross
How it loses money: Sudden volatility spikes (1987, 2008, 2020) can wipe out years of collected premium in days.
Key sources: Coval & Shumway (2001); Carr & Wu (2009); Fallon, Park & Yu (2015)

Strategy: Catastrophe bonds and insurance-linked securities (cat bonds / ILS)
What to do: Buy catastrophe bonds, or funds that hold them, which pay a high floating coupon but lose principal if a defined disaster such as a major US hurricane or earthquake strikes; hold to maturity.
Why it pays: Insurers pay well above expected disaster losses (about 2–3 times on average in past studies) to offload peak catastrophe risk that would strain their capital.
Track record: ~7%/yr total return (roughly 5 points over T-bills), Swiss Re Global Cat Bond Index 2002–2023, long-only, before fund fees
How it loses money: A mega-disaster or a cluster of storms wipes out principal on many bonds at once; heavy inflows also squeeze spreads.
Key sources: Froot (2001); Lane & Mahul (2008); Braun (2016)

What to do: Own the S&P 500 (or a stock) and each month sell a one-month call option at or slightly above the current price, collecting premium but giving up gains above that level.
Why it pays: Call buyers typically pay more than the options turn out to be worth (the volatility premium), and many investors value the steady 'income'.
Markets: Equity indices & ETFs; Stocks; Options & volatility
Track record: BXM earned roughly the S&P 500's return with about two-thirds the volatility, mid-1988 to 2001; it has lagged the S&P 500 since 2009, gross
How it loses money: Keeps nearly all crash losses while capping rebounds, so it lags in strong rallies and V-shaped recoveries.
Key sources: Whaley (2002); Hill, Balasubramanian, Gregory & Tierens (2006); Israelov & Nielsen (2015)

What to do: Sell options on an index and buy options on its member stocks, hedging out price moves, so you profit if the stocks move less in sync than the index option prices imply.
Why it pays: Index options carry a premium for correlation risk, because stocks start moving together in crashes exactly when diversification is needed most.
Markets: Equity indices & ETFs; Stocks; Options & volatility
Track record: High Sharpe ratios before costs from selling S&P 100 index options against member-stock options, 1996–2003
How it loses money: In crashes correlations jump toward 1, so the short index leg loses far more than the stock options gain.
Key sources: Driessen, Maenhout & Vilkov (2009); Buraschi, Kosowski & Trojani (2014)

Strategy: Selling short-dated vs long-dated volatility (calendar spreads)
What to do: Sell near-term index options (or one-month variance swaps) and buy longer-dated ones, keeping the volatility premium that sits mostly in the shortest maturities while hedging long-lasting volatility rises.
Why it pays: Investors pay most to hedge immediate turbulence, so short-dated volatility is the most overpriced while longer-dated volatility carries little premium.
Track record: Nearly all of the S&P 500 variance premium sits in maturities of a few months or less; longer-dated forward variance earned about zero (1990s–2010s)
How it loses money: A spike hits short-dated volatility hardest, so the short front leg loses more than the long back leg gains.
Key sources: Dew-Becker, Giglio, Le & Rodriguez (2017); Johnson (2017); Aït-Sahalia, Karaman & Mancini (2020)

Strategy: Short VIX futures / inverse-VIX funds (roll-yield harvesting)
What to do: Short front-month VIX futures (or hold an inverse-VIX fund) to profit as the futures, which usually trade above the spot VIX index, drift down toward it before expiry.
Why it pays: Investors pay up for VIX futures as crash hedges, so futures usually sit above the VIX level they converge to, and short sellers earn that gap.
Track record: Inverse-VIX note XIV gained strongly 2012-2017, then lost ~96% of its value on 5 Feb 2018 and was redeemed early; long 1-month VIX futures lost ~30%/yr, 2006-2013
How it loses money: A volatility spike can double VIX futures within days, causing near-total loss (Feb 2018, Mar 2020).
Key sources: Whaley (2013); Eraker & Wu (2017); Cheng (2019)

Strategy: Systematic index put writing (CBOE PUT index)
What to do: Each month, sell one-month S&P 500 put options struck at the current index level, hold enough cash in T-bills to buy the index if exercised, and keep the premium.
Why it pays: Index puts are persistently overpriced because institutions want downside protection, so put sellers earn an insurance premium on top of equity-like returns.
Track record: Higher risk-adjusted return than the S&P 500, mid-1986 to 2018, gross (Cboe-commissioned study); index implied vol averaged 19.3% vs 15.1% realized, 1990-2018
How it loses money: Loses nearly as much as stocks in crashes (e.g., 2008) and lags badly in strong bull markets.
Key sources: Ungar & Moran (2009); Bondarenko (2014; 2019 Cboe study); Ilmanen (2012)

What to do: Buy stocks that have fallen hardest when the market fell (high downside beta, negative co-skewness) and short those that held up, rebalancing monthly.
Why it pays: Investors dislike assets that crash together with the market, so crash-prone stocks should offer extra return to be held.
Track record: ~3.6%/yr co-skewness premium (Harvey–Siddique); ~6%/yr downside-beta premium (Ang–Chen–Xing), US, largely using same-period risk measures
How it loses money: Loses exactly in market crashes, and downside risk measured in advance, as a trader must, barely predicts returns.
Key sources: Harvey & Siddique (2000); Ang, Chen & Xing (2006); Levi & Welch (2020)

What to do: Buy the commodity futures whose daily returns over roughly the past year were most negatively skewed (rare crashes) and short those most positively skewed (rare spikes).
Why it pays: Investors overpay for lottery-like upside spikes, so positively skewed futures are overpriced and negatively skewed ones underpriced.
Track record: Roughly 8%/yr long-short before costs, 27 commodity futures, 1987–2014 (Fernandez-Perez et al.)
How it loses money: The long side holds crash-prone commodities, so a sudden supply glut or demand collapse hits hard.
Key sources: Fernandez-Perez, Frijns, Fuertes & Miffre (2018)

What to do: Sell bitcoin or ether options, e.g., covered calls or out-of-the-money puts on Deribit, collecting premiums because the volatility priced into options has usually exceeded the volatility that followed.
Why it pays: Buyers pay extra for leveraged upside and crash protection, so option prices carry a volatility risk premium.
Track record: No reliable net figure; Deribit-based studies find bitcoin implied volatility usually above later realized volatility since about 2019, with sharp exceptions
How it loses money: A sudden crash or volatility spike causes losses far larger than the premiums collected.
Key sources: Alexander & Imeraj (2021); Almeida, Grith, Miftachov & Wang (2024)

What to do: On betting exchanges or prediction markets like Kalshi, sell cheap longshot contracts (for example, buy NO when YES costs under 10¢) or buy heavy favourites, because longshots win less often than their prices imply.
Why it pays: Bettors overweight small chances and enjoy lottery-like payoffs, so longshots are overpriced; bookmakers also shade longshot odds to protect against better-informed bettors.
Track record: US horse races 1992–2001: ~-5% on favourites vs ~-61% on 100-1+ longshots (both lose after the track's cut); Kalshi sub-10¢ contracts lost buyers heavily
How it loses money: Fees or the track's cut can exceed the edge, and a rare longshot win wipes out many small gains.
Key sources: Thaler & Ziemba (1988); Snowberg & Wolfers (2010); Bürgi, Deng & Whelan (2025)

What to do: Sell options on interest rates (swaptions or Treasury-futures options) while hedging out the rate direction, collecting implied volatility that usually exceeds the volatility that actually occurs.
Why it pays: Mortgage investors, banks and other hedgers pay for protection against rate swings, so option sellers earn an insurance premium.
Track record: No reliable figure; implied interest-rate volatility has on average exceeded realised volatility in US Treasury and swaption markets.
How it loses money: Sudden rate shocks, like 2022 or the March 2023 bank failures, cause losses far larger than premiums collected.
Key sources: Duarte, Longstaff & Yu (2007); Choi, Mueller & Vedolin (2017)

What to do: Sell S&P 500 options that expire the same day, often as strangles or iron condors (sold calls and puts away from the current price), and collect the premium as it decays within hours.
Why it pays: Very short-dated options carry a high price per unit of time because buyers pay for sudden jumps and lottery-like payoffs.
Track record: No reliable figure; 0DTE trading surged only from 2022, so evidence covers a few years; retail traders lost money on net
How it loses money: One sharp intraday move can cost many days of premium; spreads and fees eat thin margins.
Key sources: Andersen, Fusari & Todorov (2017); Bandi, Fusari & Renò (2023); Beckmeyer, Branger & Gayda (2023)

What to do: Short equal dollar amounts of a 3x bull and a 3x bear ETF on the same index, profiting as their daily rebalancing makes both lose value in choppy markets.
Why it pays: Daily-reset leveraged funds suffer volatility drag, so over time both bull and bear versions trail their stated multiple of the index.
Track record: No reliable figure; the decay is mathematical, but borrow fees and strong trends often absorb the profit
How it loses money: A strong one-way trend makes one shorted leg soar; hard-to-borrow fees and share recalls add cost.
Key sources: Cheng & Madhavan (2009); Avellaneda & Zhang (2010)

What to do: Sell out-of-the-money index puts, buy out-of-the-money calls (a 'risk reversal') and hedge the market exposure with futures, betting that crash protection is overpriced relative to upside calls.
Why it pays: Hedgers' heavy demand for downside puts pushes their prices above fair value, and dealers need compensation for holding that crash exposure.
Track record: No reliable standalone figure; the skew premium is large but largely overlaps the ordinary variance premium (S&P 500 options)
How it loses money: A crash makes the sold puts explode in value while the bought calls expire worthless.
Key sources: Bollen & Whaley (2004); Garleanu, Pedersen & Poteshman (2009); Kozhan, Neuberger & Schneider (2013)

Strategy: VIX term-structure timing (VIX futures basis strategy)
What to do: Short VIX futures only when they trade well above the spot VIX (a steep 'contango'), stay out or go long when they trade below it, and hedge with S&P 500 futures.
Why it pays: The gap between VIX futures and spot VIX mostly reflects a risk premium the futures lose as they converge, not an accurate forecast of where VIX is heading.
Track record: Profitable with S&P 500 futures hedging, VIX futures mid-2000s to 2011, in-sample, before costs
How it loses money: Contango can persist right up to a spike, so the signal reacts too late in sudden shocks like Feb 2018.
Key sources: Simon & Campasano (2014); Johnson (2017); Cheng (2019)

What to do: Deposit a pair of tokens into a decentralized exchange pool (e.g., Uniswap) and earn trading fees, while arbitrageurs trade against your pool whenever outside prices move.
Why it pays: Fees are meant to compensate for 'loss-versus-rebalancing' (being picked off at stale prices by faster arbitrageurs); you only profit when fees exceed it.
Track record: Uniswap v3, 17 pools, first months after 2021 launch: $199M fees vs $260M impermanent loss; about half of LPs did worse than just holding
How it loses money: Big price moves let arbitrageurs drain value faster than fees accrue, and smart-contract hacks can wipe out the pool.
Key sources: Loesch, Hindman, Richardson & Welch (2021); Milionis, Moallemi, Roughgarden & Zhang (2022); Heimbach, Schertenleib & Wattenhofer (2022)

What to do: Buy the stocks with the highest gross profit (sales minus cost of goods sold) relative to total assets, short the lowest, and rebalance yearly.
Why it pays: Gross profit is a clean measure of a firm's productivity, and markets underprice profitable firms that don't look cheap on book value.
Track record: ~0.3%/month long-short (value-weighted), US 1963–2010 (gross); also works in international developed markets
How it loses money: Profitable firms are often expensive, and the strategy lags in junk rallies when unprofitable stocks surge.
Key sources: Novy-Marx (2013); Jensen, Kelly & Pedersen (2023)

What to do: Hold the stocks with the lowest volatility or beta (how much a stock moves with the market) over the past 1–3 years, or a minimum-variance mix, long-only and rebalanced quarterly to yearly.
Why it pays: Investors who can't borrow, and fund managers judged against benchmarks, overpay for risky stocks, leaving safe stocks underpriced for their risk.
Track record: ~12%/yr alpha gap between lowest- and highest-volatility deciles, global developed large caps 1986–2006 (gross)
How it loses money: Lags in strong bull markets and junk rallies, and its bond-like stocks suffer when interest rates jump.
Key sources: Haugen & Heins (1975); Blitz & van Vliet (2007); Baker, Bradley & Wurgler (2011)

Strategy: Operating and cash-based profitability (RMW, ROE factor)
What to do: Buy the stocks with the highest operating or cash-based profits relative to book equity or assets, or with high recent return on equity, and short the least profitable.
Why it pays: Investors underreact to how persistent high profitability is, so highly profitable firms keep beating the expectations built into their prices.
Track record: RMW factor earned a positive, significant long-short premium, US July 1963–2013 (gross); cash-based operating profitability predicted returns better than accrual-based versions
How it loses money: Junk rallies, and results depend on the exact profit definition used.
Key sources: Fama & French (2015); Ball, Gerakos, Linnainmaa & Nikolaev (2016); Hou, Xue & Zhang (2015)

What to do: Score stocks on profitability, profit growth, safety (low leverage and volatility) and payouts; buy the high-quality stocks, short the low-quality 'junk', and rebalance monthly.
Why it pays: Investors don't pay enough extra for safe, profitable, well-run firms, perhaps because they chase lottery-like junk stocks.
Track record: No reliable single figure; significant risk-adjusted long-short returns in the US and 24 other countries (gross)
How it loses money: Lags in speculative junk rallies, such as 2009 and late 2020–21, when risky, unprofitable stocks surge.
Key sources: Asness, Frazzini & Pedersen (2019); Jensen, Kelly & Pedersen (2023)
