What to do: Buy firms whose earnings are mostly backed by cash (low accruals) and short firms whose earnings come mainly from accruals, i.e. non-cash accounting adjustments.
Why it pays: Investors fixate on headline earnings and miss that accrual-driven earnings persist less than cash earnings.
Track record: ~10.4% size-adjusted hedge return in the year after formation, US 1962–1991 (gross); hedge returns no longer reliably positive in later US data
How it loses money: The US edge has largely faded since hedge funds piled in, so costs can wipe out what remains.
Key sources: Sloan (1996); Green, Hand & Soliman (2011); Ball, Gerakos, Linnainmaa & Nikolaev (2016)

What to do: Each month, rank stocks by how much analysts disagree about next year's earnings, short or avoid the most-disputed fifth and buy the least-disputed fifth.
Why it pays: When opinions differ and shorting is hard, prices reflect the optimists' views, so high-disagreement stocks end up overpriced.
Track record: ~9.5%/yr, low- minus high-dispersion quintile, US stocks 1983–2000 (gross), concentrated in small, past-loser stocks
How it loses money: Profits come mostly from small, illiquid losers and have weakened since publication.
Key sources: Diether, Malloy & Scherbina (2002); Johnson (2004)

What to do: Each month, average each stock's ranks across many known anomalies (11 or more signals) into one mispricing score, buy the most underpriced and short the most overpriced.
Why it pays: Combining signals averages out noise, and most profit comes from overpriced stocks that short-selling limits protect.
Track record: No reliable single figure; composites beat single anomalies, with gains mainly from the short side, especially after high investor sentiment (US, several decades)
How it loses money: The short side is costly and crowded, and anomaly returns shrank after publication and fall together in junk rallies.
Key sources: Stambaugh, Yu & Yuan (2012); Stambaugh & Yuan (2017); Jensen, Kelly & Pedersen (2023)

What to do: Each month, buy low-beta (less market-sensitive) stocks levered up to a beta of one and short high-beta stocks scaled down to a beta of one, so the portfolio is market-neutral.
Why it pays: Investors who cannot or will not borrow buy high-beta stocks to get more return, bidding them up and flattening the risk–return link.
Track record: Sharpe ratio ~0.78, rank-weighted US BAB factor 1926–2012 (gross); much weaker when value-weighted and after costs
How it loses money: Leverage magnifies losses when high-beta junk rallies or funding costs spike, and much of the return comes from small, costly stocks.
Key sources: Black, Jensen & Scholes (1972); Frazzini & Pedersen (2014); Novy-Marx & Velikov (2022)

Strategy: Employee satisfaction ('Best Companies to Work For')
What to do: Each year, buy the listed firms on the '100 Best Companies to Work For in America' list, or those with improving online employee ratings, and hold for a year.
Why it pays: Markets undervalue intangibles like a motivated workforce, so the payoff arrives later as better-than-expected earnings.
Track record: ~3.5%/yr four-factor alpha (~2.1%/yr vs industry peers), long-only Best Companies portfolio, US 1984–2009 (gross)
How it loses money: Small, concentrated portfolio whose edge is little tested since 2011 and absent where labour laws are rigid.
Key sources: Edmans (2011); Green, Huang, Wen & Zhou (2019); Edmans, Li & Zhang (2014, NBER working paper)

What to do: Estimate each firm's bankruptcy risk (e.g. Campbell-Hilscher-Szilagyi model, Ohlson O-score, Altman Z-score), buy the safest stocks, and short or avoid the most distressed.
Why it pays: Investors overpay for lottery-like near-bankrupt stocks, and shorting and illiquidity costs stop arbitrageurs from correcting it.
Track record: No reliable figure; the most distressed US stocks earned anomalously low returns after 1981
How it loses money: Junk rallies after crises (e.g. 2009), when the most distressed stocks soar, plus short squeezes.
Key sources: Dichev (1998); Griffin & Lemmon (2002); Campbell, Hilscher & Szilagyi (2008)

What to do: Each month, rank stocks by last month's stock-specific daily volatility (moves not explained by the market, size or value), buy the calmest fifth and short the most erratic fifth.
Why it pays: Lottery-seeking investors bid up erratic stocks, and the cost and risk of short-selling stop professionals from correcting the overpricing.
Track record: ~1.06%/month raw, low- minus high-volatility quintile (value-weighted), US 1963–2000; ~1.31%/month factor-adjusted, 23 developed markets (gross)
How it loses money: Loses heavily in speculative rallies of small volatile stocks, and results are sensitive to weighting and stock-universe choices.
Key sources: Ang, Hodrick, Xing & Zhang (2006); Ang, Hodrick, Xing & Zhang (2009); Bali & Cakici (2008)

What to do: Each month, rank stocks by their biggest one-day gain over the past month, short or avoid the top tenth (biggest spikes) and buy the bottom tenth.
Why it pays: Investors overpay for stocks that look like lottery tickets, so stocks with recent extreme jumps are overpriced and later underperform.
Track record: >1%/month, lowest- minus highest-MAX decile, raw and risk-adjusted, US stocks 1962–2005 (gross)
How it loses money: Overlaps heavily with idiosyncratic volatility, loses in speculative frenzies, and its short side is small, hard-to-borrow stocks.
Key sources: Kumar (2009); Bali, Cakici & Whitelaw (2011); Bali, Brown, Murray & Tang (2017)

Strategy: Low-risk / defensive bonds (credit and Treasury betting-against-beta)
What to do: Favour short-maturity, high-quality bonds (low-leverage, profitable issuers) over long or risky ones, using leverage so both sides carry similar risk.
Why it pays: Investors who cannot borrow reach for yield in long and risky bonds and bid them up, so safer bonds earn more per unit of risk.
Track record: Treasury BAB (long short-maturity, short long-maturity, US 1952–2012) Sharpe ~0.8 gross; credit BAB Sharpe ~0.9; defensive corporate bond factors positive alphas
How it loses money: Needs leverage, and lags badly when long bonds and risky credit rally strongly.
Key sources: Frazzini & Pedersen (2014); Houweling & van Zundert (2017); Israel, Palhares & Richardson (2018)

What to do: Avoid or short instruments with built-in leverage, such as leveraged ETFs and cheap out-of-the-money options, and hold the unlevered underlying asset instead, rebalancing monthly.
Why it pays: Investors who can't or won't borrow pay up for built-in leverage, so those instruments earn low returns for their risk.
Track record: No reliable figure; the authors find high-embedded-leverage options and leveraged ETFs earn lower risk-adjusted returns (gross)
How it loses money: Shorting options or leveraged ETFs can lose heavily in sharp moves, and borrowing fees and spreads eat the edge.
Key sources: Frazzini & Pedersen (2022)

Strategy: Betting against beta across futures markets
What to do: Within equity-index, government-bond, commodity and currency futures, buy low-beta contracts levered up and short high-beta ones so the portfolio is market-neutral, rebalancing monthly.
Why it pays: The borrowing limits that flatten the risk–return trade-off in stocks appear to operate in other markets too.
Markets: Equity indices & ETFs; Bonds & rates; Commodities; FX
Track record: No reliable single figure; positive in most asset classes tested but statistically insignificant in some (Frazzini–Pedersen, gross)
How it loses money: Needs leverage and futures access, and funding stress or a high-beta rally can wipe out gains.
Key sources: Asness, Frazzini & Pedersen (2012); Ilmanen (2012); Frazzini & Pedersen (2014)

What to do: Within groups of stocks with similar volatility, buy those least correlated with the market and short the most correlated, levered to be market-neutral and rebalanced monthly.
Why it pays: If borrowing limits drive the low-risk effect, stocks that move tightly with the market are overpriced even when their own volatility is ordinary.
Track record: No reliable figure; the authors report significant positive risk-adjusted returns in US and international stocks (gross), with little independent testing
How it loses money: Shares BAB's leverage and junk-rally risk, and profits may shrink after trading costs.
Key sources: Asness, Frazzini, Gormsen & Pedersen (2020)

What to do: Count each firm's anti-takeover provisions (poison pills, staggered boards, golden parachutes); buy firms with the fewest (strong shareholder rights), short those with the most, and hold for years.
Why it pays: Investors were slow to price the cost of entrenched managers, so poorly governed firms kept disappointing until the market learned this by the early 2000s.
Track record: ~8.5%/yr alpha, long 'Democracy' (G≤5) vs short 'Dictatorship' (G≥14) firms, US large caps 1990–1999, gross; roughly zero 2000–2008
How it loses money: The edge vanished after 1999, and earlier gains may partly reflect accidental industry bets rather than governance itself.
Key sources: Gompers, Ishii & Metrick (2003); Bebchuk, Cohen & Ferrell (2009); Bebchuk, Cohen & Wang (2013)

What to do: Buy an ETF or basket of companies that have raised their dividend every year for a long stretch (25+ years for the S&P 500 Dividend Aristocrats, 10+ for VIG's index) and hold.
Why it pays: Long dividend-raising records pick profitable, stable, low-volatility firms, so returns mostly reflect quality and low-risk premiums, not the dividends themselves.
Track record: S&P 500 Dividend Aristocrats roughly matched the S&P 500 (~10%/yr) with somewhat lower volatility, May 2005–early 2025, index total return before fees.
How it loses money: Lags in growth-led bull markets because it holds little tech, trailing the S&P 500 by roughly 3 points a year over the past decade.
Key sources: Grullon, Michaely & Swaminathan (2002); Hartzmark & Solomon (2019); Asness, Frazzini & Pedersen (2019)

What to do: Screen out or short stocks with high Beneish M-scores, a formula combining eight accounting ratios that flags likely earnings manipulation.
Why it pays: Firms showing manipulation red flags tend to disappoint when the accounting reverses or is exposed, and investors underweight those red flags.
Track record: No reliable figure
How it loses money: Many false positives, flagged stocks are costly to short, and there are few independent out-of-sample tests.
Key sources: Beneish (1999); Beneish, Lee & Nichols (2013)

What to do: Each year, buy firms that produce the most patents or patent citations per dollar of past R&D spending and short the least efficient innovators.
Why it pays: Investors find innovation output hard to judge and underreact to a firm's proven ability to turn R&D into patents.
Track record: No reliable figure
How it loses money: Patent data arrive with long delays, and the evidence rests on a few US studies that may be data-mined.
Key sources: Hirshleifer, Hsu & Li (2013); Cohen, Diether & Malloy (2013)

What to do: Among expensive 'growth' stocks, score eight yes/no signals (profitability, cash flow, stability of earnings and sales growth, R&D, capex and advertising intensity); buy high scorers, short low scorers.
Why it pays: Investors over-extrapolate growth stories, so growth firms whose fundamentals don't back up the hype later disappoint.
Track record: Significant long-short excess returns, mostly from the short side, US low book-to-market stocks 1979–1999 (gross)
How it loses money: Profits come mainly from shorting small growth stocks, which is costly and dangerous in bubbles.
Key sources: Mohanram (2005)

What to do: Hold shares of alcohol, tobacco and gambling companies, which many ethical and institutional investors shun, for the long term.
Why it pays: Norm-bound institutions avoid sin stocks, keeping their prices low and expected returns higher for willing holders.
Track record: Beat comparable stocks by a few %/yr, US 1926–2006 (gross); later largely explained by their high profitability and low investment
How it loses money: Regulation, lawsuits and shrinking demand can hurt, and little edge remains once quality factors are accounted for.
Key sources: Fabozzi, Ma & Oliphant (2008); Hong & Kacperczyk (2009); Blitz & Fabozzi (2017)

What to do: Each week, rank stocks by how lopsided (skewed toward big upside jumps) their recent daily returns are, buy the least skewed and short the most skewed.
Why it pays: Investors who love long-shot payoffs overpay for stocks prone to big upside jumps, which lowers their future returns.
Track record: ~0.19%/week, low- minus high-realised-skewness decile, US stocks 1993–2013 (gross)
How it loses money: Skewness is noisy to measure, overlaps with size and volatility, and weekly trading costs eat much of the gain.
Key sources: Boyer, Mitton & Vorkink (2010); Conrad, Dittmar & Ghysels (2013); Amaya, Christoffersen, Jacobs & Vasquez (2015)

Also moves with: Carry & Yield; Short Volatility & Insurance Selling
What to do: Overweight corporate bonds that trade rarely or come from small issuers, and underweight heavily traded bonds of large issuers, holding for months to collect the extra yield.
Why it pays: Investors demand extra return for bonds that are costly or slow to sell, especially when market liquidity dries up.
Track record: No reliable net figure; more illiquid and smaller-issuer US corporate bonds show higher yields/gross returns in studies of roughly the 1990s-2010s; net-of-cost profits uncertain
How it loses money: Illiquid bonds fall hardest and become hard to sell in crises like 2008 and March 2020.
Key sources: Bao, Pan & Wang (2011); Lin, Wang & Wu (2011); Houweling & van Zundert (2017)

What to do: Rank stocks by how much their price moves per dollar traded (the Amihud illiquidity measure), hold the most illiquid and avoid or short the most liquid, rebalancing yearly.
Why it pays: Investors demand extra return for stocks that are costly and slow to trade, especially in sell-offs.
Track record: Significant illiquid-minus-liquid premium across 45 countries 1990-2011 (gross; ~0.7%/month developed, ~1.3% emerging); US premium has shrunk, now mostly in tiny stocks
How it loses money: Trading costs can eat most of the premium, and illiquid stocks crash and become hard to sell in liquidity crises.
Key sources: Amihud (2002); Amihud, Hameed, Kang & Zhang (2015); Ben-Rephael, Kadan & Wohl (2015)

What to do: Hold small companies that are also profitable, stable and financially safe (e.g. a small-cap index that requires positive earnings) and avoid small loss-making 'junk' firms.
Why it pays: Small junk stocks drag down the raw size premium; removing them reveals a premium for the risk and illiquidity of small, sound firms.
Track record: No reliable single figure; controlling for junk restored a significant size premium in the US and 24 international markets in the authors' tests (gross)
How it loses money: Small caps can lag mega-caps for years, as since 2018, and results depend on one group's definition of quality.
Key sources: Asness, Frazzini, Israel, Moskowitz & Pedersen (2018); Hou & van Dijk (2019)

What to do: Buy the smallest coins by market value (above a minimum size, e.g., $1m) and short or underweight the largest, rebalancing weekly.
Why it pays: Compensation for the illiquidity and the high crash, delisting and failure risk of tiny coins, which are also hard to short.
Track record: No reliable net figure; large gross weekly long-short returns 2014–2018, driven by tiny, illiquid coins
How it loses money: Small coins can collapse to zero, get delisted or be untradeable in size, and the short side is rarely available.
Key sources: Liu, Tsyvinski & Wu (2022); Shen, Urquhart & Wang (2020)

What to do: Each year, buy the stocks whose returns have fallen most when market-wide liquidity dried up and short the least sensitive.
Why it pays: Stocks that lose value exactly when the whole market becomes hard to trade are unattractive, so they must offer higher returns.
Track record: ~7.5%/yr risk-adjusted, high- minus low-liquidity-sensitivity stocks, US 1966–1999 (gross); later replications find it weak and construction-sensitive
How it loses money: Loses in liquidity crises by design, and results swing a lot depending on how liquidity sensitivity is estimated.
Key sources: Pastor & Stambaugh (2003); Acharya & Pedersen (2005); Li, Novy-Marx & Velikov (2019)

Strategy: Private equity buyout funds (private-market illiquidity premium)
What to do: Commit capital for about 10 years to buyout funds that buy whole companies with heavy borrowing, expecting returns above public stocks as a reward for locking money up.
Why it pays: Said to pay for illiquidity and operational improvements; critics show returns resemble small cheap stocks plus leverage, with appraisal-smoothed valuations.
Track record: ~3%/yr above S&P 500 net of fees, US buyout funds 1984–2008 vintages; roughly matched public stocks (~11%/yr) 2006–2019
How it loses money: Fees of several percent a year and smoothed valuations hide levered equity losses, and money stays locked up when you need it.
Key sources: Harris, Jenkinson & Kaplan (2014); Phalippou (2020); Stafford (2022)

What to do: Hold the smallest listed companies by market value (e.g. the bottom 10–20%) instead of large caps, rebalancing yearly.
Why it pays: Small firms are riskier, less liquid and less researched, so investors demand a higher return to hold them.
Track record: SMB (small minus big) ~0.2%/month (~2%/yr), US 1926–2020s (gross); near zero since the early 1980s
How it loses money: Can lag large caps for decades; outside microcaps and Januarys the US premium has been near zero since the 1980s.
Key sources: Banz (1981); Horowitz, Loughran & Savin (2000); Alquist, Israel & Moskowitz (2018)

What to do: Commit money for 10+ years to funds that buy stakes in young private start-ups, betting that a few huge winners repay the many failures and beat public stocks.
Why it pays: Pays for illiquidity and extreme risk; top firms' networks and deal access give persistent edges, but those funds rarely admit new investors.
Track record: US VC funds beat public stocks for 1990s vintages but trailed them for 2000s vintages, net of fees (Harris-Jenkinson-Kaplan, Burgiss data)
How it loses money: Returns hinge on rare giant winners; the average or late-to-the-boom fund can lag public stocks for a decade while money is locked up.
Key sources: Kaplan & Schoar (2005); Harris, Jenkinson & Kaplan (2014); Harris, Jenkinson, Kaplan & Stucke (2023)

What to do: Pick related stocks whose price spread statistically returns to a long-run level (cointegrated); when the spread strays about two standard deviations, buy the cheap leg, short the rich leg, and exit when it reverts.
Why it pays: Economically linked firms share fundamentals, so spread gaps caused by temporary order flow tend to close.
Track record: ~0.85%/month before costs, ~0.33% after (copula version 0.43% / 0.05%), US stocks 1962–2014
How it loses money: The statistical link found in past data breaks (merger, business change), so the spread trends away instead of reverting.
Key sources: Vidyamurthy (2004); Rad, Low & Faff (2016); Krauss (2017)

What to do: Find stock pairs whose prices tracked each other most closely over the past year; when a pair drifts about two standard deviations apart, buy the laggard, short the leader, and exit when they reconverge or after six months.
Why it pays: You absorb temporary, non-news buying or selling in one of two close substitutes, and bear the risk that the gap is really news.
Track record: Up to ~11%/yr excess (top pairs, self-financing), US 1962–2002; much smaller and cost-sensitive since the 1990s
How it loses money: The gap keeps widening because one firm's fundamentals truly changed, e.g. a takeover, fraud or industry shock.
Key sources: Gatev, Goetzmann & Rouwenhorst (2006); Do & Faff (2010); Jacobs & Weber (2015)

What to do: Each day, strip out each stock's market, sector and factor moves (using principal components or sector ETFs), then buy stocks whose leftover price is unusually low and short unusually high ones, holding a few days.
Why it pays: Stock-specific moves driven by temporary order flow rather than news tend to revert; the strategy is paid as a liquidity provider.
Track record: Sharpe ~1.44 after assumed ~10bp round-trip costs, US stocks 1997–2007; only ~0.9 in 2003–2007
How it loses money: Crowded deleveraging, as in August 2007, when many quant funds dump the same positions at once.
Key sources: Avellaneda & Lee (2010); Khandani & Lo (2011)

Strategy: Implied-vs-actual volatility gap in stock options (Goyal-Saretto) and related option sorts
What to do: Each month, buy straddles (call plus put) on stocks whose option-implied volatility is far below their recent actual volatility, sell straddles where it is far above, and hedge out stock-price moves.
Why it pays: Option prices overreact to recent volatility and investor demand, and implied volatility tends to snap back toward actual volatility.
Track record: ~22% per month on straddle premium (not total capital), long-short, US stock options 1996–2006, gross; quoted bid-ask spreads absorb much of it
How it loses money: Option bid-ask spreads and hedging costs can erase profits; short legs suffer in market-wide volatility spikes.
Key sources: Goyal & Saretto (2009); Cao & Han (2013); Vasquez (2017)

What to do: Each month, buy stocks that fell most compared with their industry (or with what a market-size-value model predicted) and short those that rose most compared with it.
Why it pays: Removing industry and factor moves isolates temporary non-news price pressure, which reverses, while industry-wide moves tend to persist.
Track record: No reliable figure; residual reversal had about twice the risk-adjusted return of plain one-month reversal in US tests and stayed profitable after costs in large caps post-1990
How it loses money: Stock-specific news drives the move so it doesn't reverse, and margins after trading costs are thin.
Key sources: Blitz, Huij, Lansdorp & Verbeek (2013); Da, Liu & Schaumburg (2014); Hameed & Mian (2015)

What to do: Feed dozens to hundreds of stock characteristics into a machine-learning model that forecasts next month's return, buy the top predicted tenth and short the bottom tenth.
Why it pays: Flexible models pick up interactions among known signals (momentum, reversal, liquidity, volatility) that simple rankings miss.
Track record: Out-of-sample long-short Sharpe above 1 (value-weighted), US 1987–2016 (gross); much smaller excluding microcaps and after costs
How it loses money: High turnover and reliance on tiny stocks mean costs can erase gains, and models may be overfitted.
Key sources: Gu, Kelly & Xiu (2020); Freyberger, Neuhierl & Weber (2020); Avramov, Cheng & Metzker (2023)

What to do: Each month, buy the stocks with the worst returns last month and short those with the best returns, holding for one month.
Why it pays: Temporary buying or selling pressure and bid-ask bounce push prices too far; reversal traders are paid for supplying liquidity.
Track record: ~2.5%/month extreme-decile long-short spread, US stocks 1934–1987, before trading costs
How it loses money: Trading costs eat most of the gross profit, and losers keep falling when the drop reflected real news.
Key sources: Jegadeesh (1990); de Groot, Huij & Zhou (2012)

Strategy: Weekly / daily stock reversal (contrarian stat arb)
What to do: Every day or week, buy stocks that just underperformed the market and short those that just outperformed, sizing each position by how far it moved, and hold for a few days.
Why it pays: Impatient traders push prices too far for a few days; contrarians are paid for absorbing that pressure, much like market makers.
Track record: Daily version ~1.4%/day in 1995 falling to ~0.13%/day by 2007, US stocks, before costs
How it loses money: Very high turnover lets costs dominate, and crowded unwinds like August 2007 cause sudden sharp losses.
Key sources: Lehmann (1990); Lo & MacKinlay (1990); Khandani & Lo (2007, 2011)

What to do: Each month, buy the corporate bonds that fell the most last month and sell those that rose the most, betting the moves were temporary price pressure.
Why it pays: Dealers and forced sellers push bond prices away from value briefly, and buyers are paid for supplying liquidity.
Track record: Large gross reversal profits in US corporate bonds, but much likely reflects bid-ask bounce and trading costs; no reliable net figure.
How it loses money: Trading costs on illiquid bonds eat the edge, and in crises recent losers keep falling.
Key sources: Chordia, Goyal, Nozawa, Subrahmanyam & Tong (2017); Bai, Bali & Wen (2019)

Strategy: Crack and crush spread mean reversion
What to do: Trade the margin between a raw commodity and its products (crude oil vs gasoline/heating oil, soybeans vs meal/oil), buying the spread when unusually narrow and selling when unusually wide.
Why it pays: Refiners and processors raise or cut output as margins change, pulling margins back toward normal; seasonal demand adds predictable swings.
Track record: No reliable figure; profits shown mainly in 1980s–1990s samples and sensitive to costs and rule choice
How it loses money: Refinery outages, regulation or structural shifts can push margins to extremes and keep them there.
Key sources: Girma & Paulson (1999); Simon (1999); Dunis, Laws & Evans (2006)

What to do: Find coins whose prices have historically moved together (e.g., BTC and ETH, or a small basket); when the gap between them widens unusually, buy the cheap one and short the dear one until it narrows.
Why it pays: Temporary flow imbalances push related coins apart, and traders who bet on convergence are paid for supplying liquidity and bearing the risk the link breaks.
Track record: No reliable net figure; late-2010s backtests on a handful of major coins are short and highly sensitive to trading costs
How it loses money: The historical link breaks (one coin collapses, forks or is delisted) and the gap keeps widening.
Key sources: Leung & Nguyen (2019); Fischer, Krauss & Deinert (2019)

What to do: Each day or week, buy the smaller coins that fell the most and sell those that rose the most, betting on a snap-back; avoid the largest coins, which tend to keep trending instead.
Why it pays: Traders who absorb temporary selling pressure in illiquid coins are paid for providing liquidity.
Track record: No reliable net figure; daily reversal is concentrated in small, illiquid coins, where trading costs are highest
How it loses money: Falling coins keep falling or collapse, and wide bid-ask spreads wipe out the edge.
Key sources: Zaremba et al. (2021); Shen, Urquhart & Wang (2020)

What to do: Train random forests, boosted trees or neural nets on recent daily returns of S&P 500 stocks; each day buy the ~10 predicted winners and short the ~10 predicted losers.
Why it pays: The models mainly learn short-term reversal patterns, so they are paid for providing liquidity after temporary price moves.
Track record: ~0.45%/day before costs, S&P 500 stocks 1992–2015, fading to about zero after costs since ~2010
How it loses money: Daily turnover makes costs decisive, and the edge appears to have been competed away since about 2010.
Key sources: Krauss, Do & Huck (2017); Fischer & Krauss (2018)

Also moves with: Market Making & HFT; Calendar & Seasonal; Event-Driven
What to do: Read the exchange's published buy/sell imbalance before the opening or closing auction, submit offsetting orders (e.g., sell into excess buying), and unwind once the price pressure fades, often next morning.
Why it pays: Index funds and rebalancers must trade at the close regardless of price, so whoever absorbs that temporary pressure profits when prices revert.
Track record: No reliable net figure. US closing-auction price distortions largely reverse by the next day's open (2010s data).
How it loses money: The imbalance reflects real news or keeps growing, so prices don't revert and you carry an overnight loss.
Key sources: Cushing & Madhavan (2000); Bogousslavsky & Muravyev (2023)

Strategy: Short-term index dip-buying rules (e.g. Connors RSI(2))
What to do: Buy a stock index ETF or future after a short, sharp fall (e.g. 2-day RSI, a short-term overbought/oversold gauge, below 10) and sell after a few days' bounce.
Why it pays: Since 2000, index funds, futures and arbitrage trading have made daily index returns mildly mean-reverting, and dip buyers are paid for absorbing panicky selling.
Track record: No reliable net figure; daily index return autocorrelation flipped from positive (pre-1990s) to negative (2000s–2010s) across about 20 major indices
How it loses money: In a real crash dips keep dipping, so it buys repeatedly into a falling market; the edge flips if index returns start trending again.
Key sources: Lo & MacKinlay (1988); Connors & Alvarez (2008); Baltussen, van Bekkum & Da (2019)

Strategy: Support and resistance levels (round-number order clustering in FX)
What to do: Within the day, expect a currency to stall or bounce at widely published support/resistance levels (often round numbers) and to speed up once it breaks through them.
Why it pays: Traders bunch take-profit orders at round numbers, which causes bounces, and stop-loss orders just beyond them, which makes breakouts run.
Track record: Small but statistically significant power to predict where intraday trends stop, major FX pairs 1996–1998; no net-of-cost profit ever shown.
How it loses money: The effect is small next to spreads, and the levels are subjective, so most trades are noise.
Key sources: Osler (2000); Osler (2003); Menkhoff & Taylor (2007)

What to do: Run a short-term reversal strategy but make it bigger when market fear (the VIX index) is high and smaller when markets are calm.
Why it pays: When volatility spikes, market makers retreat and liquidity becomes scarce, so whoever supplies it earns unusually high compensation.
Track record: No reliable figure; in-sample, US reversal returns rose with the VIX and peaked in late 2008
How it loses money: In a real liquidity crisis prices keep falling before rebounding, while your own funding or risk limits get cut.
Key sources: Nagel (2012)

Strategy: Intraday mean reversion (fading big opening moves)
What to do: After a large jump or drop at the open in a stock-index future, bet that part of the move reverses before the close.
Why it pays: Overreaction and temporary order imbalances at the open are partly absorbed by liquidity providers within hours.
Track record: No reliable figure; reversals after big opens are statistically real in index futures but not profitable after costs
How it loses money: Trend days keep going (intraday momentum is also documented), and costs exceed the small average retracement.
Key sources: Fung, Mok & Lam (2000); Grant, Wolf & Yu (2005); Gao, Han, Li & Zhou (2018)

What to do: Back every outcome at different bookmakers when the best odds imply probabilities adding up to under 100%, or on Polymarket, Kalshi or PredictIt buy one contract on every outcome when the full set costs less than its guaranteed $1 payout.
Why it pays: Bookmakers sometimes post generous odds as loss leaders and update slowly, while prediction markets are fragmented, charge fees and cap positions, so prices don't add up.
Track record: Bookmaker-vs-exchange surebets in 19.2% of top-5 European league soccer matches; ~$40m arbitrage profit taken on Polymarket in 2024–25 (all traders combined)
How it loses money: Bookmakers void bets or limit winning accounts, odds move before every leg is placed, and fees or position caps erase thin margins.
Key sources: Franck, Verbeek & Nüesch (2013); Saguillo, Ghafouri, Kiffer & Suarez-Tangil (2025)

What to do: Lend money by buying an S&P 500 index 'box' (a bull call spread plus a bear put spread on the same strikes), which pays a fixed amount at expiry; box-spread ETFs now do this for you.
Why it pays: Box rates exceed Treasury yields because Treasuries carry a safety/convenience premium and option-based borrowers pay up for cheap leverage.
Track record: Box-implied rates averaged ~35–40 bp/yr above maturity-matched Treasury yields (larger below 3 months, ~4x in 2008), SPX options 2004–2018; narrower in recent years
How it loses money: The small extra yield can be lost to commissions, wide spreads or a mis-entered leg.
Key sources: van Binsbergen, Diamond & Grotteria (2022); St. Louis Fed, 'Are U.S. Treasuries Still Convenient?' (2025)

What to do: When a corporate bond's spread is above the company's CDS (credit insurance) spread, buy the bond and buy CDS protection, locking in the difference until it closes or the bond matures.
Why it pays: Cash bonds need funding and balance sheet while CDS do not, so bonds trade cheap when capital is scarce.
Track record: No reliable return figure; bonds traded several hundred basis points cheap to CDS in late 2008 before the gap largely closed.
How it loses money: Funding cuts force sales that widen the gap further, as in 2008.
Key sources: Garleanu & Pedersen (2011); Mitchell & Pulvino (2012); Bai & Collin-Dufresne (2019)

Also moves with: Sentiment, Flows & Alt Data; Value & Long-Term Reversal; Size & Illiquidity
What to do: Buy closed-end funds trading at unusually wide discounts to the value of their holdings (optionally hedging those holdings) and sell when the discount narrows.
Why it pays: Discounts swing with retail investor sentiment and are costly to arbitrage, so extreme discounts tend to shrink, faster when activists push for open-ending.
Markets: Equity indices & ETFs; Bonds & rates; Credit
Track record: Funds at ~20% discounts had ~6% higher next-12-month returns than undiscounted US funds (Pontiff 1995), gross; discounts often 5–20% and revert slowly
How it loses money: Discounts widen further in sell-offs as retail sentiment sours, and can persist for years without a catalyst.
Key sources: Thompson (1978); Lee, Shleifer & Thaler (1991); Pontiff (1995, 1996)

What to do: Buy convertible bonds, which are often cheap when newly issued, and short the issuer's stock as a hedge, collecting the coupon and the bond's discount while staying roughly market-neutral.
Why it pays: Issuers sell convertibles at a discount to raise money quickly, and arbitrageurs are paid for supplying capital and holding illiquid bonds.
Track record: Steady positive hedge-fund index returns in the 1990s–2000s (net of fees), then losses of roughly a third in 2008.
How it loses money: Forced selling by crowded, leveraged funds hits as credit spreads blow out (2005, 2008).
Key sources: Mitchell, Pedersen & Pulvino (2007); Choi, Getmansky & Tookes (2009); Agarwal, Fung, Loon & Naik (2011)

What to do: Borrow dollars, swap them into yen or euros with an FX forward, and invest in safe local bills, earning the gap by which the hedged foreign yield beats dollar borrowing costs.
Why it pays: Since 2008, bank capital rules make balance sheet costly, so banks no longer close these gaps and those who can still do it get paid.
Track record: Average absolute G10 basis ~24 bp (3-month) and ~27 bp (5-year) a year, 2010–2016, before balance-sheet costs; larger for yen (5-yr near -90 bp end-2015) and at quarter-ends
How it loses money: In dollar-funding crunches (e.g. March 2020) the gap widens sharply, forcing mark-to-market losses or costly early unwinds.
Key sources: Du, Tepper & Verdelhan (2018); Borio, McCauley, McGuire & Sushko (2016); Avdjiev, Du, Koch & Shin (2019)

What to do: Buy a cryptocurrency on the exchange where it is cheaper and at the same time sell it where it is dearer, then move coins or cash to rebalance between exchanges.
Why it pays: Slow transfers, capital controls and counterparty risk across fragmented exchanges stop arbitrageurs closing price gaps, especially between countries.
Track record: At least ~$2bn of estimated gross arbitrage profit across exchanges, Dec 2017–Feb 2018; gaps largest across countries (e.g., South Korea).
How it loses money: An exchange freezes withdrawals or fails (e.g., FTX in 2022), transfers lag while prices move, or capital controls trap your money.
Key sources: Makarov & Schoar (2020); Crépellière, Pelster & Zeisberger (2023)

What to do: Run bots that, inside one blockchain transaction, buy a token on one decentralized exchange and sell it on another, or liquidate risky loans for a bonus, paying fees for priority (excludes predatory 'sandwich' attacks).
Why it pays: Public blockchains leave exchange prices stale and expose pending trades, and only the fastest, best-connected bots can capture the gap.
Track record: ~$540M extracted by bots (arbitrage, liquidations, sandwiches) on Ethereum over 32 months to Aug 2021, gross; now largely bid away to validators
How it loses money: Priority-fee bidding wars and failed transactions eat profits, and code bugs can be exploited by rival bots.
Key sources: Daian et al. (2020); Qin, Zhou & Gervais (2022); Weintraub et al. (2022)

What to do: When two share lines with fixed claims on the same company's profits (e.g. Royal Dutch vs Shell, or two share classes) drift from their fixed ratio, buy the cheaper and short the dearer.
Why it pays: Different home investors, index memberships and local sentiment push the twins apart, and nothing forces them back, so arbitrageurs earn a risk premium.
Track record: Up to ~10%/yr abnormal return but with multi-year drawdowns, 12 dual-listed companies 1980–2002
How it loses money: The gap can widen for years before closing; LTCM lost heavily on Royal Dutch/Shell in 1998.
Key sources: Rosenthal & Young (1990); Froot & Dabora (1999); De Jong, Rosenthal & van Dijk (2009)

Strategy: ETF market making and authorised-participant (create/redeem) arbitrage
What to do: Quote ETF shares all day, hedging with the holdings or futures; when the ETF trades above (below) its holdings' value, sell (buy) it and create (redeem) fund shares.
Why it pays: Only authorised participants (approved dealers) can create or redeem ETF shares cheaply at scale, so they are paid to keep ETF prices in line with holdings.
Markets: Equity indices & ETFs; Bonds & rates; Credit
Track record: No reliable figure. Gaps are tiny in big US stock ETFs, but large bond ETFs hit roughly 5% discounts to their holdings in March 2020.
How it loses money: In a crisis the underlying assets (e.g., corporate bonds) become hard to trade, leaving positions you can't hedge or sell at fair value.
Key sources: Ben-David, Franzoni & Moussawi (2018); Petajisto (2017); Haddad, Moreira & Muir (2021)

What to do: When a stock-index future trades away from fair value (index plus financing cost minus dividends), sell the rich side and buy the cheap side, e.g. short futures and buy the stocks.
Why it pays: Order-flow imbalances briefly push futures and the stock basket apart; arbitrageurs earn the gap for capital, speed and execution skill.
Track record: No reliable figure; 1980s S&P 500 futures mispricings were sizeable, today's gaps are tiny and speed-driven
How it loses money: Faster competitors leave little edge, and slippage across hundreds of stocks or dividend surprises erase the thin margin.
Key sources: MacKinlay & Ramaswamy (1988); Brennan & Schwartz (1990); Chung (1991)

What to do: When a commodity's futures price is far above its spot price (steep contango), buy the physical commodity, store it in tanks, warehouses or idle tankers, and sell futures to lock in the gap.
Why it pays: In gluts, owners of storage space and capital are paid to hold surplus inventory; the futures premium cannot stay above full storage and financing costs for long.
Track record: No reliable figure; profits are episodic (e.g. 2009 and 2020 oil gluts) and go mainly to owners of cheap storage
How it loses money: Storage, shipping or financing costs jump, space runs out, or delivery and quality problems eat the locked-in spread.
Key sources: Working (1949); Brennan (1958); Fama & French (1987)

What to do: Buy SPAC shares at or below the cash held in their trust (about $10 a share), redeem for that cash at the merger vote, and keep the free warrants or rights.
Why it pays: Trust cash in Treasury bills puts a floor under the shares, so you earn T-bill yield plus a free option that sponsors give away to secure capital.
Track record: Roughly 9–24%/yr annualized for IPO-stage SPAC investors who redeemed or sold, incl. warrants: 11.6% mean for 2019–20 mergers (Klausner et al.); 23.9% (Gahng, Ritter & Zhang, RFS)
How it loses money: Paying above trust value, capital tied up through delays, and warrants expiring worthless once SPAC hype fades.
Key sources: Klausner, Ohlrogge & Ruan (2022); Gahng, Ritter & Zhang (2023)

What to do: After a strong US market day, buy international or thinly traded open-end mutual funds at a daily price (NAV) still based on hours-old foreign closing prices, then sell a day or two later.
Why it pays: Funds priced foreign holdings at stale closes, so the next day's NAV move was predictable; the profit came out of long-term shareholders' pockets.
Track record: Estimated ~35–70%/yr gains in international funds and 10–25%/yr in small-cap and high-yield funds, ~1998–2001, gross (Zitzewitz 2003)
How it loses money: Fair-value pricing, redemption fees and fund bans on frequent traders, adopted after the 2003 scandal, now remove the edge or get accounts blocked.
Key sources: Goetzmann, Ivkovic & Rouwenhorst (2001); Boudoukh, Richardson, Subrahmanyam & Whitelaw (2002); Zitzewitz (2003)

Strategy: TIPS vs nominal Treasury mispricing (breakeven relative value)
What to do: Buy TIPS (inflation-protected Treasuries) and swap their inflation payments for fixed ones, creating a synthetic ordinary Treasury cheaper than the real one, then short the real Treasury.
Why it pays: TIPS are less liquid and get dumped in crises, so they trade cheap, and only arbitrageurs with ample balance sheet can hold the gap.
Track record: Treasuries were almost always rich versus matched synthetic TIPS, by over $20 per $100 face in late 2008 (US, 2004–2009).
How it loses money: The gap widens in liquidity crises (2008, March 2020) just as funding gets harder.
Key sources: Fleckenstein, Longstaff & Lustig (2014); D'Amico, Kim & Wei (2018)

What to do: Buy the cash Treasury that is cheapest to deliver into a futures contract, short the futures, and fund the bond with repo (secured borrowing), collecting the small price gap by delivery.
Why it pays: Asset managers want bond exposure through futures, which pushes futures prices up; hedge funds supply it by holding the bonds with borrowed money.
Track record: No reliable return figure; the basis is typically narrow (tens of basis points a year), so the trade relies on very high repo leverage.
How it loses money: Spikes in margin or repo rates force fire-sale unwinds, as in March 2020.
Key sources: Barth & Kahn (2021; J. Monetary Economics 2025); Schrimpf, Shin & Sushko (2020)

What to do: Buy the cheaper of a company's US-listed depositary receipt (ADR) or its home-market shares, after adjusting for currency and conversion ratio, short the dearer, and convert one into the other to close.
Why it pays: Time-zone gaps, currency moves, fees and capital controls let the two prices drift apart; arbitrageurs earn the gap for bearing those frictions.
Track record: No reliable figure; average ADR-vs-home gap only ~5 bps across hundreds of ADRs, with occasional large spikes
How it loses money: Conversion delays, fees or sudden capital controls in the home market stop the gap closing when you need it to.
Key sources: Gagnon & Karolyi (2010); Pasquariello (2014)

What to do: Buy (or sell) a middle-maturity bond against a rate-matched mix of shorter and longer bonds when it looks cheap (or expensive) versus a fitted curve model, expecting the gap to close.
Why it pays: Supply, index and hedging flows temporarily distort certain maturities, and arbitrageurs with balance sheet are paid to absorb them.
Track record: No reliable live figure; Duarte, Longstaff & Yu report significant simulated excess returns for model-based US yield-curve arbitrage.
How it loses money: Mispricings keep widening while high leverage forces exits, as in the 1998 LTCM crisis.
Key sources: Litterman & Scheinkman (1991); Duarte, Longstaff & Yu (2007)

What to do: Use a credit model to compare a firm's CDS spread with what its share price and volatility imply, then sell whichever looks expensive and buy the cheaper one.
Why it pays: Stock and credit investors are different groups who absorb news at different speeds, so the two prices can disagree.
Track record: Simulated returns comparable to other fixed-income arbitrage strategies, US CDS 2001–2004, with large losses on individual trades.
How it loses money: Stock and credit prices diverge further, as with GM and Ford in 2005.
Key sources: Yu (2006); Duarte, Longstaff & Yu (2007); Kapadia & Pu (2012)

What to do: Put bitcoin into the Grayscale Bitcoin Trust at asset value and sell the shares after a six-month lock-up while they traded at a premium; later, buy shares at a discount betting on ETF conversion.
Why it pays: Before US spot ETFs, investors lacked easy bitcoin access and paid a premium; later, high fees and no redemptions created a discount.
Track record: No reliable figure; premium flipped to a discount in 2021 that neared 50% in late 2022, then closed at ETF conversion in January 2024
How it loses money: The premium can flip to a deep discount while shares are locked up, as hurt Three Arrows Capital in 2021–22.
Key sources: No peer-reviewed source confirmed; Grayscale filings and press record

What to do: Buy ETFs trading at an unusually large discount to their holdings' value (after adjusting for stale prices) and short those at large premiums, exiting when the gap closes.
Why it pays: Arbitrage is costly for ETFs holding foreign or illiquid assets, so gaps caused by buying and selling pressure persist briefly before closing.
Markets: Equity indices & ETFs; Bonds & rates; Credit
Track record: No reliable net figure. Gross abnormal returns found in US-listed ETFs 2007–14, mostly international and illiquid-asset funds.
How it loses money: The apparent discount reflects stale prices for the holdings rather than real mispricing, or it widens further in a sell-off.
Key sources: Petajisto (2017); Ben-David, Franzoni & Moussawi (2018)

What to do: Place a bookmaker's free bet or bonus-qualifying bet, then lay (bet against) the same outcome on a betting exchange at similar odds, so you keep most of the bonus whatever happens.
Why it pays: Bookmakers give sign-up and reload bonuses to win customers they expect to keep gambling; hedging on an exchange captures the bonus without outcome risk.
Track record: No reliable figure. Guides cite keeping ~50–80% of each free bet's value, mostly from one-off sign-up offers; a 2026 UK survey of matched bettors found reported losses
How it loses money: Wrong stakes, moved odds or missed bonus terms cause real losses, and bookmakers restrict profitable accounts, ending the supply of offers.
Key sources: Bush-Evans et al. (2026)

What to do: Short the newest ('on-the-run') Treasury of a maturity and buy a slightly older, higher-yielding ('off-the-run') one, betting the yield gap shrinks as the new bond ages.
Why it pays: Investors pay extra for the most liquid, newest bond, and that liquidity premium fades once a newer issue replaces it.
Track record: The spread closes predictably, but repo costs of shorting the new bond leave near-zero profit (US 30-year bonds, 1995–1999).
How it loses money: Flights to liquidity widen the gap sharply, as in 1998 when it hurt LTCM.
Key sources: Amihud & Mendelson (1991); Krishnamurthy (2002); Pasquariello & Vega (2009)

What to do: When a parent company is worth less on the market than its stake in a listed subsidiary, buy the parent and short the subsidiary shares it owns.
Why it pays: Hyped, hard-to-short subsidiaries stay overpriced; borrowing costs and uncertain timing limit arbitrage, so the mispricing can persist.
Track record: No reliable figure; 82 US negative-stub cases found 1985–2000 (e.g. 3Com/Palm 2000)
How it loses money: Subsidiary shares become impossible or very costly to borrow, or the gap widens before the spin-off completes.
Key sources: Mitchell, Pulvino & Stafford (2002); Lamont & Thaler (2003)

What to do: Buy a well-backed stablecoin when panic pushes it below $1 (e.g., USDC below $0.90 in March 2023) and redeem or sell it when the peg recovers; sell it when it trades above $1.
Why it pays: Panicked or cash-hungry holders sell below backing value, and arbitrageurs are paid for bearing the risk that the backing really is impaired.
Track record: No reliable figure; USDC fell to about $0.88 after SVB failed (March 2023) and regained $1 within days; TerraUSD (May 2022) never recovered
How it loses money: The backing really is broken, as with TerraUSD in 2022, and the coin never recovers.
Key sources: Lyons & Viswanath-Natraj (2023); Gorton, Klee, Ross, Ross & Vardoulakis (2022); Liu, Makarov & Schoar (2023)

What to do: Bet on the gap between interest-rate swap rates and same-maturity Treasury yields, for example buying Treasuries and paying fixed on a swap when the gap looks too low or negative.
Why it pays: Bank balance-sheet costs, funding spreads and pension-fund hedging demand push swap spreads away from fair value for long periods.
Track record: No reliable figure; long-dated US swap spreads stayed negative for years after 2008, contrary to textbook arbitrage.
How it loses money: Balance-sheet or funding shocks push spreads further from fair value and force leveraged holders out.
Key sources: Duarte, Longstaff & Yu (2007); Jermann (2020); Klingler & Sundaresan (2019)

What to do: On one exchange, trade a loop of three pairs (e.g., USD to BTC to ETH back to USD) whenever the implied cross-rate is mispriced, ending with more dollars than you started with.
Why it pays: Prices across many separately quoted trading pairs briefly fall out of line, and the fastest bots are paid for snapping them back.
Track record: No reliable figure; crypto gaps are usually below retail fees, and FX evidence shows such gaps last seconds and are hard to capture
How it loses money: Fees and slippage on three legs exceed the tiny gap, or one leg fails to fill and leaves you with an open position.
Key sources: Kozhan & Tham (2012)

What to do: Estimate each outcome's true chance with a statistical model or by averaging odds across many bookmakers, and bet only when a bookmaker's price pays more than that chance implies.
Why it pays: Some bookmakers quote stale or outlying odds and bettors misjudge probabilities, so a sharper probability estimate can beat the bookmaker's margin on selected bets.
Track record: Kaunitz et al.: 5.5% profit on 407 paper bets over 3 months, then ~$958 real-money profit over 5 months before bookmakers limited the accounts
How it loses money: Model errors or tiny edges get swamped by the bookmaker's margin, and winning accounts are quickly limited or closed.
Key sources: Bolton & Chapman (1986); Benter (1994); Kaunitz, Zhong & Kreiner (2017)

What to do: Buy stocks soon after an activist hedge fund files a Schedule 13D (a public notice of a 5%+ stake with intent to push changes) and hold for months.
Why it pays: Activists push for sales, buybacks or strategy changes that raise value, and the market doesn't fully price their likely success at once.
Track record: ~7% abnormal return from 20 days before to 20 days after filing, much of it before the filing is public, US 2001–2006
How it loses money: Much of the gain comes before the public filing, and campaigns that don't end in a sale often give gains back.
Key sources: Brav, Jiang, Partnoy & Thomas (2008); Greenwood & Schor (2009); Bebchuk, Brav & Jiang (2015)

What to do: Buy stocks soon after the company announces an open-market share repurchase program, especially cheap (high book-to-market) ones, and hold for several years.
Why it pays: Managers buy back stock when they think it is undervalued, and investors underreact to that signal, especially for neglected value stocks.
Track record: +12.1% four-year abnormal return (+45.3% for value stocks), US announcements 1980–1990, long-only; drift vanished for 2003–2012 US events (Fu & Huang 2016)
How it loses money: The US edge largely disappeared for 2003–2012 announcements, and many firms never complete the buybacks they announce.
Key sources: Ikenberry, Lakonishok & Vermaelen (1995); Peyer & Vermaelen (2009); Fu & Huang (2016)

What to do: Get allocations of newly issued corporate bonds at the offering price, which usually yields a little more than the issuer's existing bonds, and sell into early secondary trading.
Why it pays: Issuers and underwriters underprice to place large deals quickly and reward informative or loyal investors, especially for riskier, little-known borrowers.
Track record: No reliable bp figure; new bonds are underpriced on average, most for riskier and less-known issuers; insurers earned ~$41bn first-day profits on allocations, 2002–2014
How it loses money: Hot deals are rationed to favoured clients, so outsiders get filled mostly on weak deals that trade below issue price.
Key sources: Cai, Helwege & Warga (2007); Goldstein, Hotchkiss & Pedersen (2019); Nikolova, Wang & Wu (2020)

Also moves with: Defensive, Quality & Low Risk; Trend & Momentum
What to do: Short or avoid stocks of companies whose bonds were just downgraded by a rating agency, holding for up to a year; upgrades give no reliable signal.
Why it pays: Investors underreact to the bad news in downgrades, especially for small, already low-rated firms where information travels slowly.
Track record: −10% to −14% abnormal stock return in the year after Moody's downgrades, US 1970–1997
How it loses money: Downgraded small stocks are costly to short and can rebound violently in junk rallies.
Key sources: Dichev & Piotroski (2001); Avramov, Chordia, Jostova & Philipov (2009)

What to do: Each month, buy stocks expected to report earnings that month (predicted from last year's report date), optionally shorting non-reporters, because prices tend to rise around announcements.
Why it pays: Announcements concentrate risk that investors want paid for, and attention-driven buying by small investors lifts prices around the news.
Track record: ~7%/yr abnormal return, long expected announcers vs short non-announcers, US 1972–2004, gross
How it loses money: Monthly turnover makes costs bite, and each holding carries a large single-stock price gap on its announcement day.
Key sources: Frazzini & Lamont (2007); Barber, De George, Lehavy & Trueman (2013); Savor & Wilson (2016)

Strategy: Earnings date shifts (late vs early reporters)
What to do: When companies schedule earnings, compare the date with last year's: buy firms that report earlier than usual and short or avoid those that push the date later, holding through the announcement.
Why it pays: Managers tend to rush out good news and delay bad news, and investors don't fully read the timing signal.
Track record: Firms that move their earnings date earlier beat those that delay by ~2.6% in the month after the change (Johnson & So 2018, US; per data-provider summary, before costs)
How it loses money: Many date changes are innocent, the edge per trade is small, and shorting costs can erase it.
Key sources: Givoly & Palmon (1982); Chambers & Penman (1984); Johnson & So (2018)

Also moves with: Value & Long-Term Reversal; Carry & Yield; Size & Illiquidity
What to do: Buy bonds just downgraded from investment grade to junk, after rule-bound investors have been forced to sell them, and hold for months while prices recover.
Why it pays: Insurers and investment-grade-only funds must dump downgraded bonds, creating temporary fire-sale discounts for patient buyers.
Track record: ICE US Fallen Angel index beat ICE BofA US High Yield in 15 of 22 calendar years; cumulative ~368% vs ~225%, end-2003 to mid-2023 (long-only, issuer-reported index data)
How it loses money: Downgraded firms keep deteriorating and default, especially in recessions.
Key sources: Ambrose, Cai & Helwege (2008); Ellul, Jotikasthira & Lundblad (2011)

What to do: Get allocated shares when a listed company sells new stock (a follow-on offering), which is usually priced a few percent below the last market price, and sell soon after.
Why it pays: Issuers and underwriters discount the price to place a large block of new supply quickly, paying buyers for absorbing it.
Track record: ~2% average offer-price discount to the prior close, US follow-on offerings 1980–1998, rising over time; before costs
How it loses money: Allocations favour weaker deals, prices can keep sliding after the sale, and shorting beforehand bars you from buying in (SEC Rule 105).
Key sources: Altinkilic & Hansen (2003); Corwin (2003)

What to do: Get allocated shares at the IPO offer price and sell on the first trading day, when prices typically jump above the offer.
Why it pays: Underwriters price new issues low to reward informed investors for participating and to make sure the deal sells.
Track record: ~18% average first-day return from offer price, US IPOs 1980–2020s, equal-weighted; rationed real allocations earn far less
How it loses money: You get big allocations of weak deals and little of hot ones (winner's curse); buying at the open captures none of the pop.
Key sources: Ritter, IPO Statistics (updated annually); Rock (1986); Ritter & Welch (2002); Loughran & Ritter (2004)

What to do: Short recently listed stocks a few days before insiders' lockup period (usually 180 days after the IPO) ends, and buy them back shortly after.
Why it pays: Expiry releases a predictable wave of insider and venture-capital selling, and limited arbitrage capital lets the price sag when it arrives.
Track record: About −1.5% abnormal return over the 3 days around expiry (much larger for VC-backed firms), US IPOs 1988–1997, 1,948 lockups, before borrow costs
How it loses money: Borrow fees on new IPO stocks are high and short squeezes can wipe out the small expected edge.
Key sources: Field & Hanka (2001); Brav & Gompers (2003)

What to do: Buy stocks where officers or directors recently bought shares on the open market, favouring non-routine (opportunistic) and multi-insider purchases, especially in small caps.
Why it pays: Insiders know more about their firm's prospects, and their public purchase filings (due within two business days) are priced in only gradually.
Track record: ~0.8%/month value-weighted abnormal return, long opportunistic insider buys vs short opportunistic sells, US 1986–2007, gross
How it loses money: The edge concentrates in small illiquid stocks where costs are high, and insiders are often simply wrong.
Key sources: Lakonishok & Lee (2001); Jeng, Metrick & Zeckhauser (2003); Cohen, Malloy & Pomorski (2012)

Also moves with: Short Volatility & Insurance Selling; Arbitrage & Relative Value
What to do: After a takeover is announced, buy the target below the offer price (and short the acquirer in all-stock deals), collecting the remaining gap when the deal closes.
Why it pays: You are paid for bearing deal-failure risk and for giving liquidity to shareholders who sell right after the announcement rather than wait.
Track record: ~4%/yr excess return after transaction costs, diversified portfolio of US deals 1963–1998
How it loses money: Deals break together in market crashes, so losses arrive all at once, like selling crash insurance.
Key sources: Mitchell & Pulvino (2001); Baker & Savasoglu (2002); Jetley & Ji (2010)

Strategy: New-issue underperformance (avoid/short IPOs, SEOs and share issuers)
Also moves with: Value & Long-Term Reversal; Defensive, Quality & Low Risk
What to do: Avoid or short companies that recently sold new shares (IPOs, follow-on offerings, stock-paid takeovers) or grew their share count most over the past year, holding for one to five years.
Why it pays: Firms tend to issue stock when it is overpriced and buy it back when cheap, and investors underreact to that signal.
Track record: Issuers returned ~5%/yr (IPOs) and ~7%/yr (SEOs) over 5 years after issue; investors needed 44% more in issuers than in size-matched non-issuers for equal wealth, US 1970–1990
How it loses money: Results depend heavily on the benchmark, post-offering underperformance faded in 2003–2012 US data, and new IPOs are costly to short.
Key sources: Loughran & Ritter (1995); Brav, Geczy & Gompers (2000); Pontiff & Woodgate (2008)

What to do: Buy new shares or convertibles directly from small, cash-hungry listed companies at a discount (often with warrants), hedging by shorting the stock only after the deal is publicly announced.
Why it pays: Issuers with few funding options pay a discount to investors who supply capital quickly and bear resale restrictions, illiquidity and information risk.
Track record: Average PIPE investor earned ~21% abnormal return over a ~384-day holding period (Lim, Schwert & Weisbach), even as issuers' shares later underperform
How it loses money: Weak issuers keep falling or fail before you can resell, and shorting tiny, hard-to-borrow stocks is costly or impossible.
Key sources: Hertzel, Lemmon, Linck & Rees (2002); Brophy, Ouimet & Sialm (2009); Lim, Schwert & Weisbach (2021)

What to do: After quarterly earnings, buy the stocks whose profits beat expectations by the most, short the biggest misses, and hold about three months while prices keep drifting the same way.
Why it pays: Investors underreact to earnings news, especially in small, illiquid, little-followed stocks, so prices take weeks to fully adjust.
Track record: ~4% over 60 trading days, long top vs short bottom earnings-surprise decile, US 1974–1986, gross
How it loses money: In US stocks the drift has largely vanished outside micro-caps since the mid-2000s, where trading costs eat most of what remains.
Key sources: Ball & Brown (1968); Bernard & Thomas (1989); Martineau (2022)

Also moves with: Sentiment, Flows & Alt Data; Short-Term Reversal & Stat Arb; Size & Illiquidity
What to do: Each spring, predict from Russell's ranking rules which stocks will switch between the Russell 1000 and 2000, buying names index funds must buy and selling those they must sell before the June rebalance.
Why it pays: Funds tracking Russell indexes must trade huge volumes at one closing price, so whoever absorbs that flow earns a liquidity premium.
Track record: No reliable figure; price pressure of several percent on switching stocks documented in 1990s–2000s, smaller since
How it loses money: Crowded front-running shrinks the edge, and wrong membership calls or post-rebalance reversals hit small illiquid names.
Key sources: Madhavan (2003); Petajisto (2011); Chang, Hong & Liskovich (2015)

Also moves with: Sentiment, Flows & Alt Data; Short-Term Reversal & Stat Arb
What to do: Buy stocks announced as joining the S&P 500 before index funds must buy them on the effective date, and buy deleted stocks after the forced selling ends.
Why it pays: Index funds must trade at a set time whatever the price, so their concentrated demand temporarily pushes prices away from fair value.
Track record: Abnormal return for added stocks fell from ~7.4% in the 1990s to under 1% in the 2010s, US
How it loses money: Traders now pre-position, so the remaining gain is tiny and often reverses around the effective date.
Key sources: Shleifer (1986); Chen, Noronha & Singal (2004); Greenwood & Sammon (2025)

Also moves with: Trend & Momentum; Sentiment, Flows & Alt Data
What to do: Buy stocks just upgraded to 'buy' by major brokers and short stocks just downgraded to 'sell', holding for one to six months.
Why it pays: Analyst views carry real information, but investors react slowly, especially to rare downgrades.
Track record: +2.4% in the month after upgrades; −9.1% over six months after downgrades, 14 US brokers 1989–1991, gross
How it loses money: Most of the move happens within days, and studies find frequent rebalancing earns little after trading costs.
Key sources: Womack (1996); Barber, Lehavy, McNichols & Trueman (2001); Jegadeesh, Kim, Krische & Lee (2004)

What to do: Buy a token right after a major exchange such as Coinbase or Binance announces it will list it, and sell into the listing-day jump within a few days.
Why it pays: A big-exchange listing brings new buyers, liquidity and attention to a thinly traded token, creating a short-lived burst of demand.
Track record: No reliable net figure; 2017–2020 studies found positive abnormal returns of several percent around listings, much of it before the public announcement; gross
How it loses money: Insiders and bots take most of the jump before or within minutes of the news, and prices often fade after listing.
Key sources: Ante (2019); Benedetti & Nikbakht (2021); Felez-Vinas, Johnson & Putniņš (2022)

Also moves with: Carry & Yield; Size & Illiquidity; Value & Long-Term Reversal
What to do: Buy the bonds or loans of companies in or near default at deep discounts and hold them through the bankruptcy or restructuring, sometimes buying enough to steer it or end up owning the firm.
Why it pays: Many holders must or want to dump defaulted debt and few can price complex bankruptcies, so patient specialists are paid for illiquidity, legal work and default risk.
Track record: No reliable long-run figure; US default-to-emergence returns 1987–2016 were weak overall but strong in 2006–2016 (Altman-Benhenni), gross
How it loses money: Recoveries come in below the price paid, restructurings drag on, or other creditors outmanoeuvre you in court.
Key sources: Hotchkiss & Mooradian (1997); Jiang, Li & Wang (2012); Altman & Benhenni (2019)

What to do: Buy stocks that start paying a dividend and short those that scrap theirs, holding about a year as prices keep moving in the announced direction.
Why it pays: Dividend changes signal management's confidence about future earnings, and investors underreact, especially to bad news like omissions.
Track record: +7.5% (initiations) and −11.0% (omissions) market-adjusted over the next year, US 1964–1988
How it loses money: Results are benchmark-sensitive, later work suggests initiation gains may be chance, and few events mean concentrated bets.
Key sources: Michaely, Thaler & Womack (1995); Boehme & Sorescu (2002)

What to do: When a well-known short-seller research firm (e.g. Muddy Waters) publishes a report alleging fraud or overvaluation, short or sell the target soon after and hold for a few months.
Why it pays: Activists publish costly research where shorting is hard; investors under-react at first, so prices keep drifting down as allegations are confirmed.
Track record: No reliable net figure; targets typically drop sharply on report day and drift lower for months (US-listed targets, 2006–2010s); gross of often-high borrow fees
How it loses money: Most of the drop happens before you can trade, borrow is costly or unavailable, and squeezes or rebuttals can send targets sharply higher.
Key sources: Ljungqvist & Qian (2016); Brendel & Ryans (2021); Paugam, Stolowy & Gendron (2021)

What to do: Buy tokens in an initial coin offering (a crowdfunded token sale) at the offer price and sell soon after they start trading on exchanges.
Why it pays: Offer prices were set low to attract buyers and hype, so early listing demand pushed prices up, much like IPO underpricing.
Track record: Avg ~179% from ICO price to first-day open (avg ~16 days), ICOs to 2018, gross; counts only tokens that listed, and many never did
How it loses money: Many tokens never list, turn out to be scams, or crash after listing; regulators can freeze or unwind sales.
Key sources: Benedetti & Kostovetsky (2021); Lyandres, Palazzo & Rabetti (2022)

What to do: Buy the new shares of companies emerging from Chapter 11 bankruptcy and hold them through roughly their first year of trading.
Why it pays: Ex-creditors who receive the shares often sell, few analysts cover them, and the market is too pessimistic about reorganized firms.
Track record: Large positive abnormal returns (roughly 25%+, benchmark-dependent) over 200 trading days after emergence, 131 US firms, 1980s–early 1990s
How it loses money: Evidence is old and small-sample, and many reorganized firms fail again, wiping out shareholders.
Key sources: Eberhart, Altman & Aggarwal (1999)

Strategy: Pre-earnings straddle buying (exit before the announcement)
What to do: Buy at-the-money straddles (call plus put) about three trading days before a scheduled earnings announcement and sell them just before the release, capturing the rise in option prices.
Why it pays: Investors seem to under-anticipate the build-up of uncertainty before earnings, so option prices climb predictably into the event.
Track record: Significantly positive average straddle returns over the ~3 days before announcements, US stock options from 1996, before costs
How it loses money: Bid-ask spreads on short-dated single-stock options can consume the small expected gain.
Key sources: Gao, Xing & Zhang (2018); Patell & Wolfson (1979)

Strategy: Pre-positioning before commodity index rolls (front-running the 'Goldman roll')
What to do: A few days before big commodity indices roll their futures (5th–9th business day each month), sell the expiring contract and buy the next one, then close out as index funds roll.
Why it pays: Huge, publicly scheduled index rolls must trade on fixed dates and push calendar spreads predictably, so traders are paid for supplying liquidity ahead of them.
Track record: Very high gross Sharpe ratios reported for 2000–2010 in an unpublished working paper (Mou); later studies find roll price impact small and short-lived
How it loses money: Crowding and changed roll schedules erased the edge, leaving a spread position exposed to random curve moves.
Key sources: Mou (2010); Stoll & Whaley (2010); Bessembinder, Carrion, Tuttle & Venkataraman (2016)

What to do: When a company offers to buy its own shares above market, buy below the offer and tender before the deadline; odd lots (under 100 shares) usually avoid being scaled back.
Why it pays: Uncertainty over how many shares will be accepted (proration) and short deadlines keep the market price below the tender price.
Track record: No reliable figure; older US studies found profits for low-cost traders in fixed-price offers, smaller in Dutch auctions
How it loses money: Proration leaves unaccepted shares that usually drop back after the offer, and firms can amend, extend or cancel it.
Key sources: Lakonishok & Vermaelen (1990); Kadapakkam & Seth (1994)

What to do: Buy shares of newly spun-off subsidiaries (and sometimes their parents) soon after the separation and hold for one to three years.
Why it pays: Parent shareholders and index funds dump the unwanted new shares, depressing prices; focused firms also more often become takeover targets.
Track record: Spin-offs and parents beat matched firms over 3 years, US 1965–1988; roughly no edge in 1989–1995 spin-offs
How it loses money: Newly listed small companies can lag for years, and outperformance has been inconsistent in later samples and outside the US.
Key sources: Cusatis, Miles & Woolridge (1993); McConnell, Ozbilgin & Wahal (2001); McConnell & Ovtchinnikov (2004)

What to do: Buy stocks soon after they announce a forward stock split (e.g. 2-for-1) and hold about a year; avoid or short stocks announcing reverse splits.
Why it pays: Splits signal management confidence after strong performance, and investors were thought to underreact to that signal.
Track record: +7.9% abnormal return in the year after 2-for-1 splits, US 1975–1990; little or none across 1927–1996 with stricter methods
How it loses money: The effect is fragile to method and period, so you may just be holding pricey past winners with no edge.
Key sources: Ikenberry, Rankine & Stice (1996); Desai & Jain (1997); Byun & Rozeff (2003)

What to do: Rank firms with a statistical takeover-probability model (size, valuation, cash, debt, takeover defences, industry deal activity); buy the likeliest targets before any bid, optionally shorting the least likely.
Why it pays: Targets are bought at large premiums; if prices underweight takeover odds, or takeover exposure is a priced risk, likely targets earn extra return.
Track record: No reliable figure; simple predicted-target portfolios show no reliable abnormal return, though one published US takeover-likelihood factor did
How it loses money: Models flag far more 'targets' than ever get bids, and the wrongly flagged ones are often small, distressed firms that underperform.
Key sources: Palepu (1986); Cremers, Nair & John (2009); Danbolt, Siganos & Tunyi (2016)

What to do: About a month before a large scheduled release of locked team or investor tokens, short the token (usually via perpetual futures) and buy it back a week or two after the unlock.
Why it pays: Insiders and early investors who get cheap unlocked tokens often sell, adding predictable new supply that thin markets only partly price in advance.
Track record: No peer-reviewed figure; a 2024 practitioner study of thousands of unlocks found prices usually drift down in the month before big unlocks, worst for team unlocks; gross
How it loses money: Unlock dates are public, so prices often fall early; squeezes, futures funding costs and token-specific rallies can swamp the effect.
Key sources: Keyrock (2024); Field & Hanka (2001)

What to do: Use new blockchain protocols (bridging, swapping, lending) before they launch a token, aiming to qualify for a free token 'airdrop', which is usually sold soon after it arrives.
Why it pays: Projects give away tokens to attract users and spread ownership, and farmers capture this marketing spend.
Track record: No reliable figure; early drops (Uniswap 2020: 400 UNI per past user) were lucrative, later ones heavily farmed and filtered for fake accounts
How it loses money: Fees and locked capital are spent, then the project excludes you as a fake 'Sybil' account or the token collapses after launch.
Key sources: Fröwis & Böhme (2019); Messias, Yaish & Livshits (2023)

What to do: Hold a stock index fund only from the last trading day of each month through the third trading day of the next month, and sit in cash the rest of the time.
Why it pays: Regular month-end cash flows such as pay cheques, pension contributions and fund inflows create predictable buying pressure around the turn of each month.
Track record: US stocks 1926–2005: outside the four turn-of-month days investors earned on average no reward for market risk; effect also found in 31 of 35 countries (gross)
How it loses money: A crash inside the four-day window still hurts, and sitting in cash most days lags buy-and-hold in strong years.
Key sources: Ariel (1987); Lakonishok & Smidt (1988); McConnell & Xu (2008)

What to do: Avoid holding stocks from Friday's close to Monday's close (or short them then) and hold them the rest of the week, because Mondays used to average negative returns.
Why it pays: Suggested causes include firms releasing bad news over weekends and individuals selling on Mondays; no risk-based explanation fits.
Track record: S&P 500 1953–1977: average Monday return about −0.17% while other days were positive; largely gone since the late 1980s
How it loses money: The pattern has disappeared or flipped in recent decades, so trading on it mostly adds costs.
Key sources: French (1980); Gibbons & Hess (1981); Schwert (2003)

Strategy: Halloween effect ('Sell in May and go away')
What to do: Hold stocks from the start of November to the end of April, and move to cash or bonds from May through October.
Why it pays: Unexplained; leading stories are lower summer participation and risk appetite and seasonal mood shifts, not differences in risk.
Track record: Winter beat summer in 36 of 37 markets, 1970–1998; a later 100+-market, centuries-long study finds Nov–Apr returns about 4 points/yr higher than May–Oct (gross)
How it loses money: Summer returns are often still positive, so sitting out often lags buy-and-hold, and winter crashes still hit you.
Key sources: Bouman & Jacobsen (2002); Andrade, Chhaochharia & Fuerst (2013); Zhang & Jacobsen (2021)

What to do: Buy small-cap stocks (or go long small caps and short large caps) in the last days of December and hold them through January.
Why it pays: Year-end tax-loss selling and fund 'window dressing' push small stocks down in December, and they rebound once that pressure lifts in January.
Track record: US 1963–1979: a large share of the small-minus-large size premium came in January, concentrated in the first trading days (gross); persistence since then is contested
How it loses money: The premium has shrunk and partly moved into December, and small-stock trading costs can eat what is left.
Key sources: Rozeff & Kinney (1976); Keim (1983); Haug & Hirschey (2006)

What to do: Hold stocks, or tilt toward high-beta (market-sensitive) stocks, only on days with scheduled inflation, jobs or Fed rate announcements, and hold cash or low-beta stocks on other days.
Why it pays: Investors demand pay for bearing big-picture economic risk when key data are released, so market risk is rewarded mainly on those days.
Track record: US stocks 1958–2009: 11.4 bp average excess return on announcement days vs 1.1 bp on other days (gross)
How it loses money: Announcement days include some of the biggest drops, the Fed-day part has faded, and you miss gains on other days.
Key sources: Savor & Wilson (2013); Savor & Wilson (2014); Ai & Bansal (2018)

What to do: Buy a US stock index ETF or futures at the close and sell at the next morning's open, so you own the market overnight but not during the trading session.
Why it pays: Possibly pay for holding risk while markets are shut, plus attention-driven buying that lifts opening prices and selling pressure during the day.
Track record: US stocks, ETFs and index futures 1993–2006: nearly all gains came overnight; trading-hour returns near zero or negative (gross, before costs)
How it loses money: Two trades every day add costs that can swamp the small edge, and bad overnight news hits you at the open.
Key sources: Cliff, Cooper & Gulen (2008); Berkman, Koch, Tuttle & Zhang (2012)

What to do: Buy a stock index ETF or futures at about 2 p.m. the day before a scheduled Federal Reserve (FOMC) rate announcement and sell just before the 2 p.m. announcement.
Why it pays: Possibly a premium for bearing policy uncertainty before it is resolved; the original authors could not fully explain it.
Track record: S&P 500 1994–2011: about 0.49% average gain in the 24 hours before scheduled FOMC announcements, roughly 80% of annual realized excess stock returns; essentially gone since ~2015
How it loses money: The drift has largely vanished since about 2015, so you mostly carry a day of market risk for little reward.
Key sources: Lucca & Moench (2015); Kurov, Wolfe & Gilbert (2021)

What to do: Buy a stock index fund at the close two trading days before a market holiday and sell at the close of the last trading day before the holiday.
Why it pays: Holiday optimism and short-sellers closing positions before a long break may create buying pressure; differences in risk don't explain it.
Track record: US stocks 1963–1982 (Ariel): pre-holiday returns 9–14 times the normal daily return (gross); in 1983–2019 the effect survives only among small firms
How it loses money: Only about nine trading days a year qualify, so total gains are small, and the effect has faded in large US stocks.
Key sources: Lakonishok & Smidt (1988); Ariel (1990); Kim & Park (1994); Ko & Yang (2024)
