What to do: Each month, buy the stocks, country indices or commodity futures that historically did best in this same calendar month in past years and short those that historically did worst.
Why it pays: Recurring yearly patterns in flows (tax, reporting and bonus calendars) and in commodity supply, demand and storage make some assets reliably strong or weak in certain months.
Track record: US stocks 1963–2002: same-month past returns predicted returns up to 20 years later; a same-month strategy earned ~13%/yr gross 1963–2011; also seen abroad and in commodities
How it loses money: Turning over the whole portfolio monthly raises costs, and commodity seasonals are often already priced into futures.
Key sources: Heston & Sadka (2008); Heston & Sadka (2010); Keloharju, Linnainmaa & Nyberg (2016)

Strategy: Selling options over weekends and holidays (non-trading-period effect)
What to do: Sell stock options at Friday's close, hedged with shares so only the option's own value matters, and buy them back on Monday, because option prices don't fall enough over the weekend.
Why it pays: Option prices appear to treat weekends like trading days, overstating weekend risk, so option holders lose value over non-trading periods.
Track record: Option returns significantly lower over weekends than over trading days, US equity options from 1996, before costs
How it loses money: Weekend news causes gap moves, and the small per-trade edge is easily lost to bid-ask spreads.
Key sources: Jones & Shemesh (2018)

Also moves with: Short-Term Reversal & Stat Arb; Value & Long-Term Reversal; Size & Illiquidity
What to do: In mid-to-late December, buy the stocks that have fallen most over the year (the likeliest to be sold for tax losses) and hold them into January.
Why it pays: Investors dump losing stocks before year-end to book tax losses, temporarily depressing prices that rebound once the selling stops.
Track record: US prior-year losers, especially small ones, rebound strongly in early January (gross); size varies widely by study and period
How it loses money: Some losers are genuinely failing and keep falling, and the rebound may already be priced in before you buy.
Key sources: Reinganum (1983); Roll (1983); Grinblatt & Moskowitz (2004)

What to do: Short or avoid government bonds in the few days before a scheduled auction and buy right after, because prices typically dip ahead of new supply and then recover.
Why it pays: Dealers must absorb new supply and demand a temporary price discount, because outside investors are slow to step in.
Track record: Yields rise a few basis points in the days before US Treasury auctions and fall back afterwards (1980s–2000s, gross).
How it loses money: The edge is only a few basis points and is easily erased by macro news or trading costs.
Key sources: Lou, Yan & Zhang (2013); Fleming & Rosenberg (2008, NY Fed SR 299; later Fleming, Nguyen & Rosenberg 2024); Beetsma, Giuliodori, de Jong & Widijanto (2016)

What to do: Hold a currency while its home financial centre is closed and sell it while that centre trades, e.g. own euros against dollars in New York hours and dollars against euros in European hours.
Why it pays: Local firms and investors buy foreign currency during their own working hours, creating predictable selling pressure on their home currency.
Track record: No reliable figure; major currencies tended to weaken during their home trading hours (gross, small per day)
How it loses money: The intraday moves are tiny relative to spreads and news-driven swings, so costs and leverage can turn it into a loss.
Key sources: Ranaldo (2009); Breedon & Ranaldo (2013)

What to do: Each month, buy stocks expected to pay a dividend this month (because they paid one 3, 6 or 12 months ago) and short similar stocks not expected to pay.
Why it pays: Dividend-seeking investors buy shares ahead of payouts, and their predictable demand temporarily pushes prices up.
Track record: US stocks over many decades: higher average returns in predicted dividend months than other months (gross); no reliable net figure
How it loses money: The extra return is modest, monthly turnover adds costs, and dividend cuts or date shifts break the prediction.
Key sources: Hartzmark & Solomon (2013)

What to do: Just before each firm's earnings release, buy stocks whose earnings are usually highest in this quarter of the year (e.g. retailers in Q4) and short those whose earnings are usually lowest.
Why it pays: Investors anchor on recent, seasonally weaker results and are repeatedly surprised by predictably strong seasonal quarters.
Track record: No reliable figure; US firms announcing seasonally strong quarters earned higher returns around the announcement (gross)
How it loses money: Actual earnings surprises swamp any seasonal tilt, and trading around announcements is costly and volatile.
Key sources: Chang, Hartzmark, Solomon & Soltes (2017)

Also moves with: Short-Term Reversal & Stat Arb; Market Making & HFT
What to do: Buy S&P 500 futures around 2 a.m. New York time, as European markets open, and sell about an hour later, especially after heavy selling into the previous US close.
Why it pays: Dealers who absorbed sell orders at the US close are paid for holding that risk until European traders arrive to take it off their hands.
Track record: E-mini S&P 500 futures 1998–2018: a large share of the index's return came in the hour around the European open (gross); small versus trading costs
How it loses money: The bid-ask spread is large relative to the small average gain, and the drift may have faded in recent years.
Key sources: Boyarchenko, Larsen & Whelan (2023)

What to do: Count weeks from the last Fed (FOMC) meeting and hold stocks only in even-numbered weeks (0, 2, 4, 6), staying in cash during the odd weeks.
Why it pays: Fed news seems to reach markets on a two-week rhythm tied to internal Fed Board meetings, and surprisingly easy policy news lifts stocks in those weeks.
Track record: US stocks 1994–2016: essentially all of the equity premium was earned in even weeks of the FOMC cycle (gross, authors' sample)
How it loses money: It rests mainly on one study whose week-0 piece (the pre-FOMC drift) has faded, and the Fed can change how it communicates.
Key sources: Cieslak, Morse & Vissing-Jorgensen (2019)

Strategy: FX month-end London 4pm fix hedging-flow trade
Also moves with: Sentiment, Flows & Alt Data; Short-Term Reversal & Stat Arb
What to do: In the hour before the month's last 4pm London currency fix, sell currencies of countries whose stocks beat US stocks that month (buy the laggards), then unwind after the fix.
Why it pays: Funds holding currency-hedged foreign stocks reset their hedges at the month-end fix, creating predictable one-way flows that dealers absorb only at a temporary price discount.
Track record: No reliable month-end figure; related daily dollar fix-reversal trades ~12–18%/yr gross 1999–2019, short-window versions largely eaten by spreads
How it loses money: Flow estimates are often wrong or already priced in, and wide spreads around the fix can wipe out the small edge.
Key sources: Melvin & Prins (2015); Evans (2018); Krohn, Mueller & Whelan (2024)

What to do: If the stock market rises in January, stay invested for the rest of the year; if January is negative, move to Treasury bills until year-end.
Why it pays: January may reveal investors' outlook for the year, but critics see it as a weak trend signal and possible data-mining.
Track record: US stocks from 1857 (authors' sample): next-11-month returns were significantly higher after positive Januaries; mixed record since
How it loses money: A bad January is often followed by a strong recovery (e.g. 2009, 2016), so you miss big gains.
Key sources: Cooper, McConnell & Ovtchinnikov (2006)

Also moves with: Sentiment, Flows & Alt Data; Short-Term Reversal & Stat Arb
What to do: When stocks have beaten bonds over the month, sell equity futures and buy bond futures shortly before month- or quarter-end, reversing once big funds finish rebalancing.
Why it pays: Large pension and balanced funds rebalance to fixed stock/bond weights on predictable dates, and their big trades move prices temporarily.
Track record: US, recent decades: when stocks are overweight, rebalancing sales cut next-day equity returns by ~17 bp, fading within about two weeks (gross)
How it loses money: Flow estimates are noisy, other traders crowd the same trade, and market news can easily drown out rebalancing pressure.
Key sources: Harvey, Mazzoleni & Melone (2025); Etula, Rinne, Suominen & Vaittinen (2020)

What to do: Buy large-cap stocks with heavily traded options at the start of the week ending on the monthly options expiry (third Friday) and sell at that week's end.
Why it pays: As expiry nears, option dealers adjust their stock hedges and implied volatility tends to fall, which may lift prices of heavily optioned stocks.
Track record: S&P 100 stocks 1996–2008: average returns notably higher in option-expiration weeks than other weeks, concentrated in heavily optioned names (gross)
How it loses money: It rests largely on one 1996–2008 study, and weekly and daily options have since changed hedging flows around monthly expiry.
Key sources: Stivers & Sun (2013); Ni, Pearson & Poteshman (2005)

Strategy: Overnight vs intraday factor timing ('tug of war')
Also moves with: Trend & Momentum; Short-Term Reversal & Stat Arb
What to do: Hold momentum long-short stock portfolios only overnight (close to next open) and most other factor bets, such as value or size, only during the trading day (open to close).
Why it pays: Different investors dominate different hours: individuals trading near the open push momentum, while institutions trading during the day lean against it.
Track record: US stocks 1993–2013: momentum profits came entirely overnight, most other factor profits intraday (gross); no reliable net-of-cost figure
How it loses money: Trading many stocks twice a day costs more than the gross edge, and momentum crashes still apply.
Key sources: Lou, Polk & Skouras (2019); Hendershott, Livdan & Rösch (2020); Bogousslavsky (2021)

What to do: Hold stocks in Muslim-majority markets (e.g. via Turkey, Indonesia or Malaysia country ETFs) during the month of Ramadan and reduce exposure in other months.
Why it pays: Researchers attribute it to better investor mood and social solidarity during Ramadan, a sentiment explanation rather than a risk premium.
Track record: 14 Muslim-majority markets 1989–2007: returns notably higher and less volatile during Ramadan (gross, in-sample)
How it loses money: It rests mainly on one study of emerging markets, where country ETFs are costly and political shocks can swamp any seasonal edge.
Key sources: Bialkowski, Etebari & Wisniewski (2012)

Also moves with: Sentiment, Flows & Alt Data; Market Making & HFT
What to do: Each half hour, buy the stocks that rose most in this same half-hour slot on recent trading days and short those that fell most, holding for that half hour.
Why it pays: Institutions that split big orders over many days and trade at the same time each day create repeating buying or selling pressure.
Track record: US stocks, early 2000s: a stock's half-hour return predicts its return in the same slot for at least 40 trading days (gross, tiny per trade)
How it loses money: The edges are so small that you need near-zero costs and fast execution, and trading algorithms may already capture them.
Key sources: Heston, Korajczyk & Sadka (2010); Bogousslavsky (2016)

What to do: Buy a stock index fund for the last five trading days of December and the first two trading days of January, then sell.
Why it pays: Holiday optimism, thin institutional trading, year-end bonus money and the end of tax-loss selling may lift prices.
Track record: S&P 500 since 1950: about +1.3% average over the seven-day window, up roughly three years in four (practitioner figure, gross)
How it loses money: Seven days a year is a tiny sample that overlaps other year-end effects, and it has failed in some recent years.
Key sources: Hirsch, Stock Trader's Almanac (1972); Lakonishok & Smidt (1988)

What to do: Hold more US stocks in the third (pre-election) year of a presidential term and fewer in the first two years.
Why it pays: Governments may push growth-friendly policies before elections, but with so few cycles the pattern could easily be chance.
Track record: No reliable figure; pre-election years have historically averaged highest, but from only about 20–25 four-year cycles
How it loses money: With so few cycles of data the pattern may be chance, and any single year can fall sharply.
Key sources: Booth & Booth (2003); Santa-Clara & Valkanov (2003); Wong & McAleer (2009)

What to do: Hold bitcoin only on Mondays, when one 2013–2017 study found higher average returns, or trade around thin weekend markets, and stay in cash the rest of the time.
Why it pays: Possibly thin weekend liquidity and Monday's return of traditional-market flows; it may simply be a chance pattern found by data mining.
Track record: No reliable figure; BTC Monday returns were higher 2013–2017, but a simple trading rule's profits were not clearly better than random trading
How it loses money: The pattern disappears out of sample, and trading costs exceed the small daily edge.
Key sources: Caporale & Plastun (2019); Aharon & Qadan (2019)

What to do: Hold stocks in the roughly two weeks around each new moon and move to cash for the two weeks around each full moon.
Why it pays: The claim is that moon phases affect mood, but there is no convincing mechanism and the result may come from data-mining.
Track record: 48 countries: returns ~3–5% a year lower around full moons than new moons (in-sample, gross); not shown profitable after costs
How it loses money: Probably a statistical fluke with no real mechanism, and trading twice a month costs more than the claimed edge.
Key sources: Dichev & Janes (2003); Yuan, Zheng & Zhu (2006)

What to do: Lean toward stocks on sunny days in the exchange's home city and away from them on overcast days or right after daylight-saving clock changes; a seasonal version favours winter over autumn.
Why it pays: Mood shifts risk appetite: sunshine lifts optimism, while lost sleep and long autumn nights make investors more cautious.
Track record: NYC 1982–1997: ~24.8% annualized on fully sunny days vs ~8.7% on fully cloudy days (gross); gains vanish after modest trading costs
How it loses money: The effects are small and noisy, and trading on daily weather means frequent trades whose costs exceed the gain.
Key sources: Saunders (1993); Hirshleifer & Shumway (2003); Kamstra, Kramer & Levi (2003)

What to do: Using weekly CFTC Commitments of Traders data, buy the futures where commercial hedgers are most net short (speculators net long) and short those where hedgers are net long.
Why it pays: Hedgers pay speculators an insurance premium to offload price risk, so taking the other side of heavy hedging demand earns that premium.
Track record: Long-short hedging-pressure portfolios beat long-only commodity indices risk-adjusted (Basu & Miffre); later work finds the pure insurance part small
How it loses money: Positioning data is published with a lag, and the premium fades when hedging demand shifts or speculators crowd in.
Key sources: de Roon, Nijman & Veld (2000); Basu & Miffre (2013); Kang, Rouwenhorst & Tang (2020)

Strategy: Connected-firm momentum (shared analyst coverage, tech links)
What to do: Each month, buy stocks whose linked peers (firms sharing analysts or technology) rose last month and short those whose peers fell; this largely subsumes customer-supplier momentum.
Why it pays: News spreads slowly across economically linked firms because investors pay limited attention to indirect connections.
Track record: Shared-analyst connected-firm momentum factor earned ~1.68%/month alpha (t=9.67), gross, US in-sample; similar in developed international markets
How it loses money: Behaves like momentum, so it can crash in sharp market reversals; needs costly analyst or patent data.
Key sources: Ali & Hirshleifer (2020); Lee, Sun, Wang & Zhang (2019); Hou (2007)

What to do: Each month, buy suppliers whose major customers' stocks rose last month and short suppliers whose major customers' stocks fell.
Why it pays: Investors with limited attention are slow to apply news about a firm's customers to that firm's suppliers.
Track record: Over 1.5%/month long-short alpha, gross (US, sample ending 2004); a later replication finds a smaller effect that is insignificant after publication
How it loses money: Supply-chain data is now widely used, shrinking the delay, and small-cap legs are costly to trade.
Key sources: Cohen & Frazzini (2008); Menzly & Ozbas (2010); Pinchuk (2023, replication)

What to do: Using daily short-sale data, short stocks with unusually heavy new shorting and buy lightly shorted ones, holding for days to a few weeks.
Why it pays: Active short sellers, often institutions, trade on short-lived negative news and lean against temporary overpricing.
Track record: Most- minus least-shorted NYSE stocks: ~1.16% over next 20 trading days, risk-adjusted, gross (2000–2004)
How it loses money: Best results used non-public order data; public daily short-volume figures are noisy and turnover costs can erase the edge.
Key sources: Boehmer, Jones & Zhang (2008); Diether, Lee & Werner (2009); Engelberg, Reed & Ringgenberg (2012)

What to do: Using dealer or settlement data on customer currency trades, buy currencies that asset managers and other informed end-users are net buying and sell those they are selling.
Why it pays: Order flow from informed end-users carries information about fundamentals that exchange rates absorb gradually.
Track record: No reliable public trading figure; order flow explained over 60% of daily DM/$ moves (1996 data) and some customer groups' flows predict FX returns
How it loses money: Needs proprietary bank or settlement data, and flow signals can flip abruptly in risk-off episodes.
Key sources: Evans & Lyons (2002); Menkhoff, Sarno, Schmeling & Schrimpf (2016)

What to do: Underweight or short stocks that mutual funds are buying heavily because of investor inflows, and favour stocks funds are selling due to outflows, holding about a year.
Why it pays: Retail fund investors chase recent winners, and flow-driven buying lifts the stocks funds hold above fundamental value before it reverses.
Track record: Stocks most bought via fund inflows lagged least-bought ones over the next 1–3 years (US, 1980–2003); size varies by study
How it loses money: In the short run flow-driven buying keeps pushing prices up, so fading too early loses money.
Key sources: Frazzini & Lamont (2008); Lou (2012); Akbas, Armstrong, Sorescu & Subrahmanyam (2015)

What to do: Buy stocks or bonds that funds with heavy outflows (or regulated insurers) were forced to dump once the selling ends, or short them beforehand, holding while the discount recovers.
Why it pays: Forced sellers must trade regardless of value, so patient liquidity providers earn a discount that reverses as prices recover.
Track record: No reliable net figure; forced-sale stocks show large temporary price drops that reverse over subsequent quarters (US funds, 1980–2004)
How it loses money: Holdings are disclosed with a lag, some popular flow measures are flawed, and crisis selling can outlast your capital.
Key sources: Coval & Stafford (2007); Ellul, Jotikasthira & Lundblad (2011); Wardlaw (2020)

What to do: Score news stories, filings or earnings-call transcripts for positive or negative tone; buy stocks with the most positive fresh news and short the most negative, holding a day to weeks.
Why it pays: Investors underreact to soft information in text, while extreme market-wide media pessimism causes temporary overreaction that later reverses.
Track record: No reliable net figure; most predictive power fades within days and is very sensitive to trading costs
How it loses money: Speed race: machine-read news is priced within seconds, leaving slower traders mostly costs.
Key sources: Tetlock (2007); Tetlock, Saar-Tsechansky & Macskassy (2008); Ke, Kelly & Xiu (2019)

What to do: Each week, buy stocks whose call options are priced expensively relative to matching puts (higher implied volatility) and short stocks whose puts are relatively expensive.
Why it pays: Informed traders often act first in options, so lopsided option prices leak news the stock price has not yet absorbed.
Track record: ~50 bps/week long-short before costs (US, 1996–2005), shrinking over the sample period
How it loses money: Part of the signal reflects hard-to-borrow stocks, so the profitable short side is costly or impossible to trade.
Key sources: Cremers & Weinbaum (2010); Bali & Hovakimian (2009); An, Ang, Bali & Cakici (2014)

What to do: Short stocks whose out-of-the-money puts are unusually expensive versus at-the-money calls (steep skew) and buy those with the flattest skew, rebalancing weekly.
Why it pays: Informed traders expecting bad news bid up protective puts, and the stock price absorbs that information only slowly.
Track record: Steepest-skew stocks lagged flattest-skew stocks by ~10.9%/yr risk-adjusted (US, 1996–2005, in-sample)
How it loses money: Other skew measures predict the opposite sign, and the edge sits in small, less liquid optionable stocks.
Key sources: Xing, Zhang & Zhao (2010); Conrad, Dittmar & Ghysels (2013)

What to do: Buy stocks with unusually low put-versus-call buying or low option-to-stock trading volume, short those with high readings, and hold for about a week.
Why it pays: Informed traders, especially those with bad news, use options for leverage and to sidestep short-selling limits, so option activity leaks information.
Track record: Low put-call stocks beat high put-call stocks by roughly 1% the next week, US 1990–2001, using non-public CBOE order data; public-data versions are weaker
How it loses money: Public volume data hold far less information than the private data studied, and the short-lived edge is costly to trade.
Key sources: Pan & Poteshman (2006); Johnson & So (2012)

What to do: Identify retail trades from sub-penny price improvement in exchange data; buy stocks with net retail buying last week and short those with net retail selling.
Why it pays: Aggregated retail orders carry some information and supply liquidity that institutions later pay for.
Track record: Net-retail-buy stocks beat net-sell stocks by ~10 bps the next week (~5%/yr, gross, US 2010–2015)
How it loses money: The retail-identification method misclassifies many trades, and weekly turnover costs can eat the small edge.
Key sources: Boehmer, Jones, Zhang & Zhang (2021); Kelley & Tetlock (2013); Barber, Huang, Jorion, Odean & Schwarz (2024)

Also moves with: Defensive, Quality & Low Risk; Size & Illiquidity
What to do: Each month, short or avoid stocks whose borrowing fee, lending utilisation or shorting demand has jumped, and favour cheap-to-borrow stocks.
Why it pays: Rising borrow demand reveals informed pessimism, while high fees and recall risk limit arbitrage, leaving these stocks overpriced.
Track record: Stocks with rising shorting demand earned about -2.98% abnormal return the next month (Cohen, Diether & Malloy, gross); borrow fees absorb much of the short-side gain; no reliable net figure
How it loses money: Borrow fees, share recalls and squeezes on the short side can exceed the price drop you are betting on.
Key sources: Cohen, Diether & Malloy (2007); Engelberg, Reed & Ringgenberg (2018); Muravyev, Pearson & Pollet (2022)

Also moves with: Defensive, Quality & Low Risk; Size & Illiquidity
What to do: Run anomaly long-short portfolios, especially shorting speculative, hard-to-value stocks, more heavily after months when the public Baker-Wurgler investor-sentiment index is high.
Why it pays: Optimism inflates small, young, volatile, hard-to-short stocks, so their later underperformance is biggest after high-sentiment periods.
Track record: Anomaly long-short profits notably larger after high-sentiment months, mostly from the short leg (11 US anomalies, 1965–2008)
How it loses money: Sentiment can stay high for years, so shorting speculative stocks early (e.g., 1999, 2020–21) is painful.
Key sources: Baker & Wurgler (2006); Stambaugh, Yu & Yuan (2012); Baker, Wurgler & Yuan (2012)

Strategy: Short interest / days-to-cover (avoid heavily shorted stocks)
Also moves with: Value & Long-Term Reversal; Defensive, Quality & Low Risk
What to do: Each month, avoid or short the stocks with the highest short interest or days-to-cover (shares sold short divided by average daily volume), and buy those with the lowest.
Why it pays: Short sellers are often well informed, and the cost and risk of shorting stop prices from fully reflecting their pessimism.
Track record: Heavily shorted Nasdaq stocks lagged by 0.76–1.13%/month risk-adjusted (1988–1994); much weaker value-weighted
How it loses money: Short squeezes: heavily shorted stocks can spike violently, and borrowing them is costly or impossible.
Key sources: Desai, Ramesh, Thiagarajan & Balachandran (2002); Asquith, Pathak & Ritter (2005); Hong, Li, Ni, Scheinkman & Yan (2015)

What to do: After each quarter's 13F holdings filings (due 45 days after quarter-end), buy the stocks top hedge funds or famous investors hold most heavily or recently added.
Why it pays: Some managers have real stock-picking skill, and their highest-conviction ideas may keep paying after the disclosure delay.
Track record: Copying Berkshire Hathaway's disclosed buys beat the S&P 500 by ~10%/yr in one study (1976–2006); broad hedge-fund clones far less
How it loses money: Stale data and crowding: managers hide their best ideas, and popular hedge-fund names sell off together when funds deleverage.
Key sources: Martin & Puthenpurackal (2008); Frank, Poterba, Shackelford & Shoven (2004); Agarwal, Jiang, Tang & Yang (2013)

What to do: After months when investors switch heavily from bond funds into stock funds, cut stock-index exposure; after heavy switches out of stock funds, add exposure, holding a few months.
Why it pays: Flow-driven buying by retail fund switchers pushes index prices away from value, and most of that move later reverses.
Track record: Most of the flow-linked market move reversed within about 4 months (US, 1984–2008); no tradable net figure
How it loses money: Flows can keep chasing a rising market for years, so fading them early means missing rallies.
Key sources: Ben-Rephael, Kandel & Wohl (2012)

What to do: Cut stock-market exposure when total (trend-adjusted) short interest across US stocks is high, and raise it when low, reviewing monthly.
Why it pays: Short sellers collectively anticipate bad market-wide cash-flow news, so their combined positioning forecasts index returns.
Track record: Reported annual out-of-sample R² ~13% for US market returns (1973–2014); little post-publication or live evidence
How it loses money: Like most market-timing signals it may fail out of sample and leave you underinvested in rallies.
Key sources: Rapach, Ringgenberg & Zhou (2016)

Strategy: Alternative-data nowcasting (satellite, card spending, web traffic)
What to do: Estimate company sales or commodity inventories before official reports from satellite images, card transactions or web/app traffic; buy where data beat consensus, short where they miss.
Why it pays: Real-time data reveal fundamentals before official reports, and investors without it only update at announcements.
Track record: No reliable public figure; studies find the edge concentrated around earnings and shrinking as datasets spread
How it loses money: Expensive data that decays as more buyers get it; one bad read before earnings can be costly.
Key sources: Froot, Kang, Ozik & Sadka (2017); Zhu (2019); Mukherjee, Panayotov & Shon (2021)

Strategy: Change in breadth of fund ownership
What to do: Each quarter, buy stocks held by a growing number of mutual funds and avoid or short stocks that funds are abandoning, holding about a year.
Why it pays: With shorting constrained, falling ownership breadth means pessimists have stepped aside, so the price mostly reflects optimists and later falls.
Track record: Falling-breadth stocks lagged rising-breadth stocks by a few %/yr after risk adjustment (US, 1979–1998); little recent evidence
How it loses money: Holdings data arrive with a lag and the effect is modest, so costs and stale signals can erase it.
Key sources: Chen, Hong & Stein (2002)

What to do: Overweight commodities as a group when total futures open interest (contracts outstanding) has grown strongly over the past year, and underweight them when it has shrunk.
Why it pays: Rising open interest reflects growing hedging demand and economic activity before prices fully adjust, because arbitrage capital in futures is limited.
Track record: No reliable figure; evidence comes mainly from predictive regressions, not a traded strategy
How it loses money: The signal is noisy and slow, and open interest can rise on index inflows that carry no information.
Key sources: Hong & Yogo (2012)

Strategy: Contrarian sentiment-indicator timing (AAII surveys, put/call ratio, fear indices)
Also moves with: Macro & Asset Allocation; Short Volatility & Insurance Selling
What to do: Buy the stock index when investor surveys, put/call ratios or search-based fear indices show extreme pessimism, and cut exposure at extreme optimism.
Why it pays: Crowds of individual investors extrapolate recent moves, so extreme mood can push index prices temporarily away from value.
Track record: No reliable figure; little power at weekly–monthly horizons, some at 1–3 years in US data (overlapping-horizon tests)
How it loses money: Pessimism can deepen for months in a real bear market, so buying fear early brings large drawdowns.
Key sources: Fisher & Statman (2000); Brown & Cliff (2005); Da, Engelberg & Gao (2015)

What to do: Buy a coin when online attention (Google searches, Twitter/X mentions) is unusually high or rising, and cut exposure when it fades.
Why it pays: Retail-driven crypto prices react with a lag to bursts of attention as new buyers pile in.
Track record: No reliable net figure; attention proxies forecast bitcoin returns over the following weeks in-sample, roughly 2011–2018
How it loses money: Attention spikes often mark tops, the data are noisy and revised, and the signal is easily crowded.
Key sources: Liu & Tsyvinski (2021); Benedetti & Kostovetsky (2021)

What to do: When an ETF sees heavy share creations (inflows), short it or its holdings; after heavy redemptions, buy; hold days to weeks as the price pressure fades.
Why it pays: Flow-driven, non-fundamental demand for ETFs is passed by arbitrageurs into the underlying stocks, temporarily pushing prices away from value.
Track record: Large in-sample long-short returns reported on ETF portfolios; no reliable net or live figure
How it loses money: Flows can persist for weeks, and the effect is small relative to costs in liquid ETFs.
Key sources: Ben-David, Franzoni & Moussawi (2018); Brown, Davies & Ringgenberg (2021)

Strategy: End-of-day hedging-flow momentum (leveraged-ETF rebalancing, dealer gamma)
What to do: On big up (down) days, buy (sell) index futures in the last half-hour, ahead of forced buying (selling) by leveraged ETFs and short-gamma option dealers, and exit at the close.
Why it pays: Leveraged ETFs and option dealers who are short gamma must buy after gains and sell after losses, creating predictable flows near the close.
Markets: Equity indices & ETFs; Bonds & rates; Commodities
Track record: No reliable net figure; late-day moves are small, and how much comes from leveraged ETFs is debated
How it loses money: The flows are widely anticipated and partly offset, so per-trade gains are tiny and costs or a late reversal can erase them.
Key sources: Cheng & Madhavan (2009); Baltussen, Da, Lammers & Martens (2021); Ivanov & Lenkey (2018)

What to do: Using currency option prices, buy currencies where insurance against volatility is cheap (implied volatility low versus expected actual volatility) and sell those where it is expensive, rebalancing monthly.
Why it pays: Option prices reveal where investors are paying up to hedge, and those currencies tend to underperform, likely because hedging pressure meets limited arbitrage capital.
Track record: No reliable figure; returns came mainly from exchange-rate moves rather than interest gaps, with low correlation to carry
How it loses money: The signal is noisy and leans on emerging-market currencies, which can gap sharply in crises.
Key sources: Della Corte, Ramadorai & Sarno (2016)

What to do: Short or avoid stocks that novice retail traders (e.g., Robinhood users) pile into en masse on a given day, holding for about a month.
Why it pays: Attention-driven herding by inexperienced traders pushes prices above value, and the overshoot then reverses.
Track record: Top daily Robinhood herding stocks: roughly −5% abnormal return over the next 20 trading days (US, 2018–2020)
How it loses money: Meme-stock frenzies can squeeze shorts badly, and the public Robinhood popularity data stopped in 2020.
Key sources: Barber, Huang, Odean & Schwarz (2022); Barber & Odean (2008); Welch (2022)

What to do: Buy the stocks Wall Street analysts rate most favourably on average (consensus 'strong buy') and avoid or short the least favourably rated, updating as ratings change.
Why it pays: Analysts have some information, but ratings tilt toward glamour and momentum stocks and the edge decays within days.
Track record: Most- minus least-recommended: >4%/yr gross abnormal (US, 1986–1996) with daily rebalancing; not reliably positive after costs
How it loses money: High turnover eats the small edge, and analysts' favourites can crash together, as in 2000–2001.
Key sources: Barber, Lehavy, McNichols & Trueman (2001); Jegadeesh, Kim, Krische & Lee (2004); Womack (1996)

What to do: Buy stocks or cryptocurrencies whose Google search volume or trading volume suddenly jumps, and hold about two weeks before the attention-driven gain fades.
Why it pays: Retail investors buy what grabs their attention, creating temporary buying pressure on newly visible assets.
Track record: No reliable net figure; search spikes predicted higher prices for ~2 weeks that largely reversed within a year (US, 2004–2008)
How it loses money: Search-driven gains reverse, so mistiming the exit turns a short pop into a loss.
Key sources: Da, Engelberg & Gao (2011); Gervais, Kaniel & Mingelgrin (2001); Liu & Tsyvinski (2021)

What to do: Compare each firm's annual or quarterly report text with last year's; buy firms whose filings barely changed and short those that changed most, holding several months.
Why it pays: Investors skim boilerplate filings, yet changes in wording (especially risk factors and legal sections) foreshadow bad news.
Track record: Up to ~1.9%/month alpha in the best specification, long non-changers / short changers (US, 1995–2014, in-sample)
How it loses money: Single main study, now widely run by quants and data vendors, so the mispricing may close faster than in the backtest.
Key sources: Cohen, Malloy & Nguyen (2020)

What to do: Each month, buy stocks that received no major newspaper coverage and short the most heavily covered ones.
Why it pays: Neglected stocks must offer higher returns because fewer investors know or hold them, while heavily covered stocks attract overpaying attention.
Track record: No-coverage stocks beat high-coverage stocks by ~3%/yr risk-adjusted (US, 1993–2002), mostly among small stocks
How it loses money: Largely a small, illiquid-stock effect, so trading costs can consume it.
Key sources: Fang & Peress (2009); Merton (1987)

What to do: Buy stocks receiving well-argued bullish articles or research posts on investor social media, and avoid heavily criticised ones, holding days to a few months.
Why it pays: Crowds pool scattered information, and some contributors do genuine research that prices absorb slowly.
Track record: No reliable figure; WSB due-diligence posts predicted modest gains before 2021 but not after the GameStop surge
How it loses money: Hype and coordinated pumps mix with real research, and crowded meme names can collapse quickly.
Key sources: Chen, De, Hu & Hwang (2014); Bradley, Hanousek, Jame & Xiao (2024); Antweiler & Frank (2004)

What to do: Buy the local stock index on sunny mornings, or short it the day after the national football team is knocked out of a major tournament.
Why it pays: Mood swings unrelated to fundamentals briefly change investors' risk appetite.
Track record: Measurable but tiny effects (e.g., ~−0.5% next day after World Cup knockout losses); not profitable after costs for most
How it loses money: Effects are too small and rare to beat trading costs and everyday market noise.
Key sources: Saunders (1993); Hirshleifer & Shumway (2003); Edmans, Garcia & Norli (2007)

What to do: Keep posting orders to buy slightly below and sell slightly above the current price, earn that gap (the spread) on each round trip, and keep inventory near zero.
Why it pays: Impatient traders pay the spread for instant execution, which pays the market maker for holding inventory and sometimes trading against better-informed traders.
Markets: Stocks; Equity indices & ETFs; Bonds & rates; FX
Track record: Virtu: 1 losing day in 1,238 (2009–13, IPO filing). One Dutch-stock HFT market maker earned ~€0.88 gross per trade, 2007–08 (Menkveld).
How it loses money: Faster or better-informed traders hit its out-of-date quotes, and sudden one-way moves (e.g., the 2010 Flash Crash) leave it holding losing inventory.
Key sources: Menkveld (2013); Brogaard, Hendershott & Riordan (2014); Baron, Brogaard, Hagströmer & Kirilenko (2019)

Strategy: Floor specialist / dealer market making (pre-decimal era)
What to do: As the exchange's official dealer for assigned stocks, quote buy and sell prices and earn wide spreads set by large fixed price steps (e.g., 1/8 dollar), while seeing all waiting orders.
Why it pays: Large minimum price steps and privileged views of order flow let dealers charge wide spreads before electronic competition arrived.
Track record: No reliable figure. Spreads and specialist profits fell sharply after US decimalisation (2001) and the move to electronic trading.
How it loses money: Dealers had to keep trading during crashes (e.g., 1987), and faster electronic market makers took over the role.
Key sources: Hasbrouck & Sofianos (1993); Hendershott, Jones & Menkveld (2011)

Strategy: Latency arbitrage (stale-quote sniping, incl. futures-vs-ETF races)
What to do: When a price jumps on one exchange or in a linked instrument (e.g., S&P 500 futures), instantly trade against quotes elsewhere (e.g., the SPY ETF) that haven't updated yet, then hedge.
Why it pays: A posted quote is a free option for others, so whoever reacts microseconds faster to public price moves pockets the stale-price gap.
Track record: UK 2015: latency-arbitrage races were ~20% of FTSE 100 volume, a ~0.5bp tax on trading; top 6 firms won >80% of races. ES-SPY arbitrage windows shrank sharply over 2005-11 as speed rose.
How it loses money: Arriving microseconds late means trading at a bad price or leaving one leg unhedged, and network and co-location costs are large and fixed.
Key sources: Budish, Cramton & Shim (2015); Aquilina, Budish & O'Neill (2022); Foucault, Kozhan & Tham (2017)

Strategy: Machine-readable news and macro-release speed trading
What to do: Receive economic data, earnings or regulatory filings through ultra-fast machine-readable feeds and, within milliseconds, trade index futures, ETFs or the stock in the direction of the surprise.
Why it pays: Prices must absorb public news, and whoever reads and acts on it first captures the initial move before slower traders arrive.
Track record: Fastest traders earned tens of thousands of dollars per US macro release in SPY and S&P futures; prices adjust within milliseconds (2010s).
How it loses money: Wrong or fake headlines (e.g., the hacked AP tweet in 2013) trigger losing trades, and slower feeds lose every race.
Key sources: Chordia, Green & Kottimukkalur (2018); Groß-Klußmann & Hautsch (2011); Rogers, Skinner & Zechman (2017)

What to do: Keep quoting buy and sell prices on listed options, hedge the stock-price exposure with the underlying, and earn the spread while limiting bets on volatility and big jumps.
Why it pays: Option users pay for immediate trading, and dealers charge extra for risk they can't fully hedge, especially after selling more options than they bought.
Track record: No reliable figure
How it loses money: Sudden price gaps or volatility spikes while the dealer is net short options cause losses faster than hedging can keep up.
Key sources: Gârleanu, Pedersen & Poteshman (2009); Muravyev (2016)

Strategy: Order anticipation (trading around large institutional orders, 'back-running')
Also moves with: Trend & Momentum; Sentiment, Flows & Alt Data
What to do: Using only public trade and quote data, spot a large fund order being executed in slices, then trade the same way ahead of the remaining slices or sell it liquidity early.
Why it pays: Big orders split up over hours leave predictable footprints, so their remaining price pressure can be foreseen and partly captured.
Track record: No reliable figure. HFT trades predict later non-HFT order flow (US); HFTs first lean against, then trade with, long fund orders (Sweden).
How it loses money: Mistaking random trading for a big order, or the fund pausing or reversing, leaves you holding a losing position.
Key sources: van Kervel & Menkveld (2019); Korajczyk & Murphy (2019); Hirschey (2021)

What to do: Buy when waiting buy orders or recent buy trades clearly outweigh sell orders at the best prices (sell on the reverse), trading immediately and exiting within seconds.
Why it pays: An excess of buyers over sellers at the best prices predicts the next small price tick, and only the fastest can act before quotes adjust.
Track record: No strategy-specific figure. All HFT firms in S&P 500 E-mini futures: median annualised Sharpe ~4.3, gross (CFTC data, 2010–12, JFQA).
How it loses money: The edge per trade is tiny, so paying the spread, being slightly slower, or reacting to fleeting or fake orders turns it into losses.
Key sources: Cont, Kukanov & Stoikov (2014); Gould & Bonart (2016); Baron, Brogaard, Hagströmer & Kirilenko (2019)

Strategy: Retail order-flow internalisation (wholesaling / payment for order flow)
What to do: Pay retail brokers for their customers' stock and options orders, fill those orders in-house at or slightly better than the best public price, and hedge the leftover risk.
Why it pays: Small retail orders rarely carry inside information, so filling them is low-risk and lets the wholesaler keep part of the bid-ask spread.
Track record: No reliable public figure. A handful of wholesalers (e.g., Citadel Securities, Virtu) fill most US retail stock and options orders.
How it loses money: Regulators can ban it (UK since 2012, EU from mid-2026), and one-way retail stampedes are costly to hedge.
Key sources: Easley, Kiefer & O'Hara (1996); Bryzgalova, Pavlova & Sikorskaya (2023); Ernst & Spatt (2022)

What to do: Continuously post buy and sell quotes on crypto exchanges, earning the bid-ask spread and any maker rebates while keeping your coin inventory close to flat.
Why it pays: Impatient traders pay for immediacy, and fragmented, volatile 24/7 markets keep spreads wider than in mature markets.
Track record: No reliable figure; profits of specialist firms are private
How it loses money: Better-informed traders pick off stale quotes, and crashes or exchange outages leave you holding losing inventory.
Key sources: Barbon & Ranaldo (2021)

What to do: Post buy and sell limit orders on exchanges that pay a per-share rebate to whoever supplies liquidity, aiming to earn rebate plus spread while holding almost no inventory.
Why it pays: Exchanges pay rebates to attract resting orders, and the highest-volume firms qualify for the richest rebate tiers.
Track record: No reliable figure. Top US rebates reach ~0.3¢/share, but fills on high-rebate venues tend to come just before adverse moves.
How it loses money: Fills on high-rebate exchanges cluster just before the price turns against you, and the SEC voted in 2024 to cut the fee cap from 0.3¢ to 0.1¢.
Key sources: Malinova & Park (2015); Battalio, Corwin & Jennings (2016); Comerton-Forde, Grégoire & Zhong (2019)

What to do: In stocks or futures whose minimum price step (tick) is large relative to price, post orders the instant a new price level appears so you are first in line for fills.
Why it pays: A large tick keeps spreads artificially wide, and first-come-first-served matching hands that extra profit to whoever queues first, usually the fastest firm.
Track record: No reliable figure. Model-based studies find a front-of-queue spot is worth a meaningful share of the spread in large-tick US stocks.
How it loses money: Even front-of-queue orders get filled just before adverse moves, and tick-size cuts shrink the artificially wide spread.
Key sources: Yao & Ye (2018); Moallemi & Yuan (2017)

What to do: Hold about 60% in a stock index fund and 40% in high-quality government or investment-grade bonds, and rebalance back to those weights on a schedule, such as once a year.
Why it pays: You collect most of the equity premium plus the bond term premium (extra pay for lending long), and bonds have often cushioned stock sell-offs.
Markets: Multi-asset; Equity indices & ETFs; Bonds & rates
Track record: About 8–9%/yr nominal, US 1926–2023, long-only before fees; worst calendar year about −27% (1931)
How it loses money: Stocks and bonds can fall together when inflation and rates jump, as in 2022 when a US 60/40 lost roughly 16%.
Key sources: Asness (1996); Ilmanen (2011); Anderson, Bianchi & Goldberg (2012); Vanguard historical 60/40 return data

What to do: Buy a broad, low-cost stock index fund, reinvest the dividends and hold it for decades, sitting through bear markets instead of trying to time them.
Why it pays: Investors are paid for bearing large losses that tend to arrive in recessions, when jobs and incomes are also under pressure.
Track record: About 5.1%/yr real for world stocks and about 6.6%/yr real for US stocks, 1900–2023, long-only before costs (Dimson-Marsh-Staunton data)
How it loses money: Drawdowns of 50%+ and decade-long stretches of trailing cash (US 2000–2009, Japan after 1990).
Key sources: Mehra & Prescott (1985); Dimson, Marsh & Staunton (2002); Siegel (1994)

Strategy: Bond term premium (holding long-term government bonds)
Also moves with: Carry & Yield; Defensive, Quality & Low Risk
What to do: Hold long-term government bonds, or a long-bond fund, instead of cash or Treasury bills, to earn the extra return that longer maturities usually pay.
Why it pays: Investors want extra return for the risk that inflation or rising rates cut long-bond prices.
Track record: About 1.5–2%/yr over T-bills, long US Treasuries 1926–2023 (long-only, gross), with losing stretches lasting decades.
How it loses money: Inflation or rate rises crush long bonds; long US Treasuries fell over 40% from 2020 to 2023.
Key sources: Fama & Bliss (1987); Campbell & Shiller (1991); Dimson, Marsh & Staunton (2002)

Strategy: Country and asset-class allocation by value, carry and momentum
Also moves with: Value & Long-Term Reversal; Trend & Momentum; Carry & Yield
What to do: Rank country stock indices (and bond, currency or commodity markets) monthly; overweight those that are cheap, offer high yield ('carry') and have strong 12-month momentum, and underweight the opposite.
Why it pays: The same risk and behavioural forces behind stock-level value and momentum; combining them, since they tend to move oppositely, smooths returns.
Markets: Equity indices & ETFs; Bonds & rates; FX; Commodities
Track record: Long-short, gross, 1972–2011: value-plus-momentum combos had markedly higher Sharpe ratios than either alone across country indices and asset classes
How it loses money: Few markets means concentrated, noisy bets; value and carry legs crash in risk-off episodes and suffered in 2018–2020.
Key sources: Asness, Liew & Stevens (1997); Asness, Moskowitz & Pedersen (2013); Koijen, Moskowitz, Pedersen & Vrugt (2018)

What to do: Split money equally across your chosen assets or funds and rebalance periodically, instead of using optimiser software that estimates expected returns and correlations.
Why it pays: Errors in estimated returns and correlations swamp an optimiser's theoretical gains, so a simple rule often holds up better on new data.
Track record: None of 14 optimised models reliably beat 1/N's out-of-sample Sharpe across 7 equity datasets (DeMiguel et al.); Kritzman et al. dispute this
How it loses money: Ignores differences in risk, so the most volatile asset dominates losses; a poorly chosen asset list dilutes returns.
Key sources: DeMiguel, Garlappi & Uppal (2009); Kritzman, Page & Turkington (2010)

What to do: Weight stocks, bonds, commodities and so on so each contributes equal risk (roughly inverse to its volatility), then borrow to lift the bond-heavy mix to stock-like volatility.
Why it pays: Many investors can't or won't borrow, so they overpay for risky assets, leaving safer assets like bonds with better returns per unit of risk.
Markets: Multi-asset; Bonds & rates; Equity indices & ETFs; Commodities
Track record: Beat 60/40 risk-adjusted on US stocks/bonds 1926–2010 gross, but not robustly after realistic borrowing and trading costs (Anderson et al. 2012)
How it loses money: Leveraged bonds get hit when inflation and rates spike while stocks also fall, as in 2022.
Key sources: Qian (2005); Asness, Frazzini & Pedersen (2012); Anderson, Bianchi & Goldberg (2012)

What to do: When a holding falls below what you paid, sell it to book the tax loss and immediately buy a similar but not 'substantially identical' fund or stocks so your market exposure is unchanged.
Why it pays: Booked losses cut your tax bill now, while tax on the replacement's gains is put off until you sell, often at lower long-term rates.
Track record: ~1.08%/yr simulated after-tax 'tax alpha' before costs (0.82% obeying wash-sale rule), 500 largest US stocks, 1926–2018
How it loses money: It mostly defers tax rather than cancelling it; gains shrink as cost basis falls, and wash-sale errors or higher future tax rates erode them.
Key sources: Constantinides (1983); Arnott, Berkin & Ye (2001); Chaudhuri, Burnham & Lo (2020)

Strategy: Trend following as a crisis hedge ("crisis alpha")
What to do: Put a slice of a stock-and-bond portfolio into a diversified managed-futures (trend-following) fund or ETF and rebalance yearly, aiming to profit during prolonged sell-offs.
Why it pays: Trend behaves like a rolling option straddle ('long convexity'): big sustained moves either way pay off, so long bear markets become shorting gains.
Track record: Positive in 8 of the 10 worst 60/40 drawdowns, 1880–2016 (backtest); SG Trend Index +27% in 2022 and Barclay CTA Index ~+14% in 2008 (net)
How it loses money: Little help in sudden, quickly reversed crashes, and it drags on returns for years in calm bull markets.
Key sources: Hurst, Ooi & Pedersen (2017); Hamill, Rattray & Van Hemert (2016); Dao et al. (2016)

Strategy: Bond-market timing with forward rates (Cochrane-Piazzesi factor)
What to do: Hold more long-maturity bonds when the Cochrane-Piazzesi factor, a tent-shaped blend of 1- to 5-year forward rates, signals high expected bond returns, and fewer when it signals low.
Why it pays: Bond risk premia rise in bad times, and the shape of the forward curve partly reveals how much premium is on offer.
Track record: In-sample R² up to 44% for 1-year US bond excess returns, 1964–2003; little proven economic value out of sample.
How it loses money: The forecasting relationship is unstable out of sample, so timing calls can simply be wrong.
Key sources: Cochrane & Piazzesi (2005); Thornton & Valente (2012); Bauer & Hamilton (2018)

What to do: Hold more stocks when the market's price relative to its 10-year average inflation-adjusted earnings (Shiller CAPE) is low versus history, and fewer when it is high.
Why it pays: High valuations imply lower future earnings yields and often reflect over-optimism that later fades.
Track record: Good in-sample 10-year return forecasts, but CAPE-based timing rules added little or nothing over buy-and-hold in AQR tests since 1900, gross
How it loses money: Markets can stay expensive for decades (US since the 1990s), leaving you underweight through big rallies.
Key sources: Campbell & Shiller (1998); Goyal & Welch (2008); Asness, Ilmanen & Maloney (2017)

What to do: Cut holdings of corporate, especially high-yield, bonds when junk-rated firms make up an unusually large share of new bond issuance, and add back when that share is low.
Why it pays: Investors extrapolate good times, so when easy credit lets weak firms borrow heavily, later bond returns tend to disappoint.
Track record: High junk-issuance share predicted low US corporate bond excess returns over following 2–3 years (in-sample, long US history); no proven trading record.
How it loses money: Credit can stay 'expensive' for years, so you miss strong returns while waiting.
Key sources: Greenwood & Hanson (2013); López-Salido, Stein & Zakrajšek (2017)

What to do: Cut stock and junk-bond exposure when the extra yield on corporate bonds over Treasuries (credit spread) or a financial-conditions index widens sharply, and add risk back when it narrows.
Why it pays: Widening spreads flag tighter credit and rising default risk, which tend to precede weaker growth and stock drawdowns.
Track record: No reliable figure; the default spread fails out of sample as a stock-return predictor (Goyal-Welch), though credit spreads forecast recessions
How it loses money: Wide spreads also mean higher future returns, so de-risking at peak stress often means selling near the bottom.
Key sources: Fama & French (1989); Gilchrist & Zakrajšek (2012); López-Salido, Stein & Zakrajšek (2017)

What to do: Hold a long-term portfolio with half or more in private equity, venture capital, hedge funds and real assets and little in bonds, as Yale's endowment did under David Swensen.
Why it pays: Perpetual investors can tolerate illiquidity and supposedly earn illiquidity premiums and access to skilled managers that shorter-horizon investors cannot.
Track record: Large US endowments trailed a matched passive stock/bond index by ~1.6%/yr after 2008 (Ennis); elite endowments outperformed 1992–2005
How it loses money: High fees and illiquid, appraisal-priced holdings drag returns and can force sales of liquid assets in a crisis, as in 2008.
Key sources: Lerner, Schoar & Wang (2008); Dahiya & Yermack (2018); Ennis (2020)

Strategy: Equity-premium forecasting with macro/valuation variables (combination forecasts)
What to do: Each month, average simple forecasts of the stock market's return over cash from many indicators (dividend yield, interest rates, credit spreads, inflation) and tilt your stock/cash mix toward the average.
Why it pays: Expected returns rise in bad times when investors are more fearful; averaging many weak signals cuts the noise of any single one.
Track record: Single predictors mostly fail out of sample; averaged forecasts gave a small positive out-of-sample fit (R² a few % quarterly), US post-war data
How it loses money: Relationships drift or vanish, so the model can tilt the wrong way for years; the edge is tiny next to estimation error.
Key sources: Goyal & Welch (2008); Rapach, Strauss & Zhou (2010); Goyal, Welch & Zafirov (2024)

What to do: Shift money between stock investing styles ('factors' such as value, momentum, quality, low-volatility) toward those that look cheapest or have performed best recently, and away from the rest.
Why it pays: Style premia vary with risk and crowding; cheap or recently strong styles have earned somewhat more, but the signals are weak.
Track record: No reliable figure; timing by valuation spreads added little (Asness et al. 2017), though Haddad et al. (2020) report sizeable gains
How it loses money: Signals are noisy and can stay wrong for years; value looked 'cheap' through 2018–2020 while it kept falling.
Key sources: Asness, Chandra, Ilmanen & Israel (2017); Haddad, Kozak & Santosh (2020); Ehsani & Linnainmaa (2022)

Strategy: Fed policy regime timing ('Don't fight the Fed')
What to do: Hold more stocks after the Fed starts cutting interest rates (its policy or discount rate) and shift toward cash or bonds after it starts raising them, until the direction changes.
Why it pays: Easier money lowers discount rates and funding costs and supports growth, so expected stock returns seem to vary with the monetary-policy cycle.
Track record: In-sample: S&P 500 ~14%/yr real in easing vs ~2%/yr in tightening regimes, 1966–2020, before costs (authors' 2022 update)
How it loses money: The Fed often cuts because a recession is starting, so stocks can keep falling for months after easing begins (2001–02, 2007–09).
Key sources: Jensen, Mercer & Johnson (1996); Conover, Jensen & Johnson (1999); Durham (2003)

Strategy: Gold allocation as inflation and crisis hedge
What to do: Keep a fixed slice (often 5–10%) of a portfolio in gold or a gold ETF, rebalancing periodically, to cushion against inflation, currency debasement and stock-market crashes.
Why it pays: Gold has no credit risk and attracts panic and central-bank buying in crises, but its long-run real return is low and its inflation link weak over practical horizons.
Track record: Real price fell ~85% from the Jan 1980 peak to 2001; the $850 nominal peak was not regained until 2008
How it loses money: It pays no income and can lose most of its real value for decades; its safe-haven boost in crashes is often short-lived.
Key sources: Baur & Lucey (2010); Baur & McDermott (2010); Erb & Harvey (2013)

What to do: While young, hold up to about 2x your savings in stocks (e.g. via deep in-the-money index call options), then cut leverage and later go below 100% stocks as savings grow.
Why it pays: Young savers' future earnings act like a bond, so their total wealth holds too little stock; early leverage evens out lifetime risk.
Track record: No reliable live figure; simulations on US data back to 1871 showed higher retirement wealth than target-date-style paths at similar risk
How it loses money: An early-career crash can wipe out leveraged savings, and borrowing costs or forced selling can lock in losses.
Key sources: Ayres & Nalebuff (2010); Ayres & Nalebuff (2013)

What to do: Hold an equal-weighted, regularly rebalanced basket of fully cash-backed commodity futures, rolling each contract before expiry, as a long-term portfolio allocation.
Why it pays: Producers pay speculators to take their price risk (Keynes's 'normal backwardation'), and rebalancing many volatile, loosely related commodities adds a diversification return.
Track record: Equity-like ~5%/yr above T-bills, equal-weighted rebalanced index, 1959–2004; broad commodity indices weak over most of 2008–2020
How it loses money: Long stretches of contango (paying to roll contracts) plus falling prices can produce a lost decade.
Key sources: Gorton & Rouwenhorst (2006); Erb & Harvey (2006); Bhardwaj, Gorton & Rouwenhorst (2015)

What to do: Go long markets whose economic backdrop has trended favourably over the past year (e.g., rising growth for stocks, falling inflation for bonds) and short those trending unfavourably.
Why it pays: Markets under-react to gradual changes in macroeconomic data, so prices drift in the direction of trending fundamentals.
Markets: Multi-asset; Equity indices & ETFs; Bonds & rates; FX; Commodities
Track record: No reliable figure
How it loses money: Mostly practitioner backtests; data revisions and sudden economic turning points flip signals too late.
Key sources: Brooks (2017); Dahlquist & Hasseltoft (2020)

What to do: Hold 25% each in a stock index, long-term Treasury bonds, gold and cash (T-bills), and rebalance back to equal slices about once a year.
Why it pays: No extra premium beyond its parts: each slice suits a different climate (growth, recession, inflation, deflation), trading lower return for smaller drawdowns.
Markets: Multi-asset; Equity indices & ETFs; Bonds & rates; Commodities
Track record: No reliable peer-reviewed figure; practitioner backtests since the 1970s show returns below stocks with much smaller drawdowns
How it loses money: Long stretches of lagging stocks; cash and gold drag, and stocks plus long bonds can fall together in inflation shocks.
Key sources: Browne (1987); Browne (1999)

Strategy: Protective / Vigilant / Defensive asset allocation (Keller's canary rules)
What to do: Monthly, rotate into the few ETFs with the best recent momentum, moving part or all of the portfolio to bonds/cash when 'canary' assets (emerging-market stocks, aggregate bonds) show negative momentum.
Why it pays: Weak momentum across many markets at once can be an early crash warning, so going defensive early aims to dodge most of a bear market.
Markets: Multi-asset; Equity indices & ETFs; Bonds & rates; Commodities
Track record: No reliable figure; only the authors' own backtests (1970s–2010s), which are heavily optimised in-sample and not independently tested
How it loses money: Overfitted rules give false crash alarms and leave you in cash during rallies; frequent switching adds costs and taxes.
Key sources: Keller & Keuning (2016); Keller & Keuning (2017); Keller & Keuning (2018)

Also moves with: Value & Long-Term Reversal; Short Volatility & Insurance Selling
What to do: On a fixed schedule, sell some of the assets that have risen and buy those that have fallen to get back to your target weights.
Why it pays: Mechanically buying low and selling high adds a small 'diversification return' when assets are volatile, weakly correlated and partly mean-reverting; mostly it stops risk drifting.
Track record: No reliable figure; the extra return is small for stock/bond mixes and larger for volatile, uncorrelated baskets such as equal-weight commodities
How it loses money: In long trends it keeps buying the loser, lagging buy-and-hold; it behaves like a short-volatility bet.
Key sources: Booth & Fama (1992); Willenbrock (2011); Granger, Greenig, Harvey, Rattray & Zou (2014)

Strategy: Small bitcoin allocation in a diversified portfolio
What to do: Keep a small fixed slice (e.g., 1–5%) of a stock-and-bond portfolio in bitcoin, rebalancing back to target periodically so you trim after rallies and top up after crashes.
Why it pays: Bitcoin's large but volatile returns and historically low correlation with stocks and bonds raised risk-adjusted portfolio returns in past data.
Track record: No reliable forward-looking figure; 2010s studies show higher Sharpe ratios in-sample, driven by bitcoin's extraordinary past gains
How it loses money: Bitcoin can fall 75–85% (as in 2018 and 2022) and since 2020 has often dropped together with stocks in sell-offs.
Key sources: Platanakis & Urquhart (2020); Adrian, Iyer & Qureshi (2022, IMF blog)

Strategy: Variance-risk-premium market timing (VIX minus actual volatility)
What to do: Hold more stocks when the VIX (option-implied volatility) is far above the market's recent actual volatility, and fewer when that gap is small or negative.
Why it pays: A wide gap means investors are paying a high price for protection, which tends to be followed by higher stock returns as that fear premium is earned.
Track record: Predicted next-quarter US stock-market returns in-sample, 1990–2007; out-of-sample timing gains are less certain
How it loses money: The gap can widen further in a crisis, so you add stocks just before they fall more.
Key sources: Bollerslev, Tauchen & Zhou (2009); Bollerslev, Marrone, Xu & Zhou (2014)

Also moves with: Defensive, Quality & Low Risk; Trend & Momentum
What to do: Each month, scale exposure to the market or a factor inversely to its recent volatility, holding more when markets are calm and less when they are turbulent.
Why it pays: Volatility spikes are not matched by higher expected returns, so cutting exposure in turbulent periods improves return per unit of risk.
Track record: Higher Sharpe ratios in-sample for the market and many factors, US 1926–2015; mostly not robust in real-time out-of-sample tests
How it loses money: Needs leverage in calm periods, misses sharp rebounds after crashes, and gains often vanish out-of-sample after costs.
Key sources: Barroso & Santa-Clara (2015); Moreira & Muir (2017); Cederburg, O'Doherty, Wang & Yan (2020)

What to do: When short-term rates rise above long-term rates (e.g. the 3-month T-bill yield above the 10-year Treasury yield), cut stocks and favour bonds or cash ahead of a likely recession.
Why it pays: An inverted curve signals tight money and expected rate cuts; historically it preceded US recessions, usually by about 6–24 months.
Track record: No reliable figure; inversions preceded each US recession since the late 1960s, but stock-timing gains are small and inconsistent
How it loses money: Long, variable lags mean you exit early and miss late-cycle rallies; stocks rallied strongly through the 2022–24 inversion.
Key sources: Harvey (1988); Estrella & Hardouvelis (1991); Estrella & Mishkin (1998)

Also moves with: Short-Term Reversal & Stat Arb; Short Volatility & Insurance Selling
What to do: In option-expiry week, bet that a stock or index will close near its 'max pain' strike (where option buyers collectively lose most) or a heavily traded strike, trading toward it or selling options there.
Why it pays: Dealers hedging large option positions trade against moves near big strikes, nudging prices toward them at expiry; the claim that prices are steered to max pain lacks support.
Markets: Stocks; Equity indices & ETFs; Options & volatility
Track record: Pinning shifted optionable US stocks' expiry-day returns by at least 0.165% on average (1996–2002); no evidence a max-pain rule beats costs
How it loses money: The pull is small and easily overwhelmed by news or big flows; short-option versions can lose heavily on a sharp expiry-day move.
Key sources: Avellaneda & Lipkin (2003); Ni, Pearson & Poteshman (2005); Golez & Jackwerth (2012)

What to do: Spot shapes on a price chart, such as a head-and-shoulders top or a triangle, and trade in the direction the pattern supposedly predicts once it completes.
Why it pays: Said to reveal crowd psychology; tests find patterns carry slight statistical information but no reliable profit after costs and selective pattern-spotting.
Track record: No reliable figure; patterns slightly shifted subsequent return distributions in US stocks 1962–1996, but net trading profits were not shown.
How it loses money: Patterns are subjective and often fail, and remembering only the winners hides frequent false breakouts.
Key sources: Lo, Mamaysky & Wang (2000); Osler & Chang (1995); Savin, Weller & Zvingelis (2007)

What to do: Stay in stocks while both the Dow Jones Industrial and Transportation averages make higher highs, and move to cash when both break below their prior lows.
Why it pays: Claimed logic: goods made must be shipped, so joint moves confirm a durable economic trend; in practice it is a slow, partly subjective trend-following rule.
Track record: Hamilton's 1902–1929 calls trailed buy-and-hold in raw return (Cowles) but beat it risk-adjusted by cutting volatility (BGK); no reliable figure for later versions
How it loses money: Signals arrive late, after much of a move, and whipsaws in choppy markets erode returns; vague rules invite overfitting.
Key sources: Cowles (1933); Brown, Goetzmann & Kumar (1998)

What to do: Buy when price touches the lower band (two standard deviations below its 20-day average) and sell at the upper band, or trade breakouts through the bands.
Why it pays: Assumes prices snap back inside a volatility envelope, but tests found the bands did not beat buy-and-hold after trading costs.
Track record: No reliable figure; did not beat buy-and-hold after costs in tests on North American stock indices.
How it loses money: A band touch often marks the start of a strong trend, so mean-reversion trades get run over.
Key sources: Lento, Gradojevic & Wright (2007); Leung & Chong (2003)

What to do: Overweight the stock sectors said to lead the current phase of the business cycle (e.g. cyclicals in early recovery, utilities and staples heading into recession) and underweight the rest.
Why it pays: Sector profits react differently to growth, rates and inflation, so the idea is that expected sector returns shift over the cycle.
Track record: No reliable figure; gains were small even with perfect hindsight about cycle phases, and smaller in real time (Stangl et al.)
How it loses money: Cycle phases are only clear in hindsight, so you rotate late, and sectors behave differently from one cycle to the next.
Key sources: Stangl, Jacobsen & Visaltanachoti (2009); Conover, Jensen, Johnson & Mercer (2008)

What to do: Hold a long VIX futures fund such as VXX as a standing hedge or as a bet that market fear will rise.
Why it pays: Holders pay the roll premium that short sellers earn: futures usually sit above spot VIX and decay toward it, so the fund steadily loses value.
Track record: Original VXX lost over 99% of its value from its January 2009 launch to its 2019 maturity, despite brief crisis spikes
How it loses money: Steady decay from rolling futures in calm markets; crisis gains vanish unless sold quickly during the spike.
Key sources: Whaley (2013); Alexander, Korovilas & Kapraun (2016); Eraker & Wu (2017)

Strategy: Buying cheap short-dated options (0DTE and weekly 'lottery tickets')
What to do: Buy cheap, out-of-the-money calls or puts that expire the same day or week, hoping for a large, quick price move.
Why it pays: Option sellers charge a premium for bearing jump risk and retail buyers pay wide bid-ask spreads, so the expected payoff is negative.
Track record: US retail option traders lost money in aggregate, roughly 2019–2022, much of it through spreads; lottery-like options earn strongly negative average returns.
How it loses money: Most such options expire worthless, and the occasional big win rarely makes up for the steady small losses.
Key sources: Bryzgalova, Pavlova & Sikorskaya (2023); Beckmeyer, Branger & Gayda (2023); Boyer & Vorkink (2014)

Strategy: Buying lottery-like stocks (penny stocks, biggest one-day jumpers)
Also moves with: Size & Illiquidity; Sentiment, Flows & Alt Data
What to do: Buy cheap, highly volatile stocks, such as penny stocks or those with the biggest one-day price jumps last month, hoping for another huge payoff.
Why it pays: Gambling-minded investors overpay for small chances of big wins, so these stocks are priced too high and earn low average returns.
Track record: Stocks with the biggest daily jumps last month trailed those with the smallest by ~1%/month, US 1962–2005 (value-weighted, gross).
How it loses money: Average returns are low and most picks fade, so steady losses outweigh the rare jackpot.
Key sources: Bali, Cakici & Whitelaw (2011); Kumar (2009)

What to do: Buy fast-growing stocks with surging quarterly earnings and strong recent price gains as they break above a recent sideways trading range, only when the market is rising; sell any that fall 7–8%.
Why it pays: It leans on real earnings and price momentum effects (investors underreact to good news), but the chart-pattern and judgement rules add no tested edge.
Track record: No reliable figure; the live IBD 50 ETF (FFTY), which follows a CAN SLIM-style list, has badly trailed the S&P 500 since its 2015 launch.
How it loses money: Breakouts often fail in choppy or falling markets, and repeated small stop-losses plus trading costs eat the returns.
Key sources: O'Neil (1988); Chan, Jegadeesh & Lakonishok (1996); George & Hwang (2004)

What to do: Buy or sell when a one- to three-day candlestick shape signals a reversal, such as a 'hammer' after a decline or a bearish 'engulfing' bar after a rise.
Why it pays: Supposed to show buyers or sellers taking control, but large tests on US and Japanese stocks found no value after costs.
Track record: No reliable figure; no profitable patterns found in Dow Jones stocks 1992–2002 or in large Japanese stocks.
How it loses money: Signals are close to random, so trading costs and spreads make it lose money over time.
Key sources: Marshall, Young & Rose (2006); Marshall, Young & Cahan (2008)

Strategy: Cash-secured put + covered call cycle ("the wheel")
What to do: Sell cash-secured puts on a stock you like; if the shares are assigned to you, hold them and sell covered calls until they are called away, then repeat.
Why it pays: Its return is mostly the stock's own return plus a modest premium, because single-stock options are less overpriced than index options.
Track record: No reliable figure; it is essentially single-stock put and call writing, where the volatility premium is smaller than in index options
How it loses money: You end up holding a falling stock with capped upside; premiums rarely offset big single-stock drops.
Key sources: Driessen, Maenhout & Vilkov (2009); Bakshi & Kapadia (2003); Israelov & Nielsen (2015)

Strategy: Chasing attention stocks (app 'top movers' and most-popular lists)
What to do: Buy the stocks at the top of a trading app's 'most popular' or 'biggest movers' lists after large, attention-grabbing price moves.
Why it pays: Attention-driven buying pushes prices above fair value for a while, so late buyers pay for a move that tends to reverse.
Track record: Stocks hit by intense Robinhood buying had roughly −5% abnormal returns over the next 20 trading days, US 2018–2020.
How it loses money: Buying after the spike means holding through the usual reversal as attention fades.
Key sources: Barber, Huang, Odean & Schwarz (2022); Barber & Odean (2008)

What to do: Buy, or switch into, the mutual funds with the best returns over the past one to three years or a top Morningstar star rating, expecting the winners to keep winning.
Why it pays: Little real edge: past winners were mostly lucky or riding momentum, and new inflows erode any skill; only high-fee losers reliably keep losing.
Track record: S&P SPIVA persistence reports: almost no top-quartile US equity funds stay top-quartile four years running, about what luck alone predicts.
How it loses money: You buy after the hot streak, pay higher fees, and get average or worse returns as past winners fade.
Key sources: Carhart (1997); Blake & Morey (2000); Berk & Green (2004)

What to do: Automatically mirror the trades of 'top' traders on a social trading platform, usually chosen for their recent returns or popularity.
Why it pays: Recent winners are often lucky or taking big risks, ranking by past returns pushes leaders to gamble, and followers pay extra fees.
Track record: No reliable figure; experiments show copying top past performers pushes both leaders and followers into excessive risk.
How it loses money: Copied traders' lucky streaks end, and their high-risk positions blow up followers' accounts too.
Key sources: Apesteguia, Oechssler & Weidenholzer (2020); Pelster & Hofmann (2018); Heimer (2016)

What to do: Buy or sell the stocks members of Congress disclose trading under the STOCK Act, directly or via congress-tracking ETFs and websites.
Why it pays: Lawmakers might trade on policy knowledge, but disclosure delays of up to 45 days and mixed skill erode any edge.
Track record: Senators' buys beat the market ~10–12%/yr in 1993–1998 (before timely disclosure); later studies find no edge (2004–2020)
How it loses money: Late, incomplete disclosures mean you buy after any move, and recent evidence shows no outperformance.
Key sources: Ziobrowski, Cheng, Boyd & Ziobrowski (2004); Eggers & Hainmueller (2013); Belmont, Sacerdote, Sehgal & Van Hoek (2022)

What to do: Run a portfolio that is mostly or entirely short, betting against overvalued, fraud-suspect or deteriorating companies, so it profits when they or the whole market fall.
Why it pays: Short sellers do tend to pick losers, but a net-short book fights the market's long-run rise and pays borrow fees, which have outweighed that skill.
Track record: No reliable figure; the main short-bias hedge fund index (Credit Suisse, from 1994) had a negative long-run average, gaining mainly in 2000–02 and 2008
How it loses money: Steady losses in bull markets and potentially unlimited losses on squeezed shorts; it pays off mainly in crashes.
Key sources: Dechow, Hutton, Meulbroek & Sloan (2001); Boehmer, Jones & Zhang (2008)

What to do: Buy a stock just before its ex-dividend date to collect the dividend, then sell it soon afterwards.
Why it pays: Prices sometimes fall by a bit less than the dividend on the ex-date because of tax differences, but costs and taxes usually absorb the gap.
Track record: No reliable figure
How it loses money: The price drops by roughly the dividend, so after taxes, spreads and commissions you usually lose.
Key sources: Elton & Gruber (1970); Kalay (1982); Lakonishok & Vermaelen (1986)

What to do: Each January, buy equal amounts of the 10 highest-dividend-yield stocks in the Dow Jones Industrial Average and hold them for a year.
Why it pays: A simple high-dividend value tilt betting that unloved blue chips rebound; any edge was small and not significant after risk and taxes.
Track record: About 3 points/yr above the Dow 1946–1995 before taxes and costs; not significant after risk, tax and data-mining adjustments.
How it loses money: Concentrated in 10 unloved stocks that can keep falling, with long stretches of lagging the index.
Key sources: McQueen, Shields & Thorley (1997); Domian, Louton & Mossman (1998); Hirschey (2000)

Strategy: Dollar-cost averaging a lump sum (instead of investing at once)
What to do: Instead of investing a lump sum straight away, split it into equal monthly purchases over, say, 6–12 months to avoid buying at a peak.
Why it pays: No return edge: holding cash while waiting lowers expected return because markets rise more often than they fall; the benefit is only less regret.
Track record: Investing at once beat a 12-month averaging plan about two-thirds of the time in historical US, UK and Australian data (Vanguard).
How it loses money: Markets usually rise while you wait, so on average you buy in at higher prices.
Key sources: Constantinides (1979); Vanguard (2012)

Also moves with: Defensive, Quality & Low Risk; Sentiment, Flows & Alt Data
What to do: Overweight companies with high ESG (environmental, social, governance) ratings or low carbon emissions and underweight low-rated or high-emitting ones, often via ESG ETFs.
Why it pays: Claimed to capture underpriced sustainability, but past gains came mainly from investor flows and rising climate concern, not a reliable premium.
Track record: No reliable figure; green stocks' 2012–2020 outperformance traced to unexpected shifts in climate concern, not a lasting premium
How it loses money: Ratings disagree widely, and when flows reverse or high emitters rally (e.g., energy in 2022) green tilts lag.
Key sources: Pástor, Stambaugh & Taylor (2022); Bolton & Kacperczyk (2021); Berg, Kölbel & Rigobon (2022)

What to do: Label market moves as repeating five-wave advances and three-wave corrections, then buy or sell according to which wave you believe the market is in.
Why it pays: Claims crowd psychology moves in fixed repeating waves, but wave counts are subjective and relabelled after the fact, making it essentially untestable.
Track record: No reliable figure
