How it loses money: Wave counts get revised after the fact, so forecasts are often wrong and there is no clear exit rule.
Key sources: Elliott (1938); Frost & Prechter (1978) (the originators' books, not tests)

Strategy: Equity collars (stock + bought put + sold call)
What to do: Own the index or a stock, buy an out-of-the-money put for crash protection, and pay for it by selling an out-of-the-money call, capping both losses and gains.
Why it pays: Protection looks cheap, but index puts are pricey relative to calls, so collars usually give up more return than their risk reduction justifies.
Markets: Equity indices & ETFs; Stocks; Options & volatility
Track record: Cut volatility but earned less per unit of risk than simply holding less stock (S&P 500); looked good mainly in 2000s bear markets (QQQ)
How it loses money: Misses big rallies above the call strike while the put cost drags on long-run returns.
Key sources: Szado & Schneeweis (2010); Israelov & Klein (2016)

Strategy: Fed model (earnings yield vs bond yield)
Also moves with: Macro & Asset Allocation; Value & Long-Term Reversal
What to do: Compare the stock market's earnings yield (earnings divided by price) with the 10-year Treasury yield; favour stocks when the earnings yield is higher and cut them when the bond yield is higher.
Why it pays: It rests on a popular belief that stocks and bonds compete for money, but it compares a real yield with a nominal one (inflation illusion).
Track record: No reliable figure; it describes how investors set P/E ratios but adds nothing to P/E alone in forecasting long-run stock returns (Asness 2003)
How it loses money: Low bond yields make stocks look 'cheap' even at very high P/E ratios, signalling buys near expensive peaks.
Key sources: Modigliani & Cohn (1979); Asness (2003)

What to do: After a big move, expect price to pull back 23.6%, 38.2%, 50% or 61.8% of that move and reverse there, and buy or sell at those levels.
Why it pays: There is no economic reason a mathematical ratio should matter; any effect could only come from many traders watching the same levels.
Track record: No reliable figure
How it loses money: With several levels to choose from, one always 'works' in hindsight, while live trades are coin flips minus costs.
Key sources: None: no credible peer-reviewed test showing an edge

What to do: Draw fixed-slope 'Gann angles' from past highs and lows and use numerology-style time cycles to predict turning dates and price levels.
Why it pays: Based on W.D. Gann's early-1900s geometric and astrological ideas, with no tested mechanism and no evidence on new data.
Track record: No reliable figure
How it loses money: Arbitrary angles and dates give signals no better than chance, while trading costs pile up.
Key sources: None: no peer-reviewed tests; rests on W.D. Gann's own 1920s–40s books

What to do: Buy bitcoin around its roughly four-yearly 'halving' (when new-coin issuance is cut in half) and sell 12–18 months later, or trade toward the stock-to-flow model's price targets.
Why it pays: Claimed supply shock from lower issuance, but halvings are scheduled years ahead, so an efficient market should already price them in.
Track record: No reliable figure; only four halvings (2012, 2016, 2020, 2024), and stock-to-flow price targets missed badly in 2021–22
How it loses money: With only four data points the pattern can simply fail, leaving you holding through a long bear market.
Key sources: PlanB (2019, blog post)

What to do: Intraday, wait for price to 'sweep' obvious highs or lows (triggering other traders' stops), then enter at 'order blocks' or 'fair value gaps' during set 'kill zone' hours.
Why it pays: Claims to follow banks' hidden order flow, but no published study shows an edge and the rules are too subjective to test cleanly.
Track record: No reliable figure
How it loses money: Judgement-based entries and high leverage on small intraday moves lead to fast losses after spreads.
Key sources: None: no peer-reviewed tests; promoted through online courses and videos

Strategy: Leveraged retail forex and CFD trading
What to do: Take short-term, highly leveraged positions in currencies, indices or commodities through spot-forex or CFD (contract-for-difference) accounts, usually on technical signals.
Why it pays: No built-in edge: traders pay spreads and overnight financing, sometimes to a broker on the other side, and leverage turns small losses into wipe-outs.
Track record: EU regulator ESMA (2018): 74–89% of retail CFD accounts lose money.
How it loses money: With leverage and costs, ordinary price noise triggers margin calls and wipes out accounts.
Key sources: ESMA (2018); Heimer & Simsek (2019)

Strategy: Leveraged stock-Treasury ETF mix (HFEA: 55% UPRO / 45% TMF)
What to do: Hold about 55% in a 3x daily-leveraged S&P 500 ETF (UPRO) and 45% in a 3x long-term Treasury ETF (TMF), rebalancing quarterly, betting that Treasuries rise when stocks crash.
Why it pays: It seeks leveraged stock and bond returns with bonds hedging stocks, but its strong backtests relied on bond yields falling steadily from 1982 to 2020.
Track record: Lost roughly two-thirds in 2022 as UPRO (about –57%) and TMF (which fell even more) dropped together; approximate, from public fund returns.
How it loses money: When stocks and long bonds fall together, as when rates jumped in 2022, both 3x legs collapse and daily-reset decay deepens losses.
Key sources: Cheng & Madhavan (2009); Avellaneda & Zhang (2010); Asness, Frazzini & Pedersen (2012)

Strategy: Market breadth signals (advance-decline line, McClellan, breadth thrust, Hindenburg Omen)
Also moves with: Sentiment, Flows & Alt Data; Trend & Momentum
What to do: Time the stock index using counts of rising vs falling stocks: buy after a sudden surge in advancing stocks (a 'breadth thrust'); sell when breadth weakens while the index makes new highs.
Why it pays: Claimed logic: rallies led by a few stocks are fragile while broad participation confirms trends; academic tests treat breadth as a sentiment gauge with little forecasting power.
Track record: No reliable figure; even proponents' counts say only about a quarter of confirmed Hindenburg Omens preceded a crash, with frequent false alarms
How it loses money: Signals are rare, loosely defined and often false alarms, so you sit out rallies or get whipsawed.
Key sources: Zweig (1986); Brown & Cliff (2004)

Also moves with: Short Volatility & Insurance Selling; Short-Term Reversal & Stat Arb
What to do: Double the position after each loss (martingale), or place layered buy and sell orders at fixed price steps (grid), expecting price to come back and recover the losses.
Why it pays: Changing bet sizes cannot turn a zero or negative expected return positive; it just swaps many small wins for rare account-ending losses.
Track record: No reliable figure; probability theory shows no betting system creates an edge from a fair or costly game.
How it loses money: One long one-way trend forces ever-larger positions until margin runs out and the account is wiped out.
Key sources: Feller (1968)

Strategy: Moving-average crossovers and MACD on single stocks (golden/death cross)
What to do: Buy a stock when its short moving average (e.g. 50-day, or the MACD line) crosses above a longer one (e.g. 200-day), and sell when it crosses back below.
Why it pays: Meant to catch lasting trends, but signals lag; academic support exists only for MA timing of whole portfolios of volatile stocks, not single names.
Track record: No reliable figure for single stocks after costs; one study found MA timing of high-volatility US stock portfolios profitable (gross).
How it loses money: Lagging signals buy late and sell late, so whipsaws and trading costs erase or reverse the gains.
Key sources: Han, Yang & Zhou (2013); Park & Irwin (2007)

What to do: Buy bitcoin when on-chain ratios say it is cheap and sell when they are high, e.g., MVRV (market value divided by the value of all coins at the price they last moved) or NVT (market value divided by on-chain transaction volume).
Why it pays: Claimed to flag bubbles when price runs far ahead of holders' cost basis or network usage; there is little rigorous out-of-sample testing.
Track record: No reliable figure; thresholds fitted to only three or four bitcoin cycles, and no peer-reviewed out-of-sample test found
How it loses money: Thresholds that marked past tops and bottoms shift each cycle, so you sell too early or buy into a longer bear market.
Key sources: Woo (2017, blog/Forbes column); Mahmudov & Puell (2018, blog post)

Strategy: Online-mood market timing (Twitter mood, Google Trends keywords)
What to do: Buy or sell the stock index (or Bitcoin) based on daily or weekly shifts in Twitter mood scores or Google searches for words like 'debt'.
Why it pays: Claimed to capture crowd mood before it reaches prices; little evidence this survives out of sample.
Track record: Backtests claimed ~87% daily direction accuracy (Twitter) and 326% (Google 'debt', 2004–2011); replications failed
How it loses money: Data-mined keyword choices: random words backtest similarly, and live attempts did not deliver.
Key sources: Bollen, Mao & Zeng (2011); Preis, Moat & Stanley (2013); Lachanski & Pav (2017)

What to do: Buy when an oscillator such as RSI or stochastics reads 'oversold' (e.g. RSI below 30) and sell when it reads 'overbought' (e.g. RSI above 70).
Why it pays: Assumes short-term overreactions snap back; the few positive studies are single-market backtests that rarely allow for costs or data-mining.
Track record: No reliable figure; isolated positive backtests (e.g. on the UK FT30 index) do not hold up across markets or periods.
How it loses money: In strong trends 'oversold' keeps getting more oversold, so betting against the trend causes large losses.
Key sources: Chong & Ng (2008); Park & Irwin (2007)

What to do: Stake a fixed sum on whether a currency, index, stock or coin will finish above or below a level at a set expiry, often minutes away, winning a fixed profit smaller than your stake or losing all of it.
Why it pays: There is no risk premium to earn: payouts are set below fair odds, so the broker, often your direct counterparty, keeps a built-in edge on every trade.
Markets: FX; Equity indices & ETFs; Stocks; Commodities; Crypto; Options & volatility
Track record: About 80% of Australian retail clients lost money (ASIC reviews, 2017 and 2019); ~A$490m retail net losses in 2018; no evidence of a profitable rule
How it loses money: Below-fair payouts make losses near-certain over many trades, and offshore brokers (retail sales banned in EU, UK, Australia) may refuse withdrawals.

What to do: Open and close positions in stocks or index futures within the same day, aiming to profit from small intraday price moves.
Why it pays: No built-in edge: retail day traders mostly trade against better-informed professionals and pay spreads, fees and taxes on every trade.
Track record: Brazil index futures 2013–2015: 97% of those who day traded 300+ days lost money; Taiwan: under 1% of day traders reliably profitable after fees.
How it loses money: Many small trades, each paying costs and slightly out-informed, add up to steady losses.
Key sources: Chague, De-Losso & Giovannetti (2019); Barber, Lee, Liu & Odean (2014); Barber, Lee, Liu & Odean (2009)

Strategy: Selling options into earnings ("IV crush" trade)
What to do: Sell straddles or strangles (a call plus a put) on a stock just before its earnings release and buy them back right after, when option prices drop as the uncertainty passes.
Why it pays: Option prices build in a big expected earnings move; you profit only if the actual move turns out smaller than the move the market priced.
Track record: No reliable figure; the post-earnings drop in option prices is predictable and largely already priced in
How it loses money: An earnings surprise far larger than priced can cost many times the premium collected.
Key sources: Patell & Wolfson (1981); Dubinsky, Johannes, Kaeck & Seeger (2019); Gao, Xing & Zhang (2018)

What to do: Buy heavily shorted stocks (high short interest, high borrow fees), hoping a price rise forces short sellers to buy back and trigger a squeeze.
Why it pays: Occasional squeezes produce huge gains, but on average heavily shorted stocks underperform.
Track record: No reliable figure; on average high-short-interest stocks underperform, the opposite of what this needs
How it loses money: Most heavily shorted stocks keep falling; rare spectacular squeezes (e.g., GameStop 2021) hide frequent losses.
Key sources: Asquith, Pathak & Ritter (2005); Boehmer, Jones & Zhang (2008)

Strategy: Sports tipsters and 'fade the public' betting systems
What to do: Follow paid tipsters' picks, or bet against the side most of the public is backing (chasing 'sharp money' and 'reverse line moves') at ordinary bookmaker odds.
Why it pays: The claimed edge is that the public overbets favourites and popular teams, but bookmakers already price this in, and you must win ~52.4% of standard -110 bets to break even.
Track record: No reliable figure. Tipsters were less accurate than betting odds in German soccer; betting-line patterns are too small to beat the bookmaker's margin
How it loses money: The bookmaker's margin steadily drains the bankroll, and tipster track records are often cherry-picked or survivorship-biased.
Key sources: Levitt (2004); Spann & Skiera (2009); Moskowitz (2021)

Strategy: Stock-picking and market-timing newsletters / tip services
What to do: Buy the stocks, or follow the market-timing calls, recommended by paid investment newsletters, TV stock pickers or tip services.
Why it pays: Published advice is priced in quickly, and newsletters with good records tend not to repeat them.
Track record: Average newsletter showed no abnormal stock-picking returns, ~150 US newsletters 1980–1996; TV picks get a brief price pop that reverses.
How it loses money: You pay fees and trading costs for picks that, on average, match or trail an index fund.
Key sources: Metrick (1999); Graham & Harvey (1996); Engelberg, Sasseville & Williams (2012)

What to do: Hold stocks for the year if a team from the original NFL wins the Super Bowl, and sell if a team from the original AFL wins.
Why it pays: There is no economic reason; it is a chance correlation found by sifting through many unrelated variables (data-mining).
Track record: No reliable figure; its early in-sample hit rate reflected chance
How it loses money: It is pure coincidence with no link to markets, so it fails whenever luck runs out.
Key sources: Krueger & Kennedy (1990)

Strategy: Systematic tail-risk hedging (buying out-of-the-money index puts)
What to do: Continuously buy out-of-the-money S&P 500 put options (strikes well below the current price), rolling them monthly or quarterly, to protect a portfolio against crashes.
Why it pays: It is insurance: buyers pay the volatility and skew premium that sellers earn, so it loses money on average outside crashes.
Track record: Protective S&P 500 puts gave worse risk-adjusted returns and no more reliable drawdown cuts than simply holding less stock (Israelov 2019)
How it loses money: Premium bleed of a few percent a year in calm markets; payoff depends on crash timing and strike choice.
Key sources: Israelov (2019); Israelov & Nielsen (2015); Ilmanen (2012)

What to do: Buy ETFs built around a hot theme such as innovation, AI, clean energy, cannabis or the metaverse, usually after its stocks have surged, and hold for the long-term story.
Why it pays: It doesn't pay on average: providers launch funds after theme stocks are already overpriced by hype, so buyers get in near peaks and pay higher fees.
Track record: Specialised US ETFs lost about 30% risk-adjusted over their first five years after launch (Ben-David et al., 2023).
How it loses money: Concentrated, richly valued holdings collapse when hype fades; ARK Innovation fell about 80% from its 2021 peak.
Key sources: Ben-David, Franzoni, Kim & Moussawi (2023); Morningstar (2021)

Strategy: Waiting for a dip to invest ('buy the dip' cash timing)
What to do: Keep new savings in cash until the market falls by a set amount (e.g. 10% from its high), then move it into a stock index fund.
Why it pays: It feels like buying at a discount, but markets rise most of the time, so cash waiting for a dip usually misses more gains than the dip saves.
Track record: Even buying only at exact market bottoms trailed steady monthly investing in about 70% of 40-year US periods since 1920 (practitioner backtest)
How it loses money: Markets can rise for years without the target dip, leaving cash idle and missing gains that later dips rarely make up.
Key sources: Shtekhman, Tasopoulos & Wimmer (2012); Maggiulli (2019)
